THE COMING SUMMER. 1 BY A " Zr.SI3IBRZBT VABMER.7, All you that be varmin' t' year plaze P hether, • An' I'll tell'ee ixaely what manner o' weather Yen've a got eurnmin' on tbe elatson avor'ee, 3.! you'll be but zo kind as 4...0 hear out my story. I've told'ee avoretime, , again an' again, 0' sajw°3 °' tin' lightning an' rain, 0' starms an o, Vluds, an' calamities sad, An' to° they've a' cum an' bin terrible bad. 11:ow. , 9.azed to infarm'ee, I've got better news. Ate dart e the weather have done wi' the blues. lies, 'a cummin' out handsome an''smilin' to year; Ye can take thess vor gospel, I tell'ee, no veer. Not as howl sets up vor a prophet like they As studies astrology all night au' day, An' pertends tec a mestery they can explain, How the stars in their coorses bring zunshine or rain. No wizard be I o' the torth, east, or west; My prophecies come vrotn the source that's the best, That's sheer c3lealation o' cause an' effec, Nine times out o' ten, zurr, you'll vind it correc. Ef you takes care to chronicle cycles o' weather, An' you knows how to putt all their lessons together, That adage by statesmen so well understood, 1 That hestory repeats itzelf mostly holds good. Mild wenters have genally brought, as a rule, Vine rummers, though p'raps in the early part cool, At zunshine en March we had better not holler, No zummees a made by the right o' one swoller. Et ull cum vary coold I'm aveard afore long, An' kill off the plants an' the buds that beard strong. Aist wends ull be tryin', an' want at all suit The orchits an' them a 3 depends upon fruit. But take et, all round RD' all auver the nation; The land will quite pay vor rum good cultivation; Yer ground wunt be deluged weth auver much rain; •Agricultur thess year wont be labour in vain. A little coold weather in April an May, Weth showers an' p'raps sleet, want much hurt vor the hay; An' ef the hot rummer don't come in so soon As what-you expected, 'twill come late in June. July wall be hot an' remarkable dry, An' to reap putty early thess year we mos' try; Vor Angus' may bring zum electrical change, An' ef harvests that's late shud be w et, 'twunt ba strange. Our loads will be heavy vrom meadow an' field, Whate an' barley will give us a capital yield. The turmuts an' wuzzles 'all do vury well, With early pertateTs in market to zell. Ef grain crops be early an' quickly got in, We once more vrom varming a profit migat win. I doant ray our Drespecs be bright altogesher, But they wunt be no wuss vor the nex rummer's weather.

The Cheapest of Lawyers—Keeping one's own counsel. A cripple on tee nem road wilt neat a racer on tne wrone. Iris only those who have done nothing who fancy that they can do everything. When has a man a right to scold about his coffee? When he has more than suEicient grounds. A little girl went timidly into a shop the other day, and asked the saopman how many sh ie-strings she could get for a penny. "How long do you want them ?" he inquired. "I want to keep them," was the answer, in a tone of slight surprise. A gentleman of indolent habits made a business of visit- ing his friends extensively. He was once cordially received by a Quaker, who treated his visitor with great attention and politeness for several days. At lest he said, "My friend, lam afraid thee wilt never visit me again." Oh, yes, I shall," said the visitor; "I have enjoyed my visit very much; I shall certainly come again." "Nay," said the Queker ; " I think thee will not visit me again." 'What makes you think I shall not come again ?" asked the visitor. "If thee does never leave," said the Quaker. "how canst thee come again ?" KEEP Yonn TROUBLES SACRED.-4 wife whose life cannot have been all sunshine writes the following advice to other married pairs :—Preserve eacredly the privacies of your house, your aatrried state, and your heart. With God's help build your own quiet world, not allowing ycur dearest earthly friend to be the confidant of aught that concerns your domestic peace. Let moments of alienation, if' they occur, be healed at once. Never speak of it outside, but to each other confess, and all will come out rignt. Never let the morrow's sun still find you at variance. Renew or re- view the vow at all tempt ttions ; it will do you both good, and thereby yoar souls will grow together, cemented in that love which is stronger than death, and you will become truly one. SPRING AND A LAl7Gif.—ln nominally bidding adieu to , winter, and welcoming whet purports to be spring, let us present to our re tders a few prose and poetical texts, de- signed to inculcate the duty of looking on the bright side : Mirth is the medicine of life; It cures its ills, it calms i s strife; It softly smoothes the brow of care, And writes a thousand graces there. Dr. Johnson us, d to say teat a habit of looking at the best side of every event is far better then a thousand pounds a year. Bishop Hall:quaintly remarks: "For every bed there might be a worse, and when one breaks his leg, let hint be thankful it was not his neck." Charles Lamb says "A laugh is worth a hundred groans in any state of the market." , No man does his lest *except when he i cheerful. A light heart maketh nimble heeds, and keep-4 the mind free and alert. CHEERFUL Crintsmalarrv.—How different would the general estimate be of all who profess to ba, who are, truly religious, if each one in his or her sphere would look upon it as a part of their daily concern in life to diffuse cheer- fulness, sweetness, pleasantry on all around! You may not think very highly of a visitor who chances to call, and he may have coma at an inconvenient season besides, but meet him in a Christian spirit, hasten to extend the welcoming hand, show hospitality without grudging, give a little of your time and your temper towards making a favourable impression, and the result cannot fail to be eminently honourable alike to yourself and the Master you serve. Men and women of the world, wise in their generation, aim at an all•embracing affability in their desire to court a good opinion and their craving for universal homage; but let a Christian be polite, attentive, attractive, from a nobler motive. Nay, even to the minor points of dress and domes- tic surroundings this principle may and ought to extend. We heir it said II ow and again, "What a pretty room Mrs. So-and-So has! How nicely it is arranged! It is quite a treat to look round." This- in contranistinction to "How can Mrs. Sucia•another-one endure to sit in so dismal and untidy a den? How uncomfortable it looked! Nothing attended to, but everything uncared for and neglected, frumpish and disagreeable." Ve*y •well ; we may be tolerably sure that the feelings inspired by the contrasted scenes are extended toward a the ladies themselves. The former will be to a certainty the more popular, the better like4and respected: a grain of good seed let fall from her lips will outweigh oceans of morality emitted by her neigh- bour : and should she add to her household attractions the charm of aa agreeable, engaging, taking manner, and that —start not aside, fair reader !—of a becoming dress, she wields in her hand a magician's wand whose power, subtle and fragile though it be, cannot be denied.—Good Mords

6ETTING OUT ON AN AFAICAN EXPEDITION. —After my arrival at Zanzibar, I set about trying to get despatched at once to the mainland in prosecution of the mission I had undertaken. The somewhat eccentric machinery of an Oriental Government, however, was hard to be moved. Daring the first fortnight nothing could be done. First "I must rest fter my voyage ;" then "I must wait till the mail was gone ;" finally "everything would be arranged when something as was settled." After about a hundred communications had been sent without visible effect, I was beginning seriously to consider how a sinecure might be made tolerable in Zanzibar, when suddenly my calculations were interrupted by a message from the Sultan. My orders were to get ready in three days to proceed up the Rovuma and examine the reported rich coal-fields in that region This was coming to the point with a vengeance. To get ready a caravan for the interior in three days was a task by no means easy. But, thanks to my previously acquired knowledge and experience, I was equal to the emergency. In two days I had completed my arrangements, made all necessary purchases, and got together sixty of my former followers under the world-famous Chuma and the energetic Makatabu. At the last moment, however, my pans narrowly escaped wreck and failure. The men had somehow got the impreszion that they were not to go on board till the morn- ing of. the fourth day; so, on the third, they indulged in a grand carouse. They all got drunk, to a man; and when the time for starting arrived, the whole military and police force of Zanzibar had to be .employed in the ludicrous task of hunting them out and carzying them to the ship. The chase was one of the most exiting imaginable, and lasted till midnight. Incidents, carious and absurd, abounded. Two of the men, for instance, bad just got married on that day, and at the "witching hour of night" they had to be -" spirited away" from their disconsolate mates, leaving these either to mourn till their naturn or get new husbands. Such is the reckless character of the Waswahili porters. At sunrise on the following morning we sailed out of the har- bour, bound for Mikindany Bay, near the mouth of the Rovursa.—Good Words. An important archmological discovery has been made close to Liege on some property belonging to M. Emile de Lave- leye. A score of antique bronzes, including two statuettes of wonien and three heads of Mercury, have been unearthed in excellent preservation. They are thought to have formed part of a large fountain, and to belong to the beginning of the third century. M. Seguin, of Paris, has patented a process for increasing the resistance of iron to tensile, torsile, and traverse strains. The metal is brought to a cherry-red heat, and then plunged into a mixture of sulphuric acid of 60 deg. strength, with an equal quantity of water. The iron is kept in the acid bath until its temperature is lowered to that of the liquid; it is then ranidly plunged into hot water. Dr. J. Nealer, who has been investigating the colouring of wines by the aniline compounds, states in Biedermann's Central-Blatt far Agrikultur Citemie that be finds under certain circumstances the magenta used for colouring may ' so entirely disappear from wine as not to be capable of de- tection, or an upper stratum of the coloured wine may be free from this colouring matter, while it may still be found in the lower portion of the fluid. The Athenount says, apropos of the impending coronation of Milan 1., King of Servia, it is interesting to know that the British Museum possesses an original charter in the Servian language, dated A.D. 1395, to which is appended, by strands of red and white silk, a wax impression of the great seal of Stephen Dabisha, King of Servia and Bosnia, which resem- bles in general characteristics of design the great seal of Richard 11. of England. Mr. Newth, as we (Atheneum) briefly noticed last week, at the Physical Society on the 11th inst., showed experi- ments illustrative of the formation of fogs. The fact that burning sulphur, and even platinum wire rendered incan- descent by an electric current, gave off solid particles in sufficient quantity to produce a fog, leads to the inference that even with gas stoves fogs will not be got rid of, though they may be of a lighter colour than those caused by coal fires.

Art EXTRAORDINARY SPRING.—In a mine near the busy centre of St. Etienne, a French mining engineer, in boring at a depth of 1,500 ft., is reported to have come upon a hot spring, whose waters rushed forth in a column to a height of nearly 80ft. above the surface of the earth. It is similar in height and 'heat to the so-called Stracke Geyser, and is strongly impregnated with carbonic acid. The French Acidroy of Sciences have determined to send a deputation to exAmiae minutely into the peculiarities of this pheno• meron.—Builder.

INGENIOUS SOUNDINEi APPARATUS. A Russian naval officer has invented a very ingenious apparatus for ascer• tlining the depth of the sea without the use of a costly and heavy line. Indeed, no line at all is used. The instrument consists of a piece of lead, a small wheel with a contrivance for reAlstering the number of revolutions, and a float. Wit,n the b)ttom is reached, the lead becomes detached, the float begins to act, and the machine shoots up to the surface, where it can easily be fished up by a net and the r4giater read off.

A NINTH CENTURY CHRISTIAN ON MAHOMEDANISM.— Sir William Muir has contributed to the Journal of the Asiatic Society an exceedingly interesting account of the "Apology of Al Kindy "—not, indeed, the work of the famous "philosopher of Islam," but of a Christian who may have belonged to the same great clan, and who was also at the court of Al Mfienfin about AD. 830. The book ie in effect a staunch defence of the Christian religion from the point of view of an Eastern apologist of the ninth century, and includes a vigorous attack upon the distinctive tenets of the religion founded by Mahomet and some severe strictures upon the personal character of the "Prophet of Islam." This curious and interesting tract has also been issued in a separate form by Messrs. Smith, Elder, and CO. EXPLORATION IN CAMBODIA.—At the meeting of the Paris Geographical Society on the 17th instant, a cornmuni cation was read describing the results of M. Delaporte's recent visit to the Kmer rains in Cambodia. M. Delaporte's previous impression that the temples had a Brahmanic origin have been confirmed by his further explorations. He has also fully examined the palace of the Kmer kings. He has taken 300 photographs, 40 casts, and a large number of fragments of great value. Sickness has ccmpelled him to return to Saigon where he is in hospital. As soon as he is able he will embark for France. The expedition of which he was the leader, and which includes three Europeans, was, however, actively continuing the exploration, and was ex- pected to do so during the current month, until the hot weather, now about due, compelled it to retreat. LEAD POISONING FRO3I THE LINING OF COOKING UTEN. SlLS.—Cooking utensils are frequently coated with a mix- ture of tin and lead, instead of with pure tin. The alloy is more easy to apply, and is somewhat cheaper; but consider- ing how p deonous lead is, how great a tendency it has to accumulate in the system, and the ease with which it is dissolved, under suitable conditions, the practice cannot be too severely reprobated. We have seen " tinned " copper veese,s, the tin of which would actually mark paper. Of coarse, such a metal would readily be corroded by weak acids, and even by rain water. It has, in fact, been very recently shown that the "tin-lined" and " tin-washed " lead pipes, so excellent in principle,are somewhat imperfect in practice. Melted tin, applied to the surface of lead, forms an alloy 80 quickly that water is ab'e to dissolve lead from the inside of the pipe, although, of course, in less quantity than from pure lead.—Lancet. INHAT WE OWE TO THE TREES.—A country cannot con- tinue to be populous nor highly civilised when its forests, or their equivalent in coal, are lost to it. But this loss has been experienced by many nations. The whole Eastern world, as well as the countries of which we have spoken, was once well wooded. The Roman and Greek writers aeeure U 3 of this. But vast regions cf Europe and Asia, by wars and wantonness and imprudence, have been stripped of their forests. A belt of woodland: stretching from the Pyrenees to the Himalayas has been swept away, and that whole region, once fertile and populous, now barely sustains a people scanty in numbers. It is a significant fact that greet deserts now occupy the ofiginal seat of the human race, and extend on every route of their migrations. Hum- boldt is reported as sayieg ;—" Men in all climates seem to bring upon the future generations two calamities at once— a want of fuel and a scarcity of water." The two come alike from the destruction of the foreets.—Harper's Maga.

Professor Riley, of Washington, U.S.A., announces that tee has discovered a new wheat peat, which he names Isoma tritici. This is the larva of a species of Chlorops, and it feeds on the interior of the wheat stalk between the joints, high up, without causing a swelling. The destruction caused by it is said to have been very great. NITRATE OF SODA ON PASTURES.—Some years ago a large quantity of nitrate of soda was applied to a pasture, ana as a result it gave a splendid crop of hay. Bat, after- wards, toe animals grazing on it suffered considerably from thirst, excess of urine, and other disorders. Since then, chemical manures have been used only in admixture with vegetable compost, and good results have followed. The case is reported by M. Serret in the Annales Agronomiques It is stated in the Central-Blatt that Kainit is a good fer- tiliser for meadow land, especially as regards clovers. More- over, it destroys caterpillars .and appears to be inimical to the existence of snails and a orms. Tide Paris Municipality has granted a plot of land at the Park of Montesouris for a School of Insectology, to be founded by the Central Society of Agriculture and Insect- I ()logy, and to comprehend a museum of (1) useful insects, (2), auxiliary insects, (3) injurious insects. An expert. mental apiary has already been constructed, and this is tsetnEr supplemented by a silkworm nursery and mulberry planta- tion. The Prefect of the Seine is about to as the Muni- cipal Council for the necessary building funds. It is pro- posed finally to add a collection of insectivorous mammals, birds and reptiles, and to institute lectures, conferences, and periodical exhibitions. AGRICULTURAL SCHOLARSHIP AT EDINBURGH UNIVER- SITY.—The Misses Steven, of Bellahoaston, have presented to the Eainbargh University the sum of £2,000 for the foundation of a scholarship in agriculture in memory of their late broth-r, the proceeds of which will be awarded annually in the usual way. With the view of the holder making himself acqhainted with the general state of the agriculture of different districts of his own country, and the advanced practices as evidenced by the exhibition of live stock and of improved implements and machines for farming purposes, he will be required to visit personally the annual exhibitions of the four leading agricultural societies, or such of them as the professor of agriculture in the said Univer- sity for the time being shall appoint—viz.' the Royal Agri- cultural Society of England, the Bath and West of England Agricultural Society, the Highland and Agricultural Society of Scotland, and the Royal Agricultural Society of Ireland, and to furnish a report on the several departments of the re,pective exhibitions, which report shall be sent for publi- cation to the agricultural journals, if approved by the pro- fessor for the time being. The first award of the said scholarship will be made at the end of the winter session 1882-3. THE Usz or, PEAT AS LiTrErt.—Peat ground to fine powder has been found by experiment to absorb about eight times its weight of water, while sawdust and straw only take up about four times their weight of liquid. A two- horse stable was covered to a depth of 4112 inches with ground-up peat, and after a lapse of six days it gave no ap- preciable ammoniacal odour. A second two-horse stable like the first was littered with straw, and at the end of six days the air in it was found to contain as much ammonia as the peat-bedded stable did at the end of fifteen days. By the.twentieth day the peat was quite damp, so half the former quantity was strewn on the top of the first bedding, and the ammonia in the air became at once reduced. A bale of peat weighing 2801bs. lasted thirty days, whereas during the same time 330105. weight of straw, costing half as much again as the peat, was employed in the other stable. The absorptive power of the peat is exercised in a regular way, and the most economical mode of application is to put down thin layers once a week. In the opinion of the experimenter the employment of peat in this way is very suitable and economical, both as regards cost and space, Vie manure of two horses for an entire year being found to occupy a space of only 36 cubic yards. Considering the increasing value of straw as food, it seems to us that the use of peat as litter is well worth trial in those localities where it may be had almost for the cost of getting it. DISEASE OF GRASS.—During the past year or two, farmers in various parts of Kent and Sussex have had their grass attacked by a minute fungus, which there is reason to be- lieve is of a deadly character, inasmuch as deaths of farm animals have occurred under such circumstances as to sip. port strongly the theory that they have died through eating grass covered with this fungoid growth. Such animals are found by post-mortem examination to have a fungoid and somewhat leather-like outgrowth on the lungs. Rabbits fel with grass attacked by this parasite are reported to have died, and their lungs to have presented the same appearance as that just noted. It is chiefly the fescue grasses which ,uffer. The fungus is most abundant upon sandy soils, and is not uncommon in chalky situations, but does not appear on clays. It is first seen in September, and it fades away usually in the following January. While it appears freely on old grass, young grass seems to be free from it. As seen on the green herbage in the meadows the fungus has the appearance of minute globules of a bright vermilion or pink coral colour, dotted all over the grass, and in this form we have kept it on cut grass for a month or two, without any change taking place. The fungus, which, like the holly- hock disease, is of Australian origin, is named Isa ria fuci- formis, and a description of the parasite has recently been communicated to the Royal Horticultural Society by Mr. W. G. Smith. The suspicion as to its poisonous character is not lessened by the fact that it is rather closely related to ergot.

Looking narrowly at the company, he single' stepping up to -a out the object of his search, and 'Atm, said, "Mr. Tone, I am very happy to see you. yr ,Amitly replied,rising, with the utmost composure he "Sir George lam happy to see you. How is Lady Hill and 9tear family'?" Beckoned into the next room by the o4:10r, he was ordered to be ironed. Flinging off his 117-o.fOrm, he cried, "These fetters shall never degrade the tevered insignia of the free nation which I have served." When his limbs were fettered, he said, "For the cause which I have embraced I feel prouder to wear these chains than if I were decorated with the star and garter of Eng- land." He was hurried to Dublin without delay, carried thither fettered and on horseback, under an escort of dragoons. A court-martial was appointed for the 10th of November, 1798. Tone appeared in the uniform of Chef de Brigade (Colonel), and was cool and collected. When called upon to plead "Guilty or not guilty," he pleaded "Guilty." urging as a reason for so doing, "I have never during my life stooped to a prevarication." He then proceeded to read a paper which he had drawn up in justification of his con- duct, from the conclusion of which it was evident that he had entertained no hope that any defence could avail him: —" I have little more to say. In a cause like this success is everything. Success in the eyes of the vulgar fixes its merits. Unfavoured by her virtue becomes vicious in the ephemeral estimation, to those who attach every merit to prosperity. In the glorious race of patriotism I have pur- sued the path chalked out by Washington in America and Kosciusko in Poland. Like the latter, I have failed to eman- cipate my country, and unlike them both, I have forfeited my life. I have done my duty, and I have no doubt the Court will do theirs. I have only to add that the man who has thought and acted as I have done should be armed against the fear of death. I conceive that I stand here in the same light with our entiqrds, and if the indulgence lay within the power of the Court, I would only request what French magnanimity allowed to Charette and to the Count de Sombreiul—the death of a soldier, and to be shot by a file of grenadiers. This is the only favour I have to ask, and I trust that men susceptible of the nice feelings of a soldier's honour will not refuse-the request. It is not from any personal feeling that I make the request, but from a re- spect to the uniform which I wear, and to the brave army in which I have fought." This final request was not granted. He was sentenced to die the death of a traitor in forty-eight hours, on the 12th of November.
OXFORD AND CA3IBRIDGE BOAT
RACE..

The thirty-ninth aquatic contest between our two great universities took place on the Thames ori Saturday, under the most favourable conditions. Instead of rowing early in the morning, before half London is awake, the race—thanks to the state of the tide—was not fi ,ed until after mid-day, and, ultimately, the clock had struck on before the great battle began. This improvement in the time of starting was not without its effect upon the number of spectators who assembled at the river side. Fortunately the weather was all that could be desired. The early morning broke fine, the sun shone brightly, and scarcely any wind was perceptible. Later on, hoc ever, a breeze sprang up. This was semewhat chilly, blowing south-south-east, but for the purposes of the racing it could not have blown from amore favourable quar- ter. It was pretty generally admitted that the number of persons who witnessed the race from start to finish was in excess of the number who have frequented the early morn- ing race of the last four or five years.
the names and weights of the crews were as follows : OXFORD.

Moore, Christ's ll 7 S. P. Smith, Ist Trinity (stroke) P. L. Hunt, Cavendish (cox) 7 5 Mr. Edmund Searle, who once more officiated as starter, had no difficulty in performing his task. As soon as the crews had doffed their outer clothing they bent forward, he gave the word, and three minutes past one the race had commenced. A more even start could not have been effected, the whole sixteen oars struck the water at the same instant, and the custo- mary excitement at once set in. The Cantabs beean at 39 strokes a minute, and Oxford at 38. Loud shouts reverberated from the adj icent shores as soon as the eventful moment had arrived, and thousands of necks were eagerly strained to catch a glimpse of the first atom of ad- vantage which either of the crews might obtain. Although both boats kept level for the first few strokes, the quicker pace of the Cambridge men enabled them durine, the first three hundred yards to secure a slight, but only a very slight, advantage. Off the Duke's Head the Light Blues led by perhaps a foot, but their opponents some crept up to their original position, an when opposite the _London Boat- house the Dark Blues held a lead of rather more than two feet. Having a trifle the best of the tide, they slowly in- creased this advantage, and led past the Creek (1 min. 12 sec.) by nearly a quarter of a length. Along the concrete wall which protects the grounds of Craven Cottage from the ravages of the tide, no alteration in the relative position of the two boats occurred. But the Cambridge men were mak- ing efforts which soon had a deteriorating effect upon their pace, and at Craven steps, reached in 2 tnin. 26 sec., their opponents led by snore than half a length. Even as early ii the race as this it was evident that the chances of Cam- bridge were hopeless. Besides loosing the best of the tide byleeeping in too near the Middlesex store, tltey were row- ing short, the time of the oars in and out of the water was irregul tr, and, notwithstanding the smoothness of the river, a great deal of splashing was visible. The Grass Wharf was breasted in 4 min. 12 sec., but Oxford were now more than clear. Crossing the water from Rosebank to the Soapworks the Cantabs fell rapidly behind, and the Oxford men shot the deserted suspension bridge at Hammersmith two lengths in front in 7 min. 43 see. from the start. The race was now virtually over, and the result, barring accidents, became a foregone conclusion. Stroke by stroke the distance between the two eights increased. At the lower end of the Eyot the stroke side oars in the Cam- bridge boat were going in and coming out of the water " anyhow," and the crew lost ground rapidly. Oxford passed Chiswick Church in llmin. 53sec. from the start, and Cambridge 19 seconds later. The leading boat, as far as could be judge 4, was fully five lengths ahead, and that this lead was being increased every moment was apparent to all who were on board the accompanying steamers. At Barnes bridge the Dark Blues had obtaineda still greater advantage; they passed underneath in 16min. 50sec.., while another 20 seconds elapsed before the Cambridge boat entered the shadow cis upon the water by the overhanging structure. Oxford, however, with the race well in hand, with a lead of some seven.or eight lengths, and with the result now reduced to a certainty, kept pounding gamely along; Cambridge got' more wild and scratchy than ever ; and, although the Oxford men seemed to ease down slightly towards the finish, they reached the goal probably ten lengths in front, their time from start to finish, as recorded by Benson's Chronograph, haying been 20min. 12sec., and that of Cam- bridge 20min. 32sec. Both crews subsequently paddled on towards Strand-on-the-Green, and disefitharked at the boat- house of the Grove Park Boat Club. The sentence upon Tone, pronounced by a court-martial, was obviously illegal, and so every lawyer knew it to be. But the people looked on as if in stupor, and dared not by look or word betray their feelings or their sympathy. There was one friend of this Illustrious Irishman, however, who was determined that the law of the land should be invoked, and one effort made to rescue this apostle of Irish Union and this martyr of Irish liberty from the jaws of death. That friend was John Philpot Curran. "Us believed," says Mitchell, "that by moving the Court of King's Bench to assert its jurisdiction some delay might be interposed—the French Government might threaten to retaliate upon some important prisoner of war; the case might thus become a political and not a criminal one, and in the end, either through threats of retaliation or by an arrangement with the British Government, Tone might be saved. As soon, then, as the Court of King's Bench was opened on the 12th of November, Curran was seen entering the Court, leading the aged father of Tone, who produced his affidavit that his son had been brought before a bench of officer calling itself a court-martial, and sentenced to death. "I do not pretend," said Mr. Curran, " that Mr. Tone is not guilty of the charges of which he is accused. I presume the officers were honourable men. But it is stated in this affidavit as a solemn fact that Mr. Tone had no commission under His Majesty, and therefore no court-martial could have cognisance of any crime imputed to him whilst the Court of King's Bench sat in the capacity of the great criminal court of the land. In times when war was raging, when man was opposed to man in thES Geld, court-martials might be endured ; but every law authority is with me whilst I stand upon this sacred and immutable principre of the constitution that martial law and civil law are incom- patible, and the former mast cease with the existence of the latter. This is not, however, the time for arguing this mo- mentous question. My client must appear in this Court. He is cast for death this very morning. He may be ordered for execution whilst I address you. I call on the Court to support the law, and move for a-habeas corpus to be directed to the Provost Marshal of the barracks of Dublin, and Major Sandys to bring up the body of Tone." After some conflict between the Lord Chief Justice and the authorities at the barracks, the Sheriff returned with the fatal news that Mr. Tone, who had wounded himself in the course of the even- ing, was not in a condition to be removed. It appears that on the night before, after writing a letter to the French Directory, and a touching adieu to his wife, while the soldiers were erecting a gibbet for him in the yard before his window he cut hi 4 throat with a penknife. But it was not effectually done. He had missed the carotid artery, and the doctor reported that he might possibly survive. "I am sorry," murmured the sufferer, "I have been so bad an anatomist." He lingered in the extremity of agony for seven days. On the seventh day he overheard the doctor whisper to the gaoler that if "the prisoner attempted to move or speak be must ,eroire instantly." Turning to the doctor Tone replied, "I can yet find words to thank you, sir. It is the most welcome news you could give me. What should I wish to live for?" Falling back with these expressions on his lips he expired, and one more prisoner was free. "Thus passed away," says Madden, "one of the master spirits of his time. The curse of Swift was upon this man —he was an Irishman. Had he been a native of any other European country his noble eualisties, his brilliant talents, would have raised him to the first honours in the State and to the highest place in the esteem of his fellow citizens. His name lives, however, and his memory is probably des- tinedko survive as long as his country has a history. Peace be to his ashes!"
The two crews dined together in the evening at the St. James's Restaurant.

THE BOAT RACE FOR THE CHAMPION- HTP THE WORLD. The great Anglo-Canadian sculling race for the cham- pionship of the world and 1;1,000 between Edward Hanlan, of Toronto, and Robert Watson Boyd, of Middlesborough, was decided on Monday afternoon on the Tyne. The morn- ing of the race was ushered in somewhat inauspiciously, the sky being dull and murky and portending a wet day. The atmosphere, too, was made heavy and oppressive by a slight drizzling rain. From an early hour the streets presented indications of the feverish excitement generally prevalent a few hours previous to a great aquatic struggle on the river. Long before the time appointed for the race huge crowds began to move from the town westwards, and the competi- tion for vacant spaces from which even the smallest view could be obtained was exceeOngly keen. Along each side of the liver every vacant space was occupied, whilst the crnsh in the upper reaches proved that so far as attendance was concerned it was the largest that has ever been seen on the Tyne. Shortly before one o'clock the Scotch mist which had rendered a stranger's visit to Newcastle anything but agreeable became worse, and a heavy fog overhung the upper reaches of the river, rendering a voyage anything but pleasant, and materially interfering with the view of the public from the wharfs, quays, arid bridges. There was very little wind, however, and the river was in bad condi- tion for rowing. The arrangements of Mr. Superintendent Stephens wore of the most perfect description, everything being done to secure a clear course for the rival scull ers, whilst excellent order was maintained regarding the position of various boats. The &st sign of the approaching struggle was the arrival of Boyd's ten-oared cutter from the west. The crew, who were dressed in blue-and-white striped jerseys, paddled to the south side, and patiently waited the time for the start. Shortly before Iwo o'clock the boats began to leave their moorings and take up their respective positions on the south side of the river, extending from the High Level Bridge to the Redheugh Bridge. The Charles Attwood, with the referee (Mr. Luke Armstrong), took up her position immediately behind the scallers, the police boat being next, and then the three boats chartered by the com- petitors. At this time the starting boats had been moored 25 yards apart, and by two o'clock all the preliminaries for the struggle were completed. Boyd's cutter appeared on the scene and indulged in a spin over about 150 yards. At ten minutes past two Hanlan's cutter pulled down. Shortly after three a ringing cheer announced the embarkation of Boyd from his boathouse in Hillgate. Hanlan took ship a moment or two previously from the timbers in front of the Mansion House, but his appearance was not greeted with the enthusiasm accorded to his opponent. The toss for choice of stations resulted in favour of the north country- man, who, of course, chose the northern berth, which is the more sheltered. At twenty minutes past two Haulm backed to his cutter and doffed his thick guernsey, rowing in a thin, blue, armless body. Boyd immediately followed suit, stripping to the buff. Boyd broke away three times, but, Hanlan not being ready, on the fourth attempt they came to an understanding. div.head: No. XIV.—THEOBALD WOLFE TONE.
div.p: No. XIV.—THEOBALD WOLFE TONE.

No seies of papers on Illustrious Irishmen would be com- plete that did not contain sorneereference to The:Asald Wolfe Tone, the organiser, if not the founder, of the Society of United Irishmen, and who, according to Goldwin Smith, "though little known among Englishmen, was near beirsi Isere almost as fatal to England as Hannibal to Rome." were not a few in Ireland at this period who regr.otied the n. i English Government as the real enemy of their. ation In their judgment it was very unfortunate that the divisions among the Catholics themselves, alid the hereditary estranoement and aversion between them and the Presby- terians made it next to ielnpossible to cree.te a united Irish nation with one sole b,ond and one single atm-.-the destruc- tion of British goy arnment in Ireland. This, however, was precisely the f"„eaat task undertaken by Tone, a young Protestant lawsr of Dublin, and who at the time when he first flung 3-sitmself into the grand revolutionary scheme of the Catholics to the body of the nation was not asseciatieig- Persiroaily acquainted with a single individual of that creed. He was then in his Sth year. It is needless to say that Lone had been a democrat from his earliest years, and had Iwatched the progress of the Revolution in France with intense pleasure. In his narrative of his own life Tone has given such a clear account of his purposes at this time that it is best to present it in his own words :—" To subvert the tyranny of our execrable Government, to break the connec- tion with England, the never-failing source of all our po- litical evils, and to assert the independence of my country —these were my objects. To unite the whole people of Ireland, to abolish the memory of all past dissensions, and to substitute the common name of Irishman in place of the denominations of Protestant, Catholic, and Dissenter—these were my means. The Protestants I despaired of from the outset for obvious reasons. Already in possession, by an un- just monopoly, of the whole power and patronage of the country, it was not to be supposed that they would ever concur in measures the certain tendency of which must be to lessen their influence as a party, how much soever the nation might gain. To the Catholics I thought it unneces- sary to address myself, because, as no change could make their political situation worse, I reckoned upon their sup- port to a Certainty; besides, they had already begun to manifest a strong sense of their wrongs and oppressions; and finally I well knew, however it might be disguised or suppressed, there existed in the breast of every Irish Catho- lic an inexterpable abhorrence of the English name and power. There remained only the Dissenters, whom I knew to be patriotic and enlightened, though all prejudice was not yet entirely removed from their minds. I sat down ac- cordingly, and wrote a pamphlet addressed to the Dissenters, and which I entitled 'An argument on behalf of the Catho- lics of Ireland,' the object of which was to convince them that they and the Catholics had but one common interest and one common enemy; that the depression and slavery of Ireland was produced and perpetuated by the divisions existing between them, and that consequently to assert the independence of their country and their own individual liberties, it was necessary to forget all former feuds, to con- solidate the entire strength of the whole nation, and to form for the future but one people." This pamphlet, which appeared in September, 1791, under the signature of a "Northern Whig," had a considerable degree of success. The Catholics were pleased with the efforts of a volunteer in their cause, and distributed it in all quarters. The people of Belfast printed a very large edition, which they dispersed through the whole North of Ireland, and the author thereof had the satisfaction of knowing that many Dissenters were converted by his arguments. Another result of this pamphlet was that his acquaintance among the Catholics was extended. He was introduced to the Catholic leaders, and soon had on his list of friends the names of men "most distinguished for their virtue, talent, and patriotism." Through the influence thus acquired he and Russell formed a club which "certainly commenced a new epoch in the politics of Ireland." Wolfe Tone was shortly after, on the recommendation of John Keogh, appointed Secretary to the "General Committee" of the Catholics, and long laboured zealously in their service. But he was not content with mere Catholic agitation. He and his friends continued with unabated zeal in the organisation of the United Irish So- ciety, which he hoped to see swallow up all others. In 1794, as we have seen in a previous communication, the Rev. William Jackson was arrested in Dublin on a charge of high treason. He had come from France, with instructions from the Government of the Republic, to have an emissary appointed by the United Irish leaders who should go to Paris and negotiate for French aid in a revolu- tionary movement. He had come by way of London, and had letters of introduction to Lord Edward Fitzgerald, who refused to bold any communication with him. He was, however, introduced to Tone, who at first entered into his views, and undertook to be himself the agent who should go to France, but at the next interview, having conceived suspicions of Cockayne (Jackson's companion), if not of Jackson himself, he drew back and declined farther negotia- tion. The evidence upon Jackson's trial clearly proving that some degree of treasonable connection had subsisted be- tween him and Tone, the latter was advised, if he consulted his safety, to withdraw from,lreland. Accordingly in the summer of 1795 he transporled himself and his family to America. At first he formed the intention of remaining in the United States, but Tone was one of those restless spirits who feel th,t they are born for great undertakings, if not for great achievements, and who, though they may not be able to wed themselves o Fortune, woo her at all haz.rds. So he finally resolved to proceed to France and labour to form the alliance which he regarded as the grand mission of his life between the French Republic and a Republic in Ireland. He arrived at Havre on the let of February, 1796, bearieg a letter of introduction to Charles De la Croix, Minister for Foreign Affairs, from the French Envoy at khiladelphia. He had another letter to Jame-, Monroe, then the representative of the United States inParis, who very kindly guided him in his proceedings to gain the ear of the French authorities. He had several interviews with Da la Croix, with Clarke, and, what was of more importance, with the illustrious Carnot, chief of the Executive Directory, who really himself controlled at that roonknt the movements of all the French armies. His progress in negotiating for sub- stantial aid from France was at first slow and somewhat dis- couraging, but at last, when Tone was almost out of funds, he was sent for to the Lnxensberg Palace, and there informed that the Directory had resolved to send out an expedition under the command of General Roche—the most rising man at that moment among the young military chiefs of the Re- public. From this time preparations were pushed forward with more or less activity, but by no means fast enough to satisfy the ardent spirit of Toue. It was not until the 15th of December, 1796, that all the troops were on board. The troops were to have amounted to 15,000 men, but they were actually a little over 13,000, with abundance of artillery and ammunition and arms for 45,000 men. Tone was on board the Indomptable. There were on the whole 17 sail of the line, 13 frigates, five corvettes, making with transports 43 sail. General Roche, and the admiral in command of the fleet, were on board a frigate, and the second general in com- mand of the laud forces was Grouchy—of unlucky memory. A wretched fatality was upon this fine expedition from the very start. The navigation, fortunately for England, yes, and for Ireand, too, was not happy for Tone. A storm separated the fleet. The ships had to pass through a strait called the Ra, which caused them to part. Roche was driven back, with seven ships of the line; but ten sail of the fine, with 6,000 troops and an abundance of arms, commanded by Grouchy, reached the Irish coast. Tone says that "he was so near the land that he could have thrown a biscuit on shore" A landing might have been most easily effected. But the instructions of the Directory were that they should proceed to Bantry Bay. There they did proceed, and there for five days ten French sail of the line lay in one of our bays. Tons, in his diary, says—" All now rests upon Grouchy. I hope he may turn out well." He did not turn out well. Twice had this man the destinies of nations in his hands, and twice he abased his trust. The expedition failed. Pious men attributed the failure to Providence, and navigators to the wind. "England," says Tone, "since the Spanish Armada, has not had such an escape, and that expe- dition, like ours, was defeated by the weather." So ended the great "Bantry Bay Expedition." The failure of the enterprise' however, did not break the spirit of Tone. For some months he served as an Adjutant- General of the Army of the Sambre and Meuse. But in 1797, in conjunction with others, he prevailed upon the Dutch to prepare for a national effort to liberate and redeem the very same people whom a century before they had so powerfully contributed, with the Prince of Orange and its Dutch Blues, to hurl prostrate under the feet of England. "How strange sometimes are the nutations of history." This second ex- pedition was prepared in the Texel, and consisted of 15 sail of the line, 11 frigates, and several sloops. There were 14,000 men on board. A second time the winds, "the only unsubsidised allies of England," conspired in he favour. The foul weather prevented them from sailing. During the whole of the two months of July and August the departure was postponed. "It is most terrible," says Tone, in his diary. "Twice within nine months has England been saved by the wind. It seems as if the very elements had conspired to perpetuate our slavery and protect the insolence and oppression of our tyrants. What can Ido at this moment? Nothing." Tone evidently believed that Dewintsr's Dutch fleet would never sail at all, and consequently obtained leave to go to Paris. But when Tone abandoned every hope of decisive action on the part of the Dutch fleet it set sail for Ireland. On the 11th October it encountered the English fleet off a place called Camperdown. After a bloody fight *Dewinter's ship struck, a sinking wreck. Ten Dutch ships of the line and two frigates .were captured ; Dancan, the English admiral, became Lord Camperdown ; and there was an end of Holland as a great naval power. But Tone did not abate one jot of hope even after the failure of the second expedition. News reached him at Paris of the rebellion, and the founder of the United Irish Society was not a man to evade the consequences and re- sponsibilities of his own acts, nor to take his ease in France, while his comrades were perishing on the field or on the gallows. He never for one moment relaxed his efforts to effect the great task of his life, which, in his own words, was "to pull down a monarchy and establish a repablic, to break a connection of six hundred years' standing, and con- tract a fresh alliance with another country." At length, a third expedition was undertaken, and had it been executed with the sagacity with which it was planned, the result might have been different. But again it failed. and Tone, who was on board the Roche French line of battle ship, one of the vessels captured by the English squadron off the Irish coast, fell into the hands of the English Government. When the ship on which Tone was struck, confounded with the other officers, he was not recognised for some time, for he had completely acquired the language and appearance or a Frenchman but he was afterwards betrayed by a friend The French Officers were invited to breakfast with the Ear! of Cavan who commanded in that district. Tone sat undis tinguished amongst them, when Sir George Hill entered the

div.head: POSTPONEMENT OF THE EXECUTION
div.p: POSTPONEMENT OF THE EXECUTION

OF LAMSON. The Home Secretary has ordered the execution of George H. Lamson to be postponed until the 18th inst., at the re- quest of the United States Government, in order that the documents bearing al the alleged insanity of the convict may receive full consideration. At the same tune the con- vict has been "distinctly warned" that the postponement in no way raises a presumption of a reprieve or commutation of the capital sentence. Conimatailm, in fact, in the shape of a mitigation of the punishment ~there cannot be. If Lamson is eventually declared to be responsible for his actions, there can be no doubt that he will be executed. If. on the other hand, proof or even strong suspicion, of hiS insanity should be established it will be the duty of the Home Secretary to order his removal to Brpadmoor Asylum. In announcing the decision of the Horne Office care is taken to state that it has been the practice when respite :1 are granted for the purpose of further inquiry, either into mat- ters of law or of fact, that where the inquiry " shows no sufficient ground for interference the sentenee of the law takes its course." The latest instance was in 1868, when the execution of Barrett, the author of the dreadful explosion at Clerkenwell, was postponed for a fortnight. One of the most remarkable of these postponements occurred in 1857, when a soldier named Marshall was executed after seven months' respite. In 1853 a young man named Barbour, who had murdered a companion at Sheffield, received notice of the postponement of his execution—" for further inquiry"— when he was actually at the foot af the scaffold, but he was executed in the following week.

div.head: POLITICAL ITEMS.
div.p: POLITICAL ITEMS.
A general meeting of the Reform Club, to consider the question of altering the procedure of election, will be held on an early day after Easter. E.irl Granville will probably preside.
Notice has been given of no fewer than 127 amendments to be moved in committee on the Rivers Conservfncy Bill, which is introduced by the President of the Local Govern- ment Board.

It is, we (Daily News) understand, propos9,d to take morn- ing sittings of the House of Commons from Tuesday, the 2nd of May, with the object of proceeding consecutive!y with the resolutions on Procedure. _

It is understood that Colonel the Hon. F. C. Bridgeman, son of the Earl of Bradford, and Mr. Arthur L. Briggs, cotton spinner, of ThBrnleigh, Sharpies, will be invited to contest the borough of Bolton in the Conservative interest at the next general election.

_ The proposal to re-open negotiations fora fresh commercial trcaty with France do not, we believe, find favour with tbe British Cabinet. Mr. Gladstone is personally strongly averse to the principle of commercial treaties, and the en- gagement with France having lapsed, the Chancellor of the Exchequer is not inclined to resume the connection.

Renly- ing to Mr. Charles Cowan, in acknowledgment of resolutions recently passed by the Penicuik and Glencoe Liberal Association in support of the Government, Mr. Gladstone says :—"We shall labour with all our heart and energy to bring the House of Commons out of its present embarrassment into a condition in which it may look more hopefully to fulfilling its legislative obligations to the people of the three kingdoms." THE EAST CORNWALL ELECTION.—The resnit of the polling in E..st Cornwall was officially declared on Satur- day, when it was announced that Mr. Charles T. Dyke Acland, the Liberal candidate, bad polled 3,720 votes, and Mr. John Tremayne, who had come forward in the Conser- vative interest, 3,519; thus giving the Liberals a majority of 201. The election of Mr. Acland makes another instance of father and son sitting and voting in the same House, ten gentlemen, a number unprecedented in our time, now having sons members with themselves of the House of Com- mons, while two—Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Bass—have each two sons members, viz., in the case of the Premier his eldest son, Mr. W. H. Gladstone (East Worcestershire), and his fourth son, Mr. H. J. Gladstone (Leeds); and in the case of Mr. Bass, his eldest son, Mr. M. A. Bass (East Staffordshire), and Mr. H. A. Bass, the second son (Tam- worth). The other instances are those of the Speaker, the Right Hon. Sir H. B. W. Brand, G.C.B. (Cambridgeshire), and his eldest son, Mr. H. R. Brand (Stroud); Sir T. D. Acland (North Devon), and his eldest son, Mr. C. T. D. Acland (East Cornwall) ; Mr. T. A'. Dickson (county Tyrone), and his eldest son, Mr. J. Dickson (Dungannon); Sir George Elliot (North Durham), and his eldest son Mr. G. W. Elliot (Northallerton); Mr. Samuel Morley (Bristol), and his fourth son, Mr. A. Morley (Nottingham) ; Sir Stafford Northcote (North Devon), and his second son, Mr. H. S. Northcote (Exeter) ; Mr. Bernhard Samuelson (Ban- bury), and his eldest son, Mr. H. B. Samuelson (Frome) ; Ind Mr. Charles Seely (Lincoln), and his eldest son, Mr. Charles Seely, jun. (Nottingham.) Of these gentlemen all, bvith the exception of Sir Stafford and Mr. Northcote and George and Mr. Elliot, belong to the Liberal party. Sir T. D. Acland and Sir S. Northcote are the only instances of colleagues among the number.
