FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
There is a rumour, persistently repeated, that the Czar in- tends to create the office of Prime Minister in Russia.

The Czar has commuted the sentence of death passed upon the Nihilkts in the Triginia trial to hard labour in the mines for an indefinite period, an exception being made in the case of Suchanoff, who is to suffer the extreme punish- ment, but who will be shot as an officer at Cronstadt. On Saturday at Port Said all the Arab coal labourers struck work, demanding double pay. Their employers re- fused, and decided that ships must coal with their own crews. The strike is said to be caused by the imposition of new and heavy taxes by Government. General Strelinkoff was murdered in Odessa last Thursday week and his assassins were captured immediately. On this news reaching the Czar, be ordered two prisoners to be exe- cuted forthwith, but at the last moment countermanded the order; but on Saturday a court martial was held, and found them guilty. On Monday they were executed. This is an approach to lynch law, and is the outcome of a revolutionary state of society. THE MEETING OF MONARCHS. Tbe Paris adjmorial Diplomatique publishes intelligence from London, stating that it is not a simple meeting between the Emperors of Austria and Russia which is projected, but an interview at which the Emperor of Germany and the Kings of Italy, Roumania, and Servia would be present, and which would be held with the object of assuring the maintenance of peace in Europe. " Nevertheless," Memorial Diplomatique,"such a proposal would necessitate much negotiation, and could only be carried out after frank and clear explanations have been given to the British and French Governments, whose susceptibilites would have to be seriously taken into account."

The Czar is reported, on information which the Berlin correspondent of the Times regards as trustworthy, to be in "a truly helpless, irresolute, and pitiable state." A few days ago the St. Petersburg police found posted up at the street corners copies of a proclamation by the moderate revolutionary party threatening the Czar unless he adopted constitutional reforms. On that day His Majesty was ex- pected to attend the annual military monster concert in com- memoration of the first capture of Paris and in aid of the army pensioners; but the assembly was disappointed. Much irritation is felt in St. Petersburg against Turkey in conse- quence of the protracted delay in the settlement of the war indemno question, and the objections offered by the Porte to the passage of the quasi-volunteer cruisers through the Dardanelles. A WALTER SCOTT COMMEMORATION IN ROME.—At three o'clock on Saturday afternoon, in the presence of the muni- cipal authorities and the British residents, the stone tablet, commemorative of Sir Walter Scott's sojourn in Rome, was unveiled by Colonel Ramsay, who, in short speech, thanked the Municipality and the other Italians who had contritmted in one form or another to the erection of the stone. The speaker also expressed his acknowledgments to the Duke of Sermoneta, an old friend of the novelist's, who was present, for the prominent share he had taken in the work, and in conclusion said he was charged by the Earl of Haddington to express the thanks of the Scotch nation to the people of Rome. The tablet is affixed to the facade of the Silvestrelli Palace, in the Mercede-street, where Scott lived. The following is the translation of the inscription which is in Italian :—" In the year 1832, the last of his life, the illustrious English novelist, Walter Scott, of Edinburgh, dwelt in this house." A SICOBELEFF ADVENTURE.—In publishing the following curious anecdote of General Skobeleff, the Czas expressly guarantees the authenticity of every detail therein set forth. It would appear that, whenever a personage of high rank and importance visits Warsaw, the Imperial police authori- ties commission their secret agents to watch every action of that personage by day and night, as far as may be com- patible with the respect due to his exalted station, and to report the results of their observations regularly every morn- ing. One of these reports, handed in to the police office of the district, in which is situated the Hotel d'Europe, where Skobeleff lodged during his recent sojourn in the Polish capital, is textually reproduced in the columns of the Ccas. It runs as follows :—" Last night, at the hour of nine, his excellency the general deigned to leave his hotel. He wore an elegant silk hat and a no less elegant overcoat. In his hand he carried a walking-stick. His excellency condes- cended to hire the droshky No. 217, and, seated therein, to drive to Ziazd, where he alighted, and straightway disap- peared. His exceltency did not return to his hotel until seven o'clock this morning, wearing, however, a jacket and cap, both of which were covered with mud. It was, more- over, his excellency's pleasure to appear considerably intoxi- cated." "This report," concludes the Czas," is absolutely authentic. We have seen it, and are fully responsible for its publication." If our Slav contemporary be in a position to prove its words, we should imagine that the police official who has betrayed the secrets of the Warsaw Detective De- partment is likely to hear of something to his disadvantage from the hot-tempered and impetuous victor of Geok Tepe. —Daily Telegraph. THE WAR IN SOUTH AMERICA.—ANOTHER GREAT

div.head: BATTLE: 200 PERUVIANS KILLED.
div.p: BATTLE: 200 PERUVIANS KILLED.

Intelligence received at Buenos Ayres states that the Peruvian forces under the command of Colonel Mas and Prefect Panizo attacked the troops under Caceres, but wore defeated in Ayacucho, with the loss of 200 men killed. Mas and Panizo were taken prisoners, and it is expected they will be shot. Caceres afterwards attacked Benito Nela, in Ica, and took him prisoner. Pierola has issued a proclamation urging the union of all parties in Peru, and advocating peace with Chili.

div.head: INSURRECTION IN HERZEGOVINA.
div.p: THE INSURRECTION IN HERZEGOVINA.

The telegrams from Vienna and Cettinge in reference to the insurrection in Herzegovina and Crivoscie differ as widely as possible. The Austrians assert that the Crivos- cians are conclusively beaten and the revolt in Hetzegovina " stamped out." On the other band, accounts from Slavonic sources, which reach us by the way of Cettinge, assert that large bodies of insurgents are gathering in readiness for re- newed operations in the spring; and a telegram from the Montenecr'rin capital states that severe fighting is goikg on, and the Austrians were beaten and pursued by the instrr- gents. A Vienna telegram of Wednesday's date says : An official despatch received to-day states that the Austrian troops despatched on the Ist inst. in pursuit of the insurgent bands remaining on the right bank of the Tara, finding that the enemy had proceeded towards the Mestrovac Planina, made a reconnaissance in that direction. On the approach of the Austrian troops the insurgents, some of whom were accompanied by their families, fled across the sandjak frontier in the direction ef Bobovo,Ogradienika, and Slatina. The despatch adds that the dispersion of the bands has had the effect of reassuring the inhabitants. During a recon- naissance made on the Ist inst. on the right and left banks of the Drina, near Veekorabrado and Bastaci, one insurgent was killed and two were wounded. The troops captured a large quantity of ammunition. THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION.

We learn by Times Alexandria telegram that about 270 more officers have been promoted, and further • promoticns, making a total of 500, are imminent. This favour shown to the military class makes the civil supporters of the present regime somewhat discontented. The dismissal of loading European officials has been much discussed, and the native papers—Taief, the organ of Arabi, and the Watan, the Copt organ—are loud in their complaints against foreign func- tionaries. The control is now Iconfined to a position of simple observation, reporting all events to their Govern- ments. The President of the Council has again promised not to interfere with the assigned portion of the revenue or the administrations connected with the public debt. The general impression in Egypt is now that Europe will leave the country to govern itself, provided order be maintained, the debt paid, and the Mixed Tribunals respected, conse- quently a fulfilment of the programme of reforms proposed by Sir Rivers Wilson. The Commission of Inquiry can no longer be counted upon. DISASTRO US COLLISION AT SEA. LOSS OF THE MAIL STEAMER DOURO.

A disastrous collision occurred late on Saturday night off Cape Finisterre, between the royal mail steamer Douro and the Spanish steamer Yrurac Bat. The Collision must have been severe, inasmuch as both vessels foundered, and it is feared that upwards of sixty lives have been lost. The Douro was homeward bound from Brazil, via Lisbon, where many passengers were landed, but on leaving that port, there were on board, it is believed, fifty-six passengers and a crew numbering eighty-one. Of these forty-one passengers and sixty-three of the crew are said to have been saved ; but the captain, four officers, and the chief and second engineers are amongst the Jost. How many persons were on the Yrurac Bat is unknown, but the crew numbered forty-two officers and men, chiefly Spaniards except the engineers, and at Corunna a number of passengers we-e embarked. Thirty-six persons are reported saved from this vessel and thirty drowned; but later news gives some hope that the loss of life on both vessels is considerably smaller than was at first supposed. There were several Manchester gentlemen en board the Douro, and anxiety is felt in the city regarding the catastrophe, for the further reason that this is the time when the buyers from the Brazils come over to the Man- chester market, and it is probable that some merchants on this errand were passengers by that steamer.

Mr. T. P. O'Connor will return immediately from the United States, and is expected to be in his place in Parlia- ment shortly after Easter. Mr. Errington, M.P., returned to Rome on Sunday night. He expects to be absent from England for some time. On Wednesday, at the fortnightly meeting of the Bolton Rural Sanitary Authority, a singular statement was made with regard to the treatment of a man suffering from small- pox. He lived in Howell Croft, Bolton, and a sanitary inspector, believing that he was suffering from smallpox, told him so. The patient said he did not know, but he felt very ill. The inspector then told the man to go to his house in Clarence-street, a considerable distance, in the morning, and he would then see. The disease had thee broken out. The inspector then walked with him to the hospital at Fish- pool ; they passed two schools on the way, and the children on seeing there was something the matter, gathered round, shouting "That man's got the smallpox." This happened Lath at St. Mark's and St. Bartholomew's Schools.—A Mem- ber said it was the most extraordinary thin!,' he had ever heard of. To think of a patient suffering from smallpox being obliged to go through the town to the house of the inspector to ascertain whether he was suffering from' small- pox !—Alderman Miles : It is the maddest way in which the inspector could have acted.—The matter will be again gone into. There is nothing more nourishing and warming in cold weather that* cup f really good Cocoa, but the difficulty has been to obtain it pure. Tots may be secured at a cost of one halfpenny for a large breakfast cup by using Cadbury's Cocoa Essence, which goes three times as far as the adulterated and starchy compounds ordinarily sold, the smallest ps..3ket muakiug :',atirteen breakfast cups of strong Cocoa.—didct.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 8, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 8, 1882.

There will be this year, as usual, .an election to nine scholarships at Rugby school—two of £BO a year. The examination will commence on June 20. It is stated that Mr. David James is about to enter into managerial responsibilities again by joining Mr. Charles Wyndham in the lesseeship of the Critet ion Theatre. Leo XIII. has sent the palm which he carried on Palm Sunday to Cardinal M`Cabe. This gift is always considered a very special mark of the Pontiff's favour. This palm is one of unusual beauty, and has, as its central ornament, a portrait of Leo the Great. Damage to the extent of between ' £15,000 and £20,000 was caused by fire, on Monday, on the premises of Messrs. Joseph Whiteley & Son, cotton spinners, Ripnonden. A rag and rope warehouse at Hull was burned down on Monday night. The loss in this case is estimated at £I:2,000. Mad'lle Sarah Bernha,rdt, the accomplished French actress, was on Tuesday somewhat romantically married in St. Andrew's, Wells-street, Oxford-street, London, to a Greek gentleman, Mr. Aristides Ambroise Damula. The event was carried out without previous notice, and no one but officials of the church had any knowledge of it. Au important work on Egypt, Turkey, and the prospects of Islam is expected after the crisis in the former country is over, from the pen of Mr. Wilfrid Scawen Blunt, who is at present the chief English interpreter of the aims of Ourabi Pasha, and the Egyptian nationalists, and whose recent articles on the prospects of Mahotnetanism have attracted much attention here.

Mr. Arthur Wells, a Nottingham solicitor, is reported to have left in charitable bequests a sum not less than £40,000. Of this the principal share falls to the London Missionary Society, that body receiving £15,000, whilst .0,000 is left to the Nottingham Congregational Institute. Mr. Wells had, during his lifetime, presented to the South Kensington Museum his extremely valuable collection of precious stones.

In reference to the Richmond murder, and the failure of the search for the head of the victim, Mrs. Thomas, it is now stated that Kate Webster, just before her execution, confessed that she dropped the bag containing the head down between two upright supports of Barnes Bridge. She alleged that it remained between the girdereuntil it reached the bottom, and its non-discovery was owing to its becoming embedded in that position. The report of the Select Committee on Post Office annui- ties and life assurance policies was issued on Saturday. The committee recommend that policies of assurance and annui- ties should be granted for any amount not exceeding £200; that the minimum limit of age for insurance and annuities should be reduced under certain restrictions to eight and five years respectively; that the maximum age for assurances should be sixty-five; and that the premium on surrendered policies should be returned after two years. A STRANGE AFFAIR.—An extraordinary affair has just come to light at Oldham. A young woman, who had been , under treatment at a hydropathic institution at Ilkley, Yorkshire, is said to have, a few days ago, cut her throat and died. A doctor gave a certificate that the woman died from irritation of the throat, and her body was conveyed at night in a coach to Oldham and buried, no inquest being held. The coroner became acquainted with the facts, and communicated with the Home Secretary, who requests an in- quest to be held.

In view of a great procession of the Salvation Army at Sheffield, on Easter Monday, the Sheffield magistrates held a meeting on Tuesday to consider what steps should be taken to prevent a disturbance similar to that which took place a couple of months ago, when Lieutenant Davidson was seriously injured. As the result of a prolonged discussion it was decided not to stop the procession, but the mayor and the chief constable were requested to endeavour to induce the leader of the army in Sheffield to curtail the procession. A London Magistrate has ruled that madiage cancels a female apprentice's indentures, but as he could find nothing in the law reports directly bearing on the point, he suggested that a mandamus should be applied for, so that the matter might be argued before a superior court. This seems to be one of the cases in which the woman's rights movement might operate to her disadvantage, for if women are to stand on the same legal footing as men, marriage would in no way affect their responsibilities to an employer. The semi-official Arabic'paper, El Jawaib, states that the Porte has received a despatch announcing a movement of French troops towards the Tripolitan frontier, and says this movement inspires the Ottoman Governmont with doubts in regard to the value of the pacific declarations of France con- cerning her policy in North Africa. The Porte consequently proposes to raise the effective strength of the Turkish troops in Tripoli to 30,000 men, 5,000 of whom will shortly embark.

Intelligence has reached the Chester police of a savage assault, committed by a gang of Boughton roughs, on two Salvationists, who were returning home on Tuesday night. The two men attacked were severely hit and kicked, and one of them, Wilber, lies in a dangerous condition. In- quiries have been made, but as yet no clue of the assailants has been obtained. It is stated that the Salvationists were returning quietly home from the services and were met by the roughs, who were in liquor. At the Carlisle City Quarter Sessions, on Wednesday, be- fore Mr. Temple, Q.C., Recorder, a young man named Richard Johnson, who has several names, was charged with breaking into the shop of Mr. Parker, Carlisle. and stealing watches and jewellery to the amount of £BO, on the Ist February. The prisoner was seen about the shop on the 31st January: On the 6th February he pawned gold chains with James Kidson, Rice-lane, Liverpool; William Brown, Park-lane; Thomas Park, St. James's-street •, John Harri- son, Great George-street; 'and David Jones, Grafton-street; all in Liverpool. He offered to pledge a chain with James Howett, 65, Beaufort-street, who gave him charge because his answers were unsatisfactory. The prisoner said he was guilty of receiving the goods, as he had got them to pledge. The jury found him guilty of the major charge. The Recorder, on finding that the prisoner had been twice con- victed of shopbreaking in Manchester, sent him to penal servitude for five years. About five o'clock on Wednesday morning a fire broke out in the cotton mill of Messrs. Heywood and Wrigley, at Hey- wood, commonly known as the Britannia Mills. The mill was five storeys high, 16 windows long, and 14 yards wide, in addition to which there was a new wina cut off from the other building by means of iron doors. The fire broke out in the top room of the first-named building, and by the time that the local steam fire engine arrived it had got a very firm hold. At six o'clock the roof was burnt through, and by seven the building was gutted, the whole of the machinery lying in the second storey. The contents of the card-room were seriously damaged by water. The machinery in the old mill, about 9,000 spindles, quite new, was destroyed, but that in the new wing was saved. A valuable 'steam engine was also seriouslydamaged. The total damages are estimated at between £lO,OOO and £12,000. It is insured. Over 100 people will be thrown out of work. The cause of the fire is not known.

THE VICTORIA UNIVERSITY.—A meeting of the Victoria University Court was held on Tuesday. The Vice Chancel- lor (Dr. Greenwood) read a statement showing the progress of the University up to the present time. The number of matriculated students was stated approximately: to .be 80, of whom 8 have already passed the preliminary examin- ations, 31 are candidates for the preliminary examinations to be held in June next, 23 are candidates for the ordinary degree of B.A. or B.Sc., and 27 candidates for a degree with with honours. This statement, the Vice Chancellor theught, might be held to offer a very encouraging prospect as to the future of the new University. Mr. Broadfield moved and Professor Roscoe seconded a resolution in favour of offering to all persons who at the date of the Charter were Associates of Owen's College a bachelor's degree. The motion was opposed by Chancellor Christie and others, on the ground that it was not expedient, however worthy the recipients of them might be, to grant degrees without examination. The motion was ultimately adopted. The Court resolved to present an Address of congratulation to Her Majesty the Queen on her recent escape from assassination. THE DISFRANCIII SEMENT BILL.—The Corrupt Practices Disfranchisement Bill enacts that after the end of the present Parliament the Parliamentary boroughs named in the first schedule to this Act shall cease to return any member or members to serve in Parliament, and after the passing of this Act an election for any such member or members shall not be held, and the registration of voters for such an elec- tion shall not take place. An election of a member or mem- bers to serve in Parliament for the Parliamentary boroughs mentioned in the second schedule to this Act shall not be held until after the end of this present Parliament. The persons scheduled of having been guilty of bribery, treating, or personation at the last general election shall be for ever incapable of voting or being registered as a voter for that borough or county in which the borough is situated. Section six of the Corrupt Practices Prevention Act, 1854, shall apply to every person disqualified under this section for being registered as a voter. Any person scheduled and prosecuted, but who has been acquitted, shall not be subject to any disqualification under this Act. The boroughs given in the first schedule to. be disfranchised are Gloucester, Macclesfield, and Sandwich. The boroughs given in the second schedule to have writs suspended during the present Parliament are Boston, Canterbury, Chester, and Oxford. In the third Schedule Knaresborough is given as a borough not to be disfranchised nor to have writ suspended. SUNDAY WORK IN A COTTON MILL AT BLACKBURN.— Before the Blackburn borough justices on Tuesday, Messrs. John Fish and Co., Limited, were summoned at the instance of Mr. Maitland, factory inspector, for employing three young persons on Sunday the sth ult. The defendants sum- moned John Thomas Slater, a drawer-in, for employing the same young persons on the date named without their know- ledge, consent, or connivance. Mr. Maitland said the case was one of the most extraordinary he had met with in his experience as an inspector, and it was also one of the worst. He had had many complaints of serious irregularities at Messrs. Fish's mill, and he bad ascertained that three boys had been assisting a loomer on Sunday, the sth ult.—Mr. Radcliffe, solicitor for Messrs. Fish, contended that Slater, the loomer and drawer-in in question, was to blame for tak- ing the boys into the mill without the consent or the know- ledge of the firm, and he called several witnesses who de- posed that no Sunday work had ever been done in the mill so far as cotton manufacture was concerned. On behalf of Slater, Mr. Brothers, solicitor, called six witnesses to prove a conversation between his client and Mr. Hindle, manager of the mill, in which the latter said it would be all right if Slater got the boys to come on the Sunday. The evidence was very contradictory, and the Bench asked Mr. Maitland if he wished to press &he case, remarking that it was a case of bard swearing on both sides. Mr. Maitland thought a penalty ought to be inflicted as it was clear an offence had been committed. Messrs. Fish were liable for what occurred in the mill, and he was obliged to press the case against them. —The Magistrates said they would have been glad if Mr. Ntaitland had withdrawn the summonses, but as he pressed for a penalty they inflicted a fine of £1 in one case and dis- missed the other summonses.

div.head: M 1 SCELLAN WHS.
div.p: M 1 SCELLAN WHS.

- On Saturday night one of the large mills at Cleckheaton, occupied by Mr. Joseph Clay, was with its contents destroyed by. lire. The damage is estimated at £20,000. The inquest on the victims of the l'rindon Grange explo- sion terminated on Saturday. The jury found that the deceased lost their lives by the explosion of gas in the pit, but how the explosion occurred there is no evidence to show., Two judges—Lord Chief Justice Coleridge and Mr. Baron Huddleston—have been specially commissioned to try the man INPLean for shooting at the Queen at Windsor Railway Station. The trial will take place at Reading on April 18th. An extraordinary circumstance has occurred in connection with the election of poor-law guardians in Chepstow Union. The retiring guardian for the parish of St. Kinsmark is the Rev. G. Ortne, and his seat at the board has been opposed by Mr. G. Dewdney, so that a contest will take place. There is only one resident in the whole parish. "The strongest man in the world" has been called as a witness in the Queen's Bench Division, in spite of Mr. Jus- tice Stephen's warning to counsel to remember what hap- pened when Samson was called on to perform. The. modern ...;amson (Victor Le Roy is his real name) said that he carried in his teeth six chairs, a table weighing 471b5., and a man sitting upon it. The next issue of gold coinage from the mint wilt, the Press Association says, bear the impress of Her Majesty from a new die. This is the second die only which has beea. taken during the reign of Queen Victoria. It represents tff6. features of the Queen as she is at present, and depicts her wearing the Imperial Crown. Thanks to the exertions of the magistrates, the Roman Catholic clergy and the Salvationist General Booth, there was no disturbance of the peace at Chester on Sunday. How • !ar this was the result of the peremptory closing of the pub- lic-houses by order of the city magistrates is an open ques- tion, but the public generally will be inclined to think that the peace was preserved because the police were well dis- played, and the Salvation Army did nothing to afford an excuse for breaking it. The estates of the late Earl of Wilton are a splendid ex- ample of the unearned increment of the rent of land in our manufacturing centres. According to the Landed Estates Gazette, "Forty years ago, the Wilton estates were worth £22,000 a year. In the Domesday Book they are returned at £31,234; but as a matter of fact the estates left by the late Earl are of the value of quite £05.000 a year." Thus, in 40 years the estates have nearly trebled in value, and all the owner has had to do has been to sign his name.—Londan Echo.

On Monday, at the Bolton County Police Court, George Ridley, of Farnwortb, was charged with keeping a dog with- out a license. The defence offered by Ridley was a remark- able one. Re wrote :—" lam summoned for keeping a dog without a license. I believe the law requires it to be a dog in every sense or the word. Gentlemen, my animal is neither a quadruped nor a biped. Although of the dog species, it is a monstrosity of nature." The ticnai lied the defendant 7s. 6d. and costs. The Marquis of Huntly surrendered at Bow-street Police Court on Monday, when Mr. Montagu Williams, for the prosecution, stated that there was evidently no intention on the part of the Marquis to defraud, and as his estates were found to be amply sufficient for covering the whole amount advanced upon them, he asked permission to wilhdraw the summons. Serjeant Ballantine, for the Marquis of Huntly, explained that his Lordship left this country without dream- ing that there was any act of his life to which culpability could be attached. Lord Huntly, whatever may have been his misfortunes or his follies, never 'intended anything dis- honourable. The summons was withdrawn.

A MEDICAL OFFICER CENSURED.—An inquest at Chester as to the death of James Fry, a seaman, who had died in the workhouse an hour after his release from prison, was concluded on Saturday. The deceased, who was 62 years of age, had been committed to Chester Castle for a month for having stolen a coat. He was in a feeble condition when committed. During his imprisonment he was kept on second-class diet, as usual with prisoners of his class. At the end of the month he was so feeble that he was removed from the prison to the workhouse in a cab. He died imme- diately on his arrival at the workhouse. In accordance with the strongly-expressed view of the coroner that the deceased should have been allowed a more generous diet during his imprisonment, the jury added to their verdict of "Died from natural causes" an opinion that the medical officer of the prison was to blame in not having treated the deceased as.a patient, and given him a more generous diet in the

jail. SUICIDES—At one time a person guilty of felo-de-se was buried in a public highway with a stake driven through his body. But a statute of the time of George IV. forbade coroners ordering this to be done. The statute, however, directed that the burial should take place within 24 hours of the finding of the inquisition, and between nine and twelve at night. This direction is proposed to be repealed in a bill introduced by Viscount Ebrington, M.P., for amending the Act. He proposes, moreover, that the interment "may be made in any of the ways prescribed or authorised" by the Burial Laws Act of 1880. In all ether respects, however, nothing contained in the measure is to authorise the per- forming a any of the rites of Christian burial, or to be taken to alter the laws or usages relating to the burial of persons who have committed suicide. BRUTAL MURDER NEAR DURHAM.—EarIy on Sunday morning a platelayer named Thomas Pyle, employed at Ushaw Moor Colliery, near Durham, where a strike exists, was found murdered in a secluded spot immediately on the outskirts of the city:of Durham. Pyle' who was a powerful man in the prime of life, was found lying in a hedge side dead, with a wound upon his chin, and was carried to the County Hospital at Durham, where the house surgeon gave it as his opinion that death had resulted from suffocation. The handkerchief of deceased was drawn tightly round leis neck. There are indications where Pyle was found as if somebody had been dragged about 20 yards. A hedge stake, which had been drawn fresh from the hedge, was found near Pyle, whose head had been repeatedly. struck. Pyle was regarded as a " blackleg " at Ushaw Moor Colliery, and recently bad to seek the protection of law against the violence, of some of the men on strike. SHOCKING BOAT ACCIDENT.—Loss OF Two LIVES.—A sad boat accident, resulting in the death of two persons, occurred at Loch Vennacher, in the Scotch Trossachs, on Saturday. The first competition of the Callender Angling Club was being held in somewhat stormy weather. While one of the boats was crossing from the north side of the lake, and when within a few hundred yards from the shore, the persons on board changed places, causing the boat to upset, and throwing the occupants into the water. In the boat were Mr. Alexander M•Niven, Inneshewn, Glen Dochart, Kuhn; Mr. Mitchel, solicitor, Edinburgh; Donald Camp- bell, senr., and Baker, Callender, boatman. They all laid hold of the boat, and were thus kept afloat for some time. Mr. Mitchell, anxious to get a better position, climbed on the top of the upset boat. Mr. M'Niven laid hold of him by, the one hand, and kept him afloat. Campbell, getting ex- hausted, laid hold of Mr. M‘Niven's coat. In this way they were all drifted into the Invertrossach Bay. Mr. M‘Niven succeeded in reaching the shore, but two others were drowned.

A CURIOUS STORY.—An ex-member of the Fenian Directory tells a curious story in the new number of Black- wood about a plot to seize Lord Derby shortly before the ex- ecution of the Manchester Fenians. Five men were at that time found guilty, but one named Maguire, who at the trial protested his innocence, and was innocent though convicted, was released. It was the release of Maguire that saved Lord Derby, who was at Knowsley, from seizure by the Fenians as a hostage for the lives of the condemned men. When the sentence against Maguire was set aside, the Brotherhood con- cluded that with a trial thus impeached the other prisoners would not be hanged, and they therefore did not pursue the scheme for seizing Lord Derby. Emissaries, however, from various towns went to Manchester on the day of the execu- tion, the arrangement being that on the hangman and his victims appearing on the scaffold a party of good riflemen should save the condemned Fenians from the indignity of the executioner's touch. But the elements were against them. A heavy fog obscured the view, the men were hanged, and from that time onwards, though Fenianism has developed abroad, it has been practically extinct in Eng- land. ALARMING ACCIDENT IN A PUBLIC HALL.—An alarming accident occurred at Plymouth on Saturday night, resulting in serious injury to several persons and in a panic which threatened to end still more disastrously. During a per- formance of Hamilton' Diorama at St. James's Hall there was a frequent commotion in the gallery, where a rough crowd had assembled. One part of the performance was followed by heavy stamping of feet by way of applause, whereupon a loud cracking noise was heard, and imme- diately afterwards a portion of the front gallery fell out into the body of the hall, carrying with it about 50 people, mostly young men who were leaning against it. The noise and cloud of dust which succeeded created a panic, and there was a rush for the doors, the groans of injured and the shrieks of women adding to the momentary disorder. The manager appealed to the audience to retain their seats, and finally assuaged their fears. Assistance was then ob- tained on behalf of the wounded, who lay helpless amongst the debris. Most of them were found to be slightly, but six were seriously injured. Two persons on the stage in costumes depicting "Alice" and "Jumbo" were temporarily speechless through fright. FENIAN THREAT TO BLOW UP MANCHESTER TOWN HALL. —There is the best possible authority for stating that defi- nite information of an intended attack on the Manchester Town Hall has been received by the police. The municipal authorities are very reticent, but an authentic statement of the origin and grounds for the police precautions has been obtained. A few days ago the Chief Constable received from the authorities at Scotland-yard intelligence of a plot to blow up the ToWn Hall, the time fixed for the intended attack being at or about Easter. The information forwarded was of such a nature as to convince the Chief Constable that there was ground for alarm, and that it was not only advisable but necessary to take measures for the safety of the building. He laid the letter pefore the 'Watch Cominittee, or some of the members, and submitted it to the Mayor, and at once in- creased the police guard of the building. Extra policemen were placed on guard in the corridors, together with detec- tives in plain clothes, during the day time, and all visitors whose business was not known were carefully looked after. Instructions were given that a sharp eye should he kept upon parcels, the contents of which were not manifest. At night the number of constables on duty was largely increased. Pedestriars were prevented approaching close to the walls, and a cordon of police was placed round the hall. The building was carefully guarded against attacks last winter, when threats to blow up public buildings were made. A strong guard was placed on duty at all such buildings and tions only apply barracks in Manchester and Salford, but the present precau- to the Manchester Town Hall, which alone , ' has been mentioned as the object of Fenian plots.
During a quarrel amongst sailors at Portrnadoc on Mon- (lay night a Welshman Was fatally stabbed by a foreigner. The latter is in custody.
Mr. }lris.:lit will deliver an address at the opening of the new reference library at Biuningham, on the Ist of May next.

The York City Council on Wednesday, by 28 votes to 9, "refused to entertain" a motion in favour of the Sunday closing of public-houses. At the Highgate Police Court, on Wednesday, John Baker was biought up for final examination on the double charge -f wilful murder and burglary at Finchley. Tile prisoner was committed for trial on both charges. The Daily _Yews publishes a report that the general com- manding the Home District sent for Colonel Burnaby on his return from his balloon expedition, severely reprimanded him, and informed him that he had incurred the serious dis- pleasure of the Duke of Cambridge. Mr. Samuel Gurney, formerly M.P. for Penryn and Fal- mouth, died at Tunbridge Wells on Tuesday morning. He succeeded his father as president of the Aborgines' Protec- tion Society, and he had also been for many years treasurer of the Metropolitan Drinking Fountains Association. He was a member of the Society of Friends.

The competition for the Sterndale Scholarship took place at the Royal Academy of Music on Monday. There were seven candidates, and the Scholarship was awarded to George F. Crowther. In the competition for tha Parepa Rosa Scholarship there were 41 candidates, and the Scholarship was awarded to Kate Winifred Payne. A branch Free Library and Newsroom, erected by the Manchester Corporation in Campfield. Deansgate, was Opened on Wednesday by the Mayor. The new building—which, with the fittings, has cost £l2,ooo—contains over 18,000 volumes, and constitutes the seventh branch library erected by the Corporation.

The representatives of Mr. Waller, a comthercial traveller, who was thrown out of a cart and killed, the accident being, as it was alleged, caused by the wheel of the cart coming in contact with the metal of a tramway which was an inch or more above the granite paving, on Wednesday recovered £5OO as damages in an action against the North Metropoli- tan Tramways Company. At Bow-street Police Court, on Wednesday, Charles Bed- ford, who acted as a referee on the occasion of the recent prize fight in a chapel, was charged with aiding and abetting. Bedford read a statement giving the Marquis of Queens- bury 's rules, and declared that the gloves used were those used in previous boxing encounters. He told the men before commencing that if either of them broke the rules he should at once disqualify him. The affair was most honourably conducted by both men. He had surrendered himself in the interests of the public because of the perjury committed by the police. All the defendants were committed for trial. MUNIFICENT BEQUESTS TO PRESTON.—The trustees of the late Mr. E. R. Harris, prothonotary of Lancashire, have decided to make the following grants to churches out of the £5,000 set apart :—£3,000 to St. George's, Preston; £l.OOO to St. Matthew's, Preston ; £5OO to Lana'ridge Church; £5OO to St. Stephen's, Preston; and £250 to St. Mark's, Preston. They have approved plans for a new orphanage, to be built and endowed near Preston out of the same fortune. It will accommodate 150 orphans. The building will cost £25,000, and the endowment fund will be £74,000. The same trust establishes a technical school for Preston, and also erects a new free library and museum, the founda- tion stone of which the Prince of Wales is expected to lay at the guild festival in the first week of September. The sites for the various buidings are, as required by the will, provided for by the trustees. Another innovation has been made by the Prisons Com- missioners, and in the opinion of the Chairman of the Pres- ton Quarter Sessions (Mr. Higgin Q.C.), it is altogether un- called for and will be productive ,of great inconvenience. The form of the calendar has been so altered that it is diffi- cult to tell whether a prisoner is charged with felony or misdemeanour; and the learned Chairman not unreasonably expressed a wish that the Commissioners would consult those who had had years upon years of experience before they made such changes. Other magistrates concurred with Mr. Higgin, and it was decided to remonstrate with this new and reforming authority on their interference. It afterwards appearing that the calendar had to be paid for- 6d, a copy,—even by jurors, the Chairman expressed in warm terms his disgust with this regulation, and the Clerk of the Peace was instructed to prevent the sale of the calen- dar on the county property. ADULTERATION OF MILK AT SOUTHPORT.—At the Town Hall, on Wednesday morning, before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton) and several other magistrates, James Brown, milk- dealer, was charged with selling adulterated milk on the 28th February. Mr. J. H. Ellis, town clerk, appeared ia support of the information, It appeared that about a quarter-past ten o'clock on the morning of the date in question, William Beeston, inspector of nuisances, purchased from the defendant three half-pints of milk, and informed him that he had bought the purpose of being analysed. The certificate of the public analyst, Mr. Holland, showed that the milk had been adulterated to the extent of 10 per cent. —Defendant said he was not aware the milk was adulterated ; he sold it just as he had received it from the farmers. He had not added any water.—A fine of 40s. and costs was inflicted. —This is the second case of milk adulteration within the last fortnight. ALLEGED EXTENSIVE JEWELLERY FRAUDS.—On Wednes- day, at Birmingham, Thomas Jagger, jewel merchant, Bedford-road, Sandy, Bedfordshire, was Charged with an ex- tensive series of frauds, by which, it is alleged, he has obtained jewellery from various London and Birmingham firms to the value of £3,000. Mr. Alfred Peet, instructed by Mr. Rosenthall, of London, appeared for the prosecution, ' and stated that the prisoner was arrested on a warrant issued by the Londan police upoa a charge of obtaining several hundreds of gold watches from Augusta Rade, of London. A second warrant had been issued by the Birmingham magistrates for the prisoner's apprehension on other charges I of obtaining £2,000 worth of goods from several manufactur- ing jewellers in the town under false pretences, his repre- sentations being that he was a jeweller doing a most exten- sive trade, which would enable him to dispose of the goods in a single week. These representations were entirely false. The prisoner was apprehended on Tuesday by Detective- inspector Black. The London police were immediately communicated with, and on Wednesday Detective-sergeant Greet arrived from Scotland-yard. The magistrates handed over the prisoner to his charge for removal to London. A GOODS TRAIN ON FIRE.—An alarming fire occurred on Tuesday night on the Bolton and Wigan section of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway. A goods train of nearly twenty waggons, several of which were laden with cotton, was proceeding from Liverpool to Bolton, and when it was near Westhoughton station, about ten o'clock, it was dis- covered that three of the cotton trucks were on fire. The train was immediately brought to a stand, but as there is no water tank at Westhoughton, no means were available of ex- tinguishing the fire. A number of the burning bales were pitched on to the platform, and water thrown on them ; whi:e the train containing the remainder of the burning material was despatched to Lostock Junction, about a mile and a half distant. At this station the burning trucks were one after the other underneath the water tank, and after considerable exertion the flames were extinguished. About thirty bales of cotton were more or less seriously damaged, a large portion, indeed, being completely destroyed. In con- sequence of the fire the passenger train from Liverpool, due at Bolton at 10-9, was detained at Lostock Junction until about half-past 11, and passengers awaiting at Bolton to pro- ceed by this train to Manchester bad to be sent on by special train. It is not known positively how the fire originated, but it is supposed to have been caused by sparks from the engine.

TRADE NOTES. The Sheffield file grinders have made a demand for an advance of 10 per cent. On Monday notice was posted at all the North Wales col- lieries that the masters wohld reduce wages 5 per cent, after the 15th instant. The journeymen tailors of Wrexham went out on strike on Monday, failing to obtain a considerable increaase of wages:

A dispute between the employers and workmen has arisen in several of the shipbuilding yards at the South-end of Liverpool, and in consequence a number of the men in some branches are out of work. The ballot of the miners of the counts, of Durham, to ascertain if they would strike if the masters refused their demand of an advance of 20 per cent., has now been made known. Although the two-thirds majority has not been obtained, there is a decided preponderance for the strike. The number in favour of the strike is 11,000 against 9.000. The suspension is announced of Messrs. William WArthur and Co., commission agents and sugar merchants, Greenock, their liabilitias being stated at about £BO,OOO. The firm is said to have been for some time engaged in extensive raw sugar speculation. The assets are believed to be fairly good.

-lii consequence of the action taken by Lord Dudley's agent in reducing coal is. per ton, mimers' wages have been reduced 4d. per day. At 20 large collieries in Halesown, Rowley, and Old Hill districts, on Monday, the men re- solved to strike, and the whole of the collieries are now idle. Large numbers of employers are annoyed at the action of Lold Dudley's agent, as by the reduction in prices they experience great inconvenience in the execution of their contracts.

THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark-lane Express says: "The weather during the past week has been changeable. On cold undrained clays and on thin poor soils wheats continue to show some loss of colour, but on slund deep soils they hold their own remarkably well ; and the crops as a whole must be considered in an exceptionally favourable position for the first week in April. The later seed beds for barley being for the most part on strong soils, will not be first rate, as the land turned up cold and quickly became hardened by the drying winds. However, sowing progresses very favourably. A large breadth of barley and oats is above ground, and looking well. Some provincial exchanges have been sparingly supplied with native wheat, whilst in ethers deliveries have been ample; in all cases, however, scarcity of fine English wheat has been very prominent, and for such samples enhanced rates have been paid, especially during the early days of the week. In London, the trade for Eng- lish wheat has been quiet at unchanged prices. Flour has been in slow request at former prices, and barley and malt seem inclined to be cheaper. Other at ticks pass quietly ins° consumption without alteration in value. Foreign breadstuffs off stands has met with slow trade throughout the week." THE LANC(ASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES: MANCHES- TER, WEDNESDAY.—Both the coal and iron trades of this district continue depressed with prices gradually easing down to meet the market. Although it is only in excep- tional cases that there has been any actually announced reduction of list rates for coal this month, the general ten.

Idency of prices is downwards, and holders of stocks are in so many cases open to offers that the selling prices in the mar- ket are very irregular. At the pit mouth the ar erage latices I inay he given at about Sc. 6.1. to 9s. for best coals, Cis 6 I. ti. lis. for seconds house coal, ss. 63. to Bs. for common house coal, and ss. to ss. Gd. for steam and forge coals. Bulgy at the pit mouth averages 4s. Gd. to ss. per ton, and good slack 3s. 9d. to 4s. 3d., but there are inferior descriptions of slack to be bought at 2s. 9d. to 3s. 3d. per ton. The shipping trade continues very dull, with steam coal offering at Liverpool and Garston at exceedingly low prices.—In the iron market the business doing during the week has been very limited in extent. The firmer tone reported in some of the outside markets has not been responded to here, and to effect sales concessions upon current rates have to be offered. Lanca- shire makers of pig iron are quoting about 485., less 2--, for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, and district brands can be bought at about 475. to 475. 6d., less VI; but the inquiries coming into the market are as a rule only for small parcels, and the business doing on the basis of these figures is so limited as scarcely to give much value to the actual prices realised. Finished-iron makers are still kept tolerably well employed on old orders, but new business comes in only very slowly. Merchants and con- sumers appear to he running off their contracts as,far as pos- sible before replacing them, in the hope of bringing down prices; whilst makers, in view of the large consumption which is undoubtedly going on, and which must bring buyers into the market before long, are working off their orders rather than push for new business at present, and prices I remain at about £6 15s. to £6 17s. 6d., with £7 per ton as the nominal quotation of some of the makers for bars delivered into the Manchester district. DIE LABOUR MARKET.—The labour market remains on the whole in a fairly satisfactory condition, though in some districts the relation of employer and employed are some- what unsettled. In' Lancashire no agreement has been arrived at on the short-time proposals, and textile opera- tives are on the whole fairly engaged. From Belfast there , has been a significant emigration of a considerable party of I flax dressers to the United States. In the Leeds district mills are working full time. In the North of England there is a slight improvement in the steam coal-trade, and generally the engineering trades are specially busy. At Birmingham there is a fair amount of orders in the hard- ware branches, and at Manchester the building trades are again more active. In the metropolis some meetings of ,tem- porarily unemployed persons have been held, but there is no special depression in any of the leading industries. In the East of London the boot and shoe trade is still unsettled, but at Stafford and Leicester the same trade shows improve- ment. At Swansea the tin-plate manufacturers have been limiting the production, but throughout South Wales the ircn and steel trades remain busy. Railway works through- out the country are being pushed forward, and navvies and labourers are in good demand. Various new undertakings are projected in Austria and also in Italy. Advices from the United States show some lull in certain of the great in- dustries, but immigration continues on an unprecedented scale. In Florida railway construction is making consider- able progress.—Labour News.

div.head: -UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE.
div.p: -UNITED KINGDOM ALLIANCE.
PUBLIC MEETING AT RUNCORN.

On Monday evening, a public meeting under the auspices of the United Kingdom Alliance, was held in Bethesda Con- gregational schoolroom, Runcorn. The chair was occupied by Mr. T. R. Frith, and there was a fair attendance. The CHAIRMAN, who was heartily received, said be was glad to find that the friends of temperance in Runcorn were determined to push the battle to the gate, and make an ernest effort to give accurate information as to what the Per- missive Bill and United Kingdom Alliance really were. It was something over 30 years ago when he first became a member of the last named association. At that time be was but young, and he was much enamoured of the advantages which he considered would result to the:nation generally if , the alliance had their way in conducting the affairs of the country, so far as related to the liquor traffic. Since the alliance movement was started, certain changes had been made in the tactics of the council, possibly on the ground that it was wise when a man could not get a whole loaf to take half a one. He was of opinion that the United King- dom Alliance had shown wisdom in going in for what they could get, rather than waiting until tliey could obtain every- thing for which they asked. (Hear, hear.) He was sure that even in the case of their own town of Runcorn, local option would prove a very great benefit indeed, and that if they had it for a fortnight, they would wish to have its operation extended to a month, and then they would go in for it being continued twelvemonths. At the end of that time many a bright and noble woman would be found who would hold up her hand in favour of the operation of the Act being made perpetual. (Applause.) He knew a man who said "I can pass one or two publichouses, but when I have to pass three or four, I cannot resist the temptation, but I go in and get one glass, and when I have had that, I want more." It was the duty of all who truly loved their fellow men to see that the number of places where tempta- tions to drink were offered was reduced. Some said that it would be an act of injustice to remove publichouses, many of which had been purchased at a great expense. Now, they might depend upon it that England would never cl 7) an unjust act—that England which paid so many millions to liberate the slaves of Jamaica. (Applause.) In conclusion, Mr. Frith expressed a hope that they would give this ques- tion their serious consideration, and after they had done so, and discovered the truth, the justice, and the right of it, they would put their hands to the plough, and try to help on the good work. Let them do what little lay in their power to aid this movement, and then they would receive a blessing in their own souls through seeing those who were now addicted to drink brought to a better state of mind. (Applause)._

• . . Mr. S. C. BEcsErr moved the following resolution :—" That this meeting is convinced that the licensed liquor traffic is the great promoter of those national evils which the Prime Minister has declared to equal in magnitude the combined results of war, pestilence, and famine, and therefore most earnestly urges upon him the pressing necessity for Her Majesty's Government, without further delay, to initiate legislation which shall entrust local communities with the power of protecting themselves from the traffic in the manner twice recommended by the votes of the House of Commons."

Mr. Wm. SHAW, in seconding the motion, said it was something terrible to see the evil which drink was doing even in so small a town as Runcorn. They could not raise their voices too high, or speak with too much firmness on this all important question. He advised them to put their shoulders to the wheel of the drink traffic machine, and do their best to upset "the whole bag of tricks." (Laughter and cheers).

Mr. C. H. Mtnnev, in supporting the resolution, referred to the statement contained in it as to the opinion of the Prime Minister of the country of the effects of the drink traffic. Mr. Gladstone was no fanatic on this question, and his opinion was deserving of the most serious consideration on the part of all thoughtful men. It was about 50 years since the temperance movement began in this country. At one of the inaugural meetings a publican attended and made the sapient remark, as he thought, that if they did not take "a drop of something good," they would all be dead in 12 months! (Laughter.) The name of every publican and beerseller in the place where the meeting was held was taken down, and they numbered 42, against 17 members of the temperance committee then formed. Fifteen years after the members of the committee brought out the list and examined it, only to find that not a single publican or beerseller, whose name was originally placed upon it, was left alive! In 20 years from the formation of the original list it was again looked at, and it was seen that 14 out of the 17 members of the committee were still living. Those who started the temperance movement in the country found that they had not only to convince people it was a right one, but to do something with the object of doing something to do away with the temptations which were set up in the shape of public-houses and beershops by law, at every corner in their towns and villages. Under the circumstances, they were led to enquire whether it was right that a Christian Government should make a profit out of that which depraved and destroyed the people. There were many men who did not see their way to entirely give up taking intoxicating drink, but who were quite willing to help in doing some- thing to bring an influence to bear upon the Government which should cause them to sweep away all the public temptations placed in the path of men to entice them to drink. The United Kingdom Alliance was so constituted, as a society, that those who were not total abstainers could be members of it. They, however, considered it was pos- sible to proceed in the work of doing away with the traffic by steps, so that it was not necessary, if the people of Run- corn were ready to abolish it, that they should wait until those at Widnes were prepared to do the same. What they really required was the Permissive Bill, so that if the rate- payers desired, they could take the traffic into their own hands and stamp it out. Then there was the question of local option, which occupied a grand position, having last year been carried in the House of Commons by a majority of 42. They had also got over 20 members of Her Majesty's Government who were prepared to vote for this principle being put in force; and Mr. Gladstone bad stated that, just as soon as the way was clear, he would carry out some im- provement in the licensing system upon the lines laid down by Sir :Wilfrid Lawson. Runcorn occupied the position of being one of the most important towns in Mid-Cheshire, and it was a remarkable fact that the members for that division did not vote in favour of the ratepayers having the right to decide this matter in their own hands, as was provided by the principle of the local option, he supposed on the ground that they did not consider they were fit to be trusted with it, but that the magistrates were the only people who were capable of dealing with it. The people who lived in the division ought to place this matter prominently before their representatives in Parliament, so that they might take a different line of ac- tion when the question again came up for discussion. The speaker then gave some facts howing what success had attended the abolition of the liquor traffic in the state of Kansas, United States, the emigration and the railway receipts never having been so large as they were to-day. (Applause.) The resolution was carried unanimously.

Mr. J. D. Jcu•rEs considered the Alliance were acting very i wisely in holding such meetings as that n Mid-Cheshire, which was a benighted spot. (Laughter.) Indeed he h ,d nearly said it was "where Satan's seat is; but he would go so. i far as that, but simply say t was the hot-bed f Toryism. However, it must be patent to all who studied ti:e signs of the time that we were on the eve of what would amount to almost a political revolution. (Hear, hear.) T:,e. rotten boroughs would be disfranchised, and there would fellow that a redistribution of seats and the lowering of rtt. county franchise. This alteration would bring in a lot ..‘t

people who had never yet voted, but who were only too eage, to do so; and the work of the United Kingdom Alliance WASO ecitiiere Th-se faru:.e voters up to a proper point, so ib,,t when the props. tii:, cs sue, they might support the r'iglit man. He eek,ised teens when eny general election took place, to see to it liar ile,y orked the 'oracle so that they had upon the caucus a numbecof temperancemen, who would be able to "put gie screw on" the future members, in case they needed it. Luckily the supportersof temperance reformation were not so weak as in former days, or such suggestions from them would simply be received with the remarks that they might go to Jericho, or some other nice , place. He had pleasure in moving, "That this meeting most earnestly calls open the social reformers, friends of temper- ance, education, religion, and public order in the various constituencies throughout the United Kingdom, to render all possible aid to the Alliance and the various temperance organizations co-operating with it, so as more fully to arouse the conscience of the nation, and inilueve the -Electors to make a determined stand against its greatest social pest and curse, and to give united electoral support to such men and measures as will suppress the facilities and temptations of intemperance, or will confer upon the people the power to veto the issue of licenses for the sale of intoxicatinm liquors within their respective parishes and districts." He believed that the time would shortly be here when 3,000 men would be enfranchised in Runcorn, and he might say that that town and Northwich had it in their hands to say who should be the two future ineinbe s for Mid-Cheshire. Such being the case, the United Kingdom Alliance might do worse than send Sir Wilfrid Lawson on a little tour among: t the electors in these towns, and in that way the temperance people would be able to work up the necessary enthusiasm. (Applause.) Mr. BisBROwN seconded the motion, and contended that the licensing matters ought to be under the control of tne general body of ratepayers, instead of in the hands of the magistrates, as at present. 'These Magnates often in some towns permitted .public-houses to be put up in certain places where they were not needed, in spite of the protest of 70 or SO per cent of the ratepayers. Mr. JAMES WHITE, of Manchester, supported the resolu- tion, which was agreed to unanimously. The proceedings were brought to a close by the passing of the customary votes of thanks.

div.head: RUNCORN BOAR!) OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOAR!) OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fornightiy meeting took place at Dutton Work- house, on Tuesday afternoon, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon I3arclay. There were also present, the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Ashton (vice-chairman), Mclntyre, Fisher, Norman, Hazlehurst, Andrews, Weir, Challoner, Handley, Challoner, .Highfield, IN'hitlow, Rigby, Percival, Darbyshire, Jackson, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

THE INCREASE IN THE COUNTY RATE. The following communication was read in reference to this subject, which came before the Board : Clerk of the Peace's Office, Chester, 22nd March, 1882.—Dear Sir,—The increase in the county rate made at the last January ttiessio,s, as compared with the corresponding rate of the January Sessions of 1881, is caused by the „greater demands of the ap- proaching quarter, as compared with those of the same quarter in last year. I enclose the treasurer's estimates presented at the January Sessions, 1881 and 1882, and you will at once see why a three farthings rate is now required irstead of a farthing rate, as then.—Y, urs truly, THOMAS ROBERTS.—H. Linaker, Esq., clerk to the Runcorn Union, Frodshatn.

The DEPUTY CLERK explained that the particulars for- vcarded showed that £l,OOO extra had been spent on main roads, and the purchase of land at Upton, for the asylum, had cost £BOO. These were both items of increased expen- ditnre.
Mr. HAZLEIII7IIST thought the explanation quite satisfac- tory.
Mr. HA2s-DLEY (laughing): Pass it round the table; it is a wonderfully instructive document. (I...tighter.) Mr. RIGBY: Is there only one copy? The DEPUTY CLEnx: That is all.
Mr. RIGBY : I would have it posted up against a wall, and framed.
It was agreed that the necessary cheque for the amount of the county rate, which had been withheld, should be for- warded.
Mr. HANDLEY said that as this was the last meeting of the Board previous to the election, he had much pleasure in moving a hearty vote of thanks to their excellent chair- man.
Mr. WEIR seconded the motion, and in supporting it Mr. ASHTON said he thought that if there was one point on which they agreed, more than another, it was that they had a capital chairman.

The resolution was carried with applause, and appro- priately acknowledged by the Chairman. A similar compliment was paid to Mr. Ashton, the vice- chairman, on the motion of Mr 1 NORMAN, seconded by the CHAIRMAN.

The Rev. J. W. N. TANNER proposed a vote of thanks to their excellent Clerk, who always gape them very sound and thoroughly satisfactory advice on the numerous matters referred to his judgment. Mr. CHALLONER, in seconding the resolution, said he had known Mr: Henry Linaker for many years, and he believed it was an acknowledged fact that he was the best clerk pos- sessed by any Board of Guardians within many miles of that place. A more honourable man he did not know. Mr. HAZLEHURST supported the proposition, which was carried with applause. Mr. H. LENTAE.Rn, in responding, said: I will take this opportunity of saying that since I was appointed clerk of this Board-some 18 years age-it has always been my wish and intention to discharge the duties of the post not only with satisfaction to the Guardians, but to the ratepayers. Although I am connected with about 37 townships, and have to do with property in 30 out of those, I. should le ashamed to think that the fact of my being associated with those townships deteriorated from my ability to perform my duty to this Board, or equally prevented me doing my duty to the ratepayers. (Applause.) The list of the Graardians' attendance during the year was laid before the Board as follows:-Messrs. Rigby 19, J. Lowe 9, Tanner 23, Knowles 7, W. Lowe 1, T. Lowe 1, T. Massey 1, Mclntyre 15, Stokes 2, Stringer 4, Percival 3, Campkin 10, J. Ashton 23, Andrews 11, Challoner 12, Wright 8, G. Whitlow 6, Midwood 13, Tickle, Harrison, and Mountield 0, Jackson 14, .Darbyshire 21. R. Ashton 7, Pickering 9, W. Whitlow 4, W. Fisher 17, Handtey 21, Hazlehurst 16, Ntrman 21, Whittaker 14, Hiahfield 13, Baguley 3, Darhyshire 3, Acton 1, Weir 14, 'Broady 4, Canon Barclay 16, C. Mounfield 2, and Nield 6. This terminated the business.

div.head: UNITED METIIODIS r FREE CHURCH,
div.p: UNITED METIIODIS r FREE CHURCH,
WIDNES.

A missionary meeting in connection with the United Methodist Free Church Missions was held in this church on Monday evening. There was only a poor attendance, and Mr. Leadbetter presided. There were also present the Revs. F. Peters and Billington, and Mr. E. Gandy. The meeting having been opened with singing and prayer, The CHAIRMAN observed that missionary efforts were practical in their character, and said he did not agree with those persons who said the results obtained in the mission field were not worth the money expended. In China their missionaries had been the means of converting many to Christianity, and though their work in Africa had been ex- pensive, with little apparent advance, there was no reason to despond. Several of their most powerful and talented mis- sionaries had succumbed to the climate, amongst them that noble woman, Mrs. Wakefield; but who knew but that the butial places of those men might some day speak in much stronger language than any human tongue, and tell the black man how the white man had bravely dared to sail across the stormy ocean to tell them of the Lord and His Son, Jesus Christ.

The Rev. J. BILLINGTON read the report, from which it appeared that there had been an increase of 440 members during the year. The hurricane in Jamaica, about twelve months ago, had caused the society damage amounting to about £4,500, schools and chapels having been blown down lin great number. The Church in England and Australia had exhibited great sympathy, and had by a special effort I raised a sum which would do much to mitigate the conse- queuc,es of the disaster. For two years the society's mission station at Sierre Leone had been without a European mis- sionary, and those at present in charge there were deserving of sympathy for the noble manner in which they had strug- gled against their adverse circumstances. The Rev. Thomas Truscott would shortly, however, be departing for the station. The total receipts of the society for the past year was £lB 274 16s. 4d., and the expenditure, with the sum of £327 16s. 11d, due to the bank, was the same amount. The Runcorn circuit, which included Widnes, had contributed £ll Os Pd. Of this sum Wines had raised £3 12s. 2,id. In conclusion, Mr. Billington made an appal for subscrip— tions.

Mr. E. GANDY, in the course of a brief address, said he had always had great pleasure in advocating the claims of the missionary society, and in doing all that lay in his power to further its aims. At the present time we seemed to stand on a more neighbourly platform than 'ever we did before, and the world was more compact than at any previous period of its history. The facilities of communication and the in- terchange of commerce were such that we ought to be thankful that the genius of our fellows had been directed in this channel, as the nearer the nath.ns were brought to- gether the brighter and better would be our days. A more helpful feeling would be engendered. Missionary work also tended to the same end, and to bring about that period, as Bobby Burns said, whim "man to man shag brudder be all the wide world over."
The Rev. T. Peters having addressed the nv Wing, a col- lection was taken on behalf of the society, and the rnecting concluded with the singing of the Doxoio2y.

GOLBORNE. , NAR ROW ESCAPE AT GOLBORNE t4TA.TION.—On Monaay an elderly woman, going to Wigan by the 12-15 noon trains had a narrow escape of being killed through tbe present system of level-crossing at Go!borne station. The up mail had barely passed throu;.;ll when the down Express came dashing up just as the woman was turning to cross the line at the end of the white railings recently filmed for the pro- tection of passengers. She would inevitably have beea killed (the noise of one train drowning the approach of Ike , other), bad not Mrs. Mapei, wife of Dr. Mapei, been provi- dentially behind the woman and pulled Let back from under the very front of the express. If exit and entrance were made by steps from the bridge to the station, crossing the line would be at pissengers' own risk, and would not be at- tended by the dangers and narrow escapes which under the present system, every day present themselves to the old and unitiated.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
A Standard Vienna telegram says the Herzegovina insur- rection is considered virtually ended.

According td latest advices from Mentone, the Duke of Albany continues to improve in health. The d!spute in the South Staffordshire and East Worces- tershire coal trada.is now at an end. On Thursday morning the Dublin police made another seizure of arms, and arrested two persons.

The men imprisoned in the Killingworth Colliery owing to an accident in the shaft were all rescued late on Wednes- day An authoritative contradiction is given to the report that the Archbishop of Canterbury contemplates resignation of his office.

The trial of Kinsella for the Tighe-street murder in Dub• lin was concluded on Thursday, when the prisoner was found guilty. Sentence was deferred. The Earl of Stamford and Warrington is suffering from severe illness at his Leicestershire seat, Bradgate House, near Leicester. It has been deemed necessaty to summon a Lon- don physician. The watnan, Annie Gouldthorpe, wife of a pawnbroker in Manchester, who is charged with attempting to poison her husband while administering medicine to him,was on Thurs- day committed for trial. Margaret Farrell and George Holborn Tarelli were con- victed at Hull on Thursday of fraud on a Manchester firm, and were sentence to nine months' imprisonment. They had been carrying on an extensive "long arm" business. The young man Harrison who is charged with the murder of Lucy Sands, at Workington, was brought bef&e the magistrates on Thursday and again remanded. During the hearing a witness was given into custody on charges of per- jury. In the Whitehall Chapel, on. Thursday, the customary Royal charities were distributed to 63 aged men and as many aged women, the number of each sex corresponding with the age of her Majesty. More than 1,300 persons were ' relieved.

The Flintshire police have resumed guard, as usual, over the Premier at Hawarden. limas at first assumed that he would not require protection, but, on reconsideration, the Chief Constable of Flintshire decided to send a posse of police to Hawarden during the recess. The first case of a volunteer being pensioned is just re- ported from Aberdeen. James M‘Donald, late of C Company, Ist Elginsbire, is to have sixpence a day for life, in con- sequence of injuries received at the Royal review last August.

Lord Roseberry on Thursday performed the ceremony of unveiling the Burns stab° at Dumfries. The freedom of the burgh was conferred upon the noble lord in recognition of his zealous attention to national affairs, and especially of his valuable assistance to measures having for their object the promotion of interests beneficial to Scotland. The arrangements for the Conservative demonstration in Liverpool have now been finally announced. On Wednes- day next the Marquis of Salisbury and Sir. Stafford North' cote will speak at a Conservative banquet, and on the follow- ing day will address a mass meeting to be held in Hengler's Circus. The noble Marquis an Sir Stafford Northcote have also promised to be present at a luncheon of the Junior Conservative Club on Friday, when they are expected to deliver political addresses. The Earl of Crawford and Balt- arres has issued a circular from Dun Echt with regard to the con. t " Wells," which was recently discovered in America, and which he thinks is likely to be one of the great events of the season. Before the middle of June it will be 2,000 times larger than when it appeared on the 10th March last. It will not only In visible, but will, it is expected, add greatly to the tempera- ture of the summer months.

Chester is promised the double honour 'of a visit from the Prince of Wales, and also from the Duke of Cambridge, who, in his official capacity of Commander-in-Chief, intends to be present atsome yeomanry inspections. The Prince of Wales's visit may also be said to be of An official character, as he will attend the inspection of the Earl of Chester's Yeomanry Cavalry, of which he is colonel. The time of the visits will be about the middle of May.

A return of the number of licenses far the sale by retail of any kind of intoxicating liquors, not to be consumed udon the premises, granted in England and Wales from 1877 to 1881 has been issued. This shows that in 1877 the total number of excise licenses granted amounted to 21,729 while in 1881 the total was 29,085. The retailers of beer had increased from 8.394 to 13,793; the sellers of table beer were 150 in 1877, and 81 in 1881. There were no retailers of beer and wine up to 1879, but in 1881 there were 915. The Chief Secretary for Ireland has written a letter to Mr. Gorst, M.P., in which he states that it was his impres- sion that the time when he was to make his statement in reference to the condition of Ireland was after Easter. He says that he was in the House when Mr. Gorst gave his notice, but that there was some conversation at the time and he did not kar the word "to-morrow." It was, therefore, with consid'REable surprise that he read in the papers the re- port of Tuesday's proceedings in Parliament. AMERICAN CITIZENS IMPRISONED IN IRELAND.

A brief digest of the correspondence between the English and American Governments on the subject of the imprison- ment of American citizens in Ireland under the Protection of Life and Property Act, has been published. President Arthur, it is stated, earnestly and repeatedly requested that these persons should be brought to trial, but the State Department does not think it would be preper to disclose at present the communications which have passsd between the two Governments. It is admitted that a despatch of the 4tln inst. announcing tat five Americans were still imprisoned was erroneous, the State Department having been advised of , their release.
THE GOVERNMENT AND ,THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC

A deputation from the Birmingham Auxiliary of the I United Kingdom Alliance waited on Thursday upon Mr. Chamberlain, at Highbury, near Birmingham, to present a statement of the views of the Alliance with respect to any measure that might be proposed by the Government affect- ing the liquor traffic, and also to urge the Government to catry out the principle of local option in harmony with the resolutions which have been endorsed on two occasions by the House of Commons. The interview, which was private, occupied about two hours, and a free isterchange of views took place, with which the deputation ,were apparently satisfied.

div.head: DEATEI OF A PAUPER BARONET.
div.p: DEATEI OF A PAUPER BARONET.

At a meeting of the .St. Saviour's (Southwark) Board of , Guardians on Thursday the death was announced of Sir Horatio Henry Wraxall, Bart., who had for some time been chargeable to the Union as a pauper. The deceased died in Wandsworth Lunatic Asylum, he having been admitted to that institution on the Ist of April, 1851, the cause of death being general paralysis. It appears that the deceased had been for many years in unfortunate circumstances, and latterly had fallen into a complete state of destitution. He followed the profession of a racing man for many years, and some six or ten years ago resided at Boulogne, where repeated losses on the turf appear to have reduced him to penury. Since then he has several times figured in police courts for obtaining goods under false pretences, once for allowing his name to appear as a director of a company and ordering goods for which he was unable to pay. Towards the end he led a most precarious existence, and was even in debt to cue of the members of the St. Saviour's Board of Guardians. The title now becomes extinct.

div.head: WORKHOUSE SCANDAL.
div.p: A WORKHOUSE SCANDAL.

scandalous affair has occurred at Oldham. It came Out at a meeting of the Board of Guardians there on Wed- nesday evening that a pig at the workhouse had been seized with illness, supposed to be pleuro-pneumonia, and had been killed by direction of the medical officer, who further ordered that the carcase should be burned. A meeting of the Guardians confirmed this order, but it is alleged that three of their number remained at the workhouse till be- tween eight and nine o'clock in the evening and then drove away with the carcase and sold it to a pork butcher at Middleton for 255. It is stated that after the transaction became the subject of gossip one of the trio, hanged over the money to the Master of the Workhous9. At the meet- ing on Wednesday evening the other Guardians expressed the opinion that their three colleagues had acte4 in a most improper manner. The sanitary authorities concerned do not appear to have taken any action in the matter as yet.
