of which Mr. L. Stanley drew attention to the diffi- culties under which Board School pupil teachers laboured in not being able to obtain admission to oertain training colleges without having to undergo a religious test, so to speak. These colleges, which re- ceive over £lOO,OOO a year in grants from the national Ifund, are all of them denominational in their cliar- actor, andfit is therefore reqiiisite either to provide other colleges of an undenominational deseription, or to remove the causes for objection very properly urged against the denominational institutions. The con- sciences of parents who send their children to a denominational school are protected by the State, and by a purity of reasoning it is only fair that pupil teachers desirous of entering a denominational achool should have their consciences protected in the same way. This difficulty could be got rid of by allowing School Boards to establish training colleges for their own teachers, and sooner or later that no doubt will be done, but meanwhile the objections complained of must be removed in order that the teachers from the denominational and boarl schools may be placed on an equality. Tory like Lord George Hamilton manifested alarm at the new code, and predicted that if adopted it would result in affording the:children of middle classes parents a secondary education in an elementary school contrary to the spirit of the Education Act. As Mr. Mundella re- marked, however, the noble lord only saw a "monster of his own creation." On the preparation of the new code, which greatly favours the teachers, the greatest care has been bestowed, and any altera- tions which have been made has been with the view of securing thoroughness in the teaching and obviating " cramming." Payment by results is still to be adhered to, but these are to have a more searching test applied to them. The third o matter referred to, and that the most gratifying, was the education esti- mates themselves, on which as we have previously shown there is an increase, though considering the marvellous results achieved in the advancement of the education of the masses there is not much cause for complaint. It is rather a cause for thankfulness that the Education Act is doing so much. The estimatas are fdr £2,749,863 as cempared with £2,683,958, for the preceding year, showing an inerease of £65,905, most of which we are told is caused by an increase in the Government grants. Last year the per centage cf passes in the "three R's" was 81 82, the highest number of passes we have ever had in one year. In some individual cases, of course, the per centage has been higher; and as an evidence of what can be done with a good staff of teachers we may mention that at one school 99 per cent., and in another 98i per cent. of the scholars presented for examina- tion passed. These are results which had been deemed almost impossible. But satisfactory as is the state of education' in England and Wales it compares very unfavourably :with that of Scotland, where the total per centage of passes reached 883. On the whole the past year's educational results in the United Kingdom show that there has not been any year since the passing of the Act in 1870, in which there is to be found more satisfactory evidence of solid progress;. and the tax-payer will not begrudge the cost for it is returned to him indirectly,—in the decreased amount demanded off him for the main- tenance of paupers and criminals. But beyond this the tone of society generally is elevated by the dissemi• nation of education, and the improvement in this res- pect is most marked.

div.head: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.

The Tories scored a "moral victory" on Friday last in East Cornwall; the Liberal victory was something more cubstantial. Although the representatism of the constituency remains unchanged, I claim that in the recent contest there has been a decisive triumph for Liberalism. I readily admit—because I can do no other—that there has been a falling off in the aggregate Liberal vote, while the aggregate Tory vote has increased; but the means m:hereby that result has been obtained are important factors to be remembered. The Conservative candidate was the very strongest that could have been put forth. He had represented tile consti- tuency before, and from his family connection with the county was a general favouThe by both parties. He had also the advantage of being first in the field. Mr. Acland, on the other hand,was best known further north, though he had some slight connection with the county; and he was rather late in entering upon the contest. From the moment that he did so enter, however, the screw was put upon all Mr. Tremayne's friends, and the party generally tried to fasten upon Mr. Gladstone and his Cabinet a sympathy with Mr. Bradlaugh's atheistical views. The Liberal candidate even, did not escape being classed as an Atheist. It is not difficult to understand how with such a character he should be looked upon with something like holy horror by those who knew no better, and that he would suffer in his candidature in consequence. After all, however, Mr. Acland has triumphed over his adversaries, and he has taken his seat in Stephen's, where he will be something more than an ornament.

Some of the London correspondents of the Irish news- papers, and a few of the Irish members of Parliament as well, have for some time back made pretty free with the name of Mr. Mitchell Henry, who, though returned for Gal- way as a Home/ Ruler, has felt it his daty to dissociate himself from the active section of that party and to give a general support to the Government in their policy. This has irritated Mr. Sexton and his friends so much that they have availed themselves of every opportunity to annoy the hon. member by representing that his constituents are anxious to turn him out, and calling upon him to resign. This, however, has had no effect, and more recently other tactics have been resorted to. An endeav our is now being made to show that the Government are anxious to shower honours upon him for what he has done, and the latest rumour of a London corre- spondent of an Irish journal is that Mr. Henry is about to be raised to the Peerage as Lord KYlmore. More unlikely taings have happened, certainly. The Pall Mall Gazette gave further publicity to the rumour, and in a letter to that journal the hon. member hints that it published a liTnited piece of information. He says "Not only one, but all the Irish members who voted with the Government on Thursday are to be raised to the peerage, and they are also to receive grants from the public purse to enable Ihem to support their now dignity. In this way Mr. Gladstone expects to over- come the vexatious opposition of the House of Lords to his Irish policy, while he depends upon the cloture for dealing wita the no-rent gentlemen who will succeed them in the Commons." Mr. Mitchell Henry says further that he first set the report rolling, and adds that the Pall Mall has been heavily bribed to give it currency. After this happy mode of dealing with the subject, Mr. Mitchell Henry's late col- leagues need not thiglr they will succeed in getting him out of temper by any of their moves. I am in a position to inform my readers that there is no probability of Mr. Bradlaugh being driven into the Bank- ruptcy Court. This is what his opponents are aiming at, but they are bound to fail. From a "usually well-informed quarter "—to use the phrase of the London correspondents —I learn that last week, immediately after the decision in Mr. Bradlaugh's case, five members of Parliament waited upon him u and offered him .£lOO each for twelve months, without interest, and as much longer as he required it. The £5OO was subsequently paid into court. It is scarcely necessary to say that Mr. Newdegate was not one of the members. Unless the last-named gentleman is possessed of the wealth of Crcesus, I should not be surprised to find him in the bankruptcy court before the hon. member for North- ampton. Mr. Newdegate is respoesible for the common informers' costs, and as it is generally believed no portion of these can be recovered—even although the defendant has been ordered to pay the fine—there must be a tidy score run up. Mr. Newdegate's Tory friends have been ready enough to back him with their voices, they will not show as much alacrity, in opening their purses. On the other hand, the masses who have supported Mr. Bradlaugh in his successes at Northampton will not desert him in his defeats in the law courts. FLACCUS.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 8, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 8, 1882.

ACCIDENT TO MR. ANNETT, OF RUNCORN. Tuesday morning, Mr. Annett, master of Holy Trinity Schools, Runcorn, fell from his bicycle in Heath-road, and hurt his head rather seriously. RIIM.TCORN COUNTY COURT.-At this court on Tuesday be- fore Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, and Mr. E. J. Nichol- son, registrar, there were heard 25 judgment summonses, 63 original plaints, and four adjourned plaints —Mrs. Millington, grocer, High-street, sued Thomas Davies, blacksmith, Handley's-fields, for £ll 3s. sd. for goods supplied. Plain- tiff proved the amount to be owing, and defendant, in defence, made some allegations against her character.—His Honour: Have you any witness? Defendant: Honour (warmly): Your defence is a most seandalous and offensive one for which there is no witness before the court. You have no real answer to the claim, and you come here and traduce the plaintiff's character.—Mr. Hitchen, on be- half of the plaintiff, asked or judgment for £1 per month. —Defendant: I can't and I sha'n't pay.—His Honour: You had better take care what language you use in this court.— Judgment was given for 15s. a month.

A BILL TRANSACTION: IMPORTANT DECISION.—An important deClision respecting the alteration of a bill, after acceptance, has been given in the Chancery Division, by Mr. Justice Fry. The bill was drawn by Messrs. J. Knight and Co., of Wi Ines, and accepted by Ed. Edwards, a Welsh farmer at Cowen, who said that the amount on the face of the bill when he accepted it was £22 25., but that it bad subse- quently been altered to £222 25., and in this form it had been paid to Messrs. Knight and Co.'s bankers, who de- manded from Mr. Edwards the latter amount. The bankers ccntended that Mr. Edwards' plea of an alteration subse- quent to acceptance should not be taken, inasmuch as there was spice enough left between the £ and the 22 2s in which .to make the alteration to £222 25., and there was also spice enough before the words "Twenty-two pounds " in which to insert the words "Two hundred and," and the stamp on the bill was sufficient to cover £3OO. The learned judge held that the bankers had received the bill on the credit of Messrs. Knight and Co., that they had made no enquiry of Mr. Edwards respecting its accuracy, that Mr. Edwards had not been guilty of negligence, and that the loss must there- fore fall on the bankers, who would have their remedy against the persons giving them the bill. Having regard, however, to the importance of the matter, he was willing to allow the bankers 14 days in which to lodge an appeal if they were so disposed. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was field at the Board Offices, Bridgewater-street, on Wed- nesday morning. Mr. John Simpson presided, and there were present the Bev. W. Fennelly,r„Messrs. Jas. Pritchard, Richard Lea, Peter Briscoe, Thos. Ncrman, and Rigby (clerk). The Clerk remarked that after paying all accounts for the half-year the Board had a balance of £3O at the Bank, and it was proposed to issue as usual a precept for £2OO for the next half-year, at the end of which it was probable there would be a balance of £3O or £4o.—Mr. Pritchard proposed that a precept for £2OO be issued to the overseers.—Mr. Norman seconded, and the motion was car- ried.—Mr. T. Bowyer, the school attendance officer, pre- sented the returns from the public elementary schools for March, which showed certified Government accommodation 2,323, number on rolls 2,818, average attendance 20924, average attendance for March 1831 1851-9, for the year 1874 1,252, accommodation in excess of average attendance 2307, number on rolls in excess of accommodation 495. These figures show an increase in the average attendance as compared with the corresponding period of last year of 240.6, and compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, an increase of 840-4. Total number in attend- ance at private schools under 9d. per week 66. At the com- mittee meeting held on the 15th ult., he reported 78 parents for the irregular attendance of their children at school. 47 parents appeared before the committee in answer to their notices,4 applications were made for half-tine and granted; 5 applied for school fees, and the fees of 12 children were recommended by the committee to be paid by the Board of Guardians. The remaining cases were adjourned, the parents being duly cautioned.—The Board then considered the 25 applications which had been received for the post of schoolmistress at Mill Brow School, and five selections were made. The appointment will be made next week.—This was the whole of the business.

FATAL HOIST ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.- —Mr. T. J. Ridg- way, coroner, held an inquest at the Lion Hotel, Runcorn, on Wednesday, touching the death of Charles Watson, a chemical wo.iks' labourer, 16 years of age.--John Watson, 9, New-street, identified the body as that of his son.—Jesse Hand, 70, Shaw-street, labourer, deposed that he knew the deceased. They worked together at" Johnson's" soapery in Runcorn. On Tuesday morning the deceased and he were working together. They had a wagon and pushed it near to a hoist in the works which they wanted to use. When they were near • the hoist he saw Samuel Lunt and Thomas Molyneux put a loaded wagon on the cage of the hoist, and he saw Lunt move the handle of the hoist in order to get the steam up to work it. There was not steam enough to put the wagon far, and Lunt dropped the wagon again and he then saw Lunt move the handle again as though shutting the steam off. He then went away, and Molyneux also went away. Witness heard Lunt say that it (meaning the hoist) would not take thA' wagon up. As soon as Lunt went away the deceased said "let's try and pull the wagon off so that we can put ours on." Witness replied, "all right," and went and got hold of the wagon in front and the deceased went to the other end. Witness pulled at the wagon and the deceased pushed, and just as it got partly off the cage of the hoist, the hoist went up and took the deceased up with it. In going up the wagon got pitched off and the deceased slipped down in the cage, and went up. itness had to spring out of the say of the wagon. Some men came to the assistance of the deceased. He thought the hoist went up because the steam had not been propezly shut off. There was no particular man to work the hoist. Deceased was witness's foreman and worked the hoist for their wagon. He did not try whether the steam was shut off nor did the deceisecl.—Thomos Lightfoot, 'foreman at the Run- corn Soap and Alkali Company's works, saidthat on Tues- day he was near where the deceased and last witness were working. He heard a wagon fall, and went to the hoist. He saw the cage at the top and one of the bars of wood forming part of the hoist. He got assistance and got deceased out. Ho was dead, and was very badly injured. His head and neck, and breast were injured. The men who put the wagon on the hoist out to have seen that the steam was shutoff. There was no one person in charge of the hoist. If the lads had looked at the lever on the hoist they could have told whether the steam was shut off. It was the deceased's duty to hoist his wagon up, and he had a full knowledge of the hoist.—Samuel Lunt, who after being cautioned was sworn, said he helped to put the wagon on the hoist and when he had put the wagon on he turned the steam on and found the hoist would not work. He then went with his mate to get some more stuff. He left the steam on thinking that by the time they returned the hoist would havelifted the wagon up. He had done so in similar cases before. He did not see the lads about when he and his mate went away.— A verdict to the effect that the deceased was accidentally killed through the incautious use of a steam hoist was re- turned. ,

SINGULAR ACTION BY A CHAPEL KEEPER AT RUNCORN.— On Tuesday at the Runcorn County Court before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, Wm. Clare, formerly chapel keeper at the Aston Wesleyan Chapel, sued Mr. John Frodsham) representing the trustees of this place of worship, for 19s. Bd. made up as follows :—Paraffin oil, 10s. Bd.; lamp glasses, is. 4d. ; repairing back-yard door, is.; cleaning school three weeks at Is. 31. per week, 35. 9d.; and income tax 2s. 11d. —The plaintiff, in answer to his Honour, slid Mr. John Frodsnam ordered him to get the oil. He was engaged to look after the chapel by Mr. John Frodsham, who told him that whatever materials he found would be paid for. He had purchased the four lamp glasses because the others were hroken.—His Honour: Who cleaned the chapel ?—Plaintiff: The cleaning of the schools was ordered by Mr. Frodsham in the bargain.—What was the bargain? We were the chapel keepers, and we had to keep it in order.—His Honour (sharply): You first say it was the chapel and now you say it was the school and the chapel; which was it?—lt was the school and chapel.—Cross-examined by Mr. Hitchen, who represented Mr. Frodsham : His house rent was £7 3s , and £3 was to be deducted for looking after the chapel. The reason the charges he claimed were not deducted was be- cause he hadn't the bill when he paid the rent to Mr. Frod- sham. There hal been an action against him in the War- rington County Court by the trustees of the chapel. but it was compromised by his paying £2 lOs , but it eid not in- clude the settlement of the present claitn,—The plaintiff's wife corroborated his statement as to the manner in whick they were engaged.—For the defence Mr. Hitchen submitted there was no case against the trustees as trustees. and said when analysed it was found to be a "make up." The plaintiff was sued in the Warrington County Court by the trustees who dvished to obtain possession of the house, the trustees claiming double rent, but a settlement was made which was understood to include all claims between the parties. He should prove that the statement by the plain- tiff to get any thing he liked, and charge the trustees was not true. When he was engaged the plaintiff was distinctly told that everything required for the chapel would be got by the chapel stewards, and he .was on no account to obtain anything without direct orders. He had ample oil supplied, and the cleaning of the school was included in his engage- ment.—Mr. Frddsham (called) confirmed the advocite's. statement, and said he clearly stated when he engaged Clare that he should not allow anything except ordered by him- self. The bill for oil for a whale year only amounted to about 3s. or 3s. 6d.—Plaintiff Did you find any timber for lighting the fire? There was nothing at all said about light- ing fires. You were engaged to light the fires.—Plaintiff: And where was the timber? Witness evaded giving a direct answer to this question.—His Honour: Will you sir, answer the question or I must order you out of court. Witness: I didn't find the wood.—His Honour: Why didn't you answer the question instead of wasting I my time here.—The Rev. Jno. Nowell, superintendent of the circuit, and Mr. Thomas Norman gave evidence that the settlement in the former county court case was understood to include all claims.—His Honour said the receipt only showed settlement of rent and costs, but still there was the obvious observation that plaintiff compromised the matter' for £2 103, which he actually paid, while at that time the plaintiff seemed to say he had a claim of 19s Bd. against the trustees. If this had been a genuine claim then was the time it should have been produced. He must give judgment for the defendants with costs.

INSPECTION Or THE WIDNES POLICE.—This annual inspection took place on Monday. The Inspecting Officer (the Hon. Captain Legge) was accompanied by Colonel Moorsom, chief constable of the county, and Superinten- dent Barker (of Prescot and Widnes). On parade were Inspector Barnett, five sergeants, and 26 policemen ; and we hear that the Insp(cting Officer expressed himself in favour- able terms as to the condition of the cells, the books, and the appearance of the men.

RUNCORN CAMDEN IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—On the evening of the 31st ult., a lecture was delivered in connec- tion with this class by Mr. John Le Couteur, on "Lost Israel found." Mr. W. J: Shore presided, and there was a good attendance. The lecturer gave a sketch of the Anglo- Israel theory, of which so much has of late been written by Mr. Hine, Sharon Turner, and others, and which has been terribly ridiculed within the last month by " Verax," the editor of the Manchester Examiner (Mr. Dunckley, who was at one time pastor of the Baptist chapel off Chapel-street, Salford). The old arguments which have been so frequently. laid before the public were dwelt upon at length. The lec- turer treated his subject in an interesting style; and at the close a vote of thanks was passed to him, op the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Joseph Speakman. WIDNES AND Goon Fatosi.-7—The streets of Widnes, yesterday, were comparatively quiet, as the beautiful weather appears to have tempted the great army of toilers, with which the town abounds, to wend their way to fresh fields and pastures new. What few trains left the two sta- tions were well filled with passengers, who appeared in capital spirits at the ilea of getting away from their smoky daily surroundings. The Welsh Wesleyans at Cornwall - street, held their annual tea party, and a similar gathering took place at the Primitive Methodist chapel, Hutchinson- street, the Rev. J. Morton, of Warriagton, being announced to preside. The Wesleyan Methodists at Albert-road, had a meeting; and in the evening the Amalgamated Society of Railway ' Servants had their annual tea and ball at the Volunteer Hall.

GOOD FRIDLY IN RUNCORN.—Yesterday the weather in Runcorn and the neighbourhood was of a description favourable to holiday making, and it was taken advantage of to the fullest extent. The sun shone brilliantly, and the only disadvantage was the fact that the wind was lather too northerly. Hundreds visited the town from the surround- ing districts, and a constant stream of passengers wended their way to and fro upon the great bridge which spans the Mersey. A number of people left Runcorn for Liverpool, Warrington, and Manchester, though in order to do this they had to cross to Widnes, as not a single train, with he ex- ception of the one which carries the newspapers from Lon- don, left the station—a state of things which we hope time will remedy. Divine service was held at the various churches, and many of the Nonconformist places of worship, though the Dissenters in this district do not observe the day with that strictness which prevails amongst many of those who worship according to the usages of the Church of England. The members of the salvation Army, under Staff Captain Barker, met at six o'clock in the morning, for the purpose of "taking in ammunition for the day." At half-past ten a service known by the name of "a captain of fire" was held. At half-past two "the King's own blood and fire warriors" opened fire on the inhabitants of Widnes; at five o'clock they had a monster tea party in the Foresters' Hall; at seven, " fireing " was resumed is the Market Place, when, in the words of their dramatic bill, those who were " wounded " were taken to the Hallelujah Hospital—the Foresters' Hall—there to have their injuries attended to. It will be seen from these statements that the men belonging to General Booth's army are no feather bed soldiers, A number 9f tea parties were held by the various denominations, and brief addresses were delivered; bat none of them was of any general public in- terest.

The will (dated February 21, 1880), with a codicil (dated February 23 following), of Mr. William Harrison Ainsworth, late of St. Mary's-road, Reigate, who died on January 3rd last, was proved on the 24th ult. by Charles Heaton Hide, the acting executor, the personal estate ex- ceeding £4,000. The testator leaves certain furniture and effects at 'Hurstpierpoirt to his daughter Fanny for I:fe, then to his daughter Mrs. Ann Blanche Swainson for life, and afterwards her three children, and he in tkes no further provision for his said daughters and his daughter Emily Mary, having already made • ample provision for them by settlement ; to his executor twenty guineas; ard• the house- hold furniture, &c., at his residence, to his wife, Mrs. Sarah Ainsworth. The residue of his real and personal estate is to be held upon trust for his wife for life, and then for his daughter Clara.—lllustrated London News.

GOOD FRIDAY AT WAR RlNGTON.—Business was entirely suspended in Warrington yesterday, being Good Friday, and and the day was observed as in previous years. In the morning services were held in the episcopal churches, and the Rev. J. Eglinton, superintendent Wesleyan minister/ preached in Bold-street Chapel. The majority of the towns- people regarded the day as one of pleasure, and large num- bers of persons left town by road and rail for the numerous pleasure esorts in the neighbourhood, the more popular places being Liverpool, Minchester, and Frodsharn. As to the weather, the pleasure seekers could not have been more highly favoured. Throughout the day the sun shone brilliantly in a cloudless sky, and a refreshing breeze pre- vailed, the day being one of the finest that has been experienced for a long time past. Those who remained in town found pleasure in strolling through the park and gardens, where the trees and shrubs are bright with the foliage just breaking into life, or along the binks of the river where the fields have assumed their most verdant garb. In the evening the missionary meeting was held in Bold- street Wesleyan chapel, and the day passed very quietly. WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS . —Wednesday, (befve Messrs. G. Artingstall and P. Stubbs).—Thomas Appleton pleaded guilty to being drunk in a highway in Orford on the 19th March, and he was fined ss. and costs. —Edward Ashton, for being drunk in Penketh on the 18th March, was mulcted in the same amount.—Ellen Greenall, for being drunk in Bakers-lane, Penketh, on the 19th March, was ordered to pay the Costs.--4lenry Grace was summoned by Edward Chester, sen., for breaking down a wooden fence, and also with breaking an earthenware vessel, the damage being estimated at Ils. 6d. Ihe offence was said to have been committed on the 19th March. From the statement of the complainant, it appeared that the question was one for the County Court rather than a magisterial inquiry, and the case was dismissed because the magistrates had no jurisdic- tion. The parties, it may be added, were neighbours, and lived in Manchester-road.—Patrick O'Brien, of Newton, (for whom Mr. Davies appeared), for indecent behavior, was fined 40s. and costs.—John Wilkinson Colley, of Sankey, pleaded guilty to stealing a brass scoop and a butcher's steel from the shop of Mr. John Lawley, Sankey Bridges, on the the 31st March, and also with having assaulted P.C. Philip whilst apprehending him. Prisoner, who is an old offender, was sent to gaol for three months with hard labour.

THE MANCHESTER, LIVERPOOL, AND NORTH LANCA- SHIRE AGRICULTURAL SrICIETY.—The journal and prize list of this society is now published and on sale. A copy has been sent us, and we have pleasure in directing atten- tion to its contents, which are of special interest to agricul- turists. In the first few pages the names of the local committee for the forthcoming show, at Preston, on sth, 6th, 7th, and Bth September, are given; and these are followed by the prize list for 1882, with the rules and regu- lations under which the prizes will be awarded. The premiums offered are, it is gratifying to note, quite equal to those given in previous years. Following the prize list are the inspectors' reports and awards of prizes for best cultivated farms as made last year, and the repoNl of the council of the society, as submitted to the annual meeting held at Warrington in November last, is also printed. An abstract of the receipts and payments for the year is among the contents, together with a comparative statement of show-yard receipts and entries for exhibition from 1861 to 1881 inclusive; and the reports on the state of agriculture in the north-eastern division of the society's district, extracts from an essay on the manufacture of butter, the report on dairy trials' and other articles, are deserving of attention and careful perusal by all engaged in agricultural pursuits. A great deal of labour has evidently been bestowed upon the preparation of the journal, and pains taken to make it as attractive as possible. INTERESTING PRESENTATION AT WARRINGTON. Owing to failing health Mr. Peers Brimelow, who for upwards of 30 years bad been in the employ of Messrs. Rylands Bros., Church-street, had been compelled to sever his connection with the works, and on Monday evening he was the recipient of a gratifying testimonial from his late fellow workmen. The presentation was made at the Ring 0' Bells, and was preceded by a supper to which about 60 persons sat down. Mr. R. Sutton occupied the chair, and called upon Mr. J. Chappell, manager at the works, to make the presentation. Mr. Chappdl, who was received with applause, said he was truly sorry his old friend's health was failing, and he felt sure there was not one in that room but deeply sympathised with Mr. Brimelow. He had worked with him for upwards of one generation and had in many ways been closely connected with him; and he had always found Mr. Brimelow a true and honest friend. He knew their employers deeply regretted his sickness and would be glad to see him restored to health and at his duties. He then presented to Mr. Brimelow a hair-seated arm chair together with a purse of gold. The chair bore a silver plate on which was the following inscription :—" This chair, along with a purse of money, Was presented to Peers Brimelow by his employers and employees of Messrs. Rylands. Brbs. as a token of respect. April 3rd, 1882." In acknowledging the presentation Mr. Brimelow expressed' his • heartfelt thanks for the honour they had done him. It showed he had suc- ceeded in gaining their esteem and the general respect of his fellow workmen; and he could assure them that it gave him no little satisfaction, now that his working days were over, to feel that his conduct while amon,st them had met with their approbation. Mr. H. Whitham briefly dwelt upon the good feeling that existed between their employers and Mr. Brimelow, and showed how willing they had been to con- tribute towards the testimonir l. Mr. B. Farrar spoke of the encouragement given to new employees by Mr. Brimelow, whose conduct was worthy of imitation. Songs and recita- tions occupied the remainder of the evening, and the pro- ceedings concluded with ii vote of thanks to the chairman.

WARRINGTON A9SESSMENT COMMITTEO.—Under the presidency of Mr. John Rylands, the last meeting of the committee, as at present constituted, was held at the Work- house on Thursday, a large number of appeals were dealt with, but they were devoid of public interest. At the con- clusion of the business a vote of thanks was passed to the chairman for his services during the year.

FORTHCOMING DRAMATIC PERFORMANCES AT LATCH- FORD—On behalf of Mr. John White, Mr. Thurnham (of Messrs. Robert Davies and Co.) applied to the borough justices on Thursday for a license to hold two amateur dramatic performances in Christ Church Schcol, Latchford, on Tuesday and Wednesday evening next. The application was granted.

QUEEN ANNE'S BOUNTY.—The following is a list of the benefices in the dioceses of Manchester and Chester to which the governors of the Queen Anne's Bounty have recently agreed to make grants, en condition of the benefactions offered to obtain them being duly completed :—The parochial charyelry of St. Eidmor's Admarsh-in-Bleasdale, Garstang, £200; St. Oswald's perpetual curacy, Knuzden, Accrington, £400; St. Luke's, Winmarleigh, Garstang, £000; the per- petual Curacy of Byley-with-Lees, Middlewich, £200; the perpetual curacy of Chel ford, Congleton, £200; the Vicarage of Over Tabley, Knutsford, £200; and the Vicarage of flelsby, Frodsham, £2OO.

INQUESTS AT 'WATIBINGTON.—The county coroner, Mr. Driffield, on Wednesday, held an inquest at the Golden Ball, on the body of Martha, wife of Peter Berry, a blact- smith, living at 46, Ashton-street. The deceased, who was CO years of age, was ascending the stairs on the 13th Feb., when she slipped down, and broke her thigh. She was at- tended by Dr. Fox, but she, on Monday last, snccombed to her injuries. Verdict accldental death.—An inquest was also held on the same day by Mr. Driffield, on the infant daugh- ter of William Thomason, brickmaker, of 11, Morris-court, Church-street. At an early hour on Tuesday morning the child was found dead in bed, apparently having died whilst in a fit. A verdict that death resulted from natural causes, probably convulsions, was returned.

*A CHILD SCALDED TO DEA'TH AT LA.TCHFORD. —Mr. H. C. Yntes, coroner, held an inquest at the Lion Inn/ Latchford, on the body of Thomas Clare, 14 months old, Son of John Clare, soap, boiler, 49, New-road, Latchford. From the evidence it appeared that on the previous Wed- day evening about eight o'clock the deceased's sister, 14 years of age, placed a can containing boiling water on the table. She left the rowin for a few minutes to refill the kettle, and difring her absence the deceased knocked the can over, and was so severely scalded on his face; neck, and arms, that he died on the following day. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

WARRINGTON BlcTax CLua.—The members of the above club held their annual general meeting at the George Inn, Sankey-street, on Tuesday evening last, when the fol- lowing gentlemen were present :—Messrs. NV. P. Skelton, Wilfrid Skelton, J. Tinsley, NV. Crompton, W. Aukland, T. Craddock, NV. H. Harrison, W. Unsworth, E. Caldwell, T. Atherton, and J. Critchley. The following officers were ap- pointed :—Captain, W. Harrison ; sub-captain, T. Craddock; secretary, J. Critchley ; treasurer, W. P. Skelton. Com- mittee :—Messrs. Caldwell, Wilfrid Skelton, T. Atherton, and W. Crompton. We would call the attention of gentle- men wishing to join to an advertisement in another part of our journal, and would advise all those who take an interest in this healthy recreation to become members of the club at once.

RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT LATCH:MED.—The ad- journed meeting of the ratepayers of Latchford was held at the Cheshire Cheese Inn, on Tuesday, the overseer, Mr. ,R. H. Kerr, presiding. The business was the passing of the overseers' accounts, which showed the total receipts for the year to be £1,641 is. 5d., and the payments £1,509 2s. 2d. , There was a balance in the bank of £362 13s. 7d. The rates uncollected amounted to £154 16s. 5d., which represented empty property; but £lOO of that sum it was considered would be received. In answer to a remark by Mr. J. R. Booth, the Chairman said it was a remarkable thing that about £lOO of the uncollected rates ought to be paid by peo- ple who drove cabs to church and that sort of thing. A vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and the meet- ing concluded. There were only six persons present. WARRINGTON MUSETTAL—The return for the quarter ending 31st March last shows that the number of visitors was 8,216, as compared with 7,366 in 1881; reading room (estimated) 12,400, against 10,200, the volumes issued being 3,544, against 2,923; and that the number of volumes issued in the lending library was 7,786, against 8,369. The fol- lowing are amongst the more important additions during the quarter :—Lending Library : Stanley's Christian Institu- tions, Wright's Logic of Christian Evidences Vignoli's Myth and Science, Winskill's Temperance Evidences, Spencer's Principles of Sociology, Fitch's Lectures on Teaching, Wilson's Steam Boilers, Young's The Stn, Davis' Practical Microscopy, Harrison's Geology of the counties, Thrupp'j; History of Coachbuilding, liodgson's Errors in English, Iluxley's Science and Culture, De Rance's Water Supbly, Box's Treatise on heat, Nortbcott's Lathe's and Turning, Gardiner's Study of English History, Green's Making of England, Trollope's Dr. Wortle's School, Payn's From Exile, Gerard's Beggar my Neighbour, Shorthouse's John lnglesant, Morley's English Literature in the Reign of Victoria, Stevenson's Familiar Studiee. Reference Library: Kelly's London Directory, Croston's Nooks and Corners of Lancashire and Cheshire, Sehliemann's Illos, Clergy List for 1882, Burgess' Notes on the Hebrew Psalms, Hamerton's Graphic Arts, Clermout's Quadrupeds of Europe.

TIrE ASSESSMENT OF THE GAS Worts.—Aldermen Davies and Holmes appeared before, the Warrington Assessment committee, on Thursday, in reference to the assessment of the Warrington Gas Works. Mr. J. Rylands occupied the chair, and the other members present were M.ssrs. Cooper, Garnett, Appleton, Darbyshire, Gillespie, Harrison, and Houghton, together with Mr. J. C. Sutton (clerk), Mr. Owen (valuer), and the assistant oversirers.—The Chairman said he thought they would remember that the last time they met the difficulty the committee had was how they could deal with the property which to all appearances was in- creased in value by the outlay of £40,000, and yet they wanted reduction. If it had been an ordinary manufactory and not a gas works enjoying a monopoly, the ccmmittee would have had no difficulty in dealing with it. Being a gas works there was a difficulty to his mind how they should deal with it, especially as he had seen a case which was somewhat parallel to it, which came before the quarter ses- sions. The deputation had probably had sent to thorn the report ef Mr. Sutton, which laid down the basis on which the committee would be prepared to deal with the assess- ment of the gas works. Perhaps they would say if they had any objection to raise to that principle.—Alderman Davies said on the contrary they very much approved of it.—The Chairman said then the only difficulty would be to get at the amount which another tenant would give as rental for the preperty.—Mr. Davies said he was very much oblige:4 to the Board and their clerk for the trouble in sending the report, which well laid down the principle acted upon in the various cases which had been decided. He was stating he thought the committee had a perfect right to call upon them to submit a statement of their receipts, when the chairman said the committee had a long list of appeals be- fore them, and as the question would be one of accounts, he thought it would be better to appoint a sup-committee to go thproughly into the matter.—This suggestion was adopted, and the Chairman, Mr. Darbyshire, Mr. Cooper, the Clerk, and the Surveyor were appointed the sub-committee.

THE WARRINGTON CORPORATION IND ELECTRIC LIGHTING.—RATEPAYERS MEETING. On Thursday, at noon, a meeting of the ratepayers was held in the Council Chan'iber of the Town Hall, for the fpurpose, if thought de- sirable, of passing a resolution authorising the Corporation to oppose in Parliament the following bills :—British Elec- tric Lighting Company (Limited) Bill; Edison Electric Bill; Siearien. Brothers, dr Company (Limited) Bill; Anglo- American Brush Electric Light Corporation (Limited) Bill; Electric Light and Power Generator Company (Limited) Bill; and to charge the costs on the borough fund. Alder- man Webster was voted to the chair. There were present Councillors Fairclougb, Monks, Mackie, Woolfall, Taylor; Messrs. W.H. Brook (Town Cclerk). J. L. Whittle (deputy Town Clerk), Wm. Bolton, Wm. Bennett, and Lea.— The Chairman observed that the meeting was a mere matter of form. The opposition to the bills was not opposition in the ordinary sense of the term. The Corporation did not desire to prevent the introduction of the electric light in the town, but wished simply to be in a position to protect their own interest against these companies. The opposition which had been made by themselves, and other bodies, had re- sulted in the Government introducing a bill in the House of Commons which they hoped would meet all their objec- tions. lulhat case there would be no further opposition. If, on the contrary, their objections were not satisfied, they should have to go forward with the opposition to the bills with a view to protecting their own interests, and not with any intention of in any way opposing the electric light. (Councillor Monks: Oh, dear no!) He concluded by mov- ing the resolution that the expenses incurred should be charged upon the borough found or any other fund applic- able thereto.—Councillor Mackie seconded the motion with very great pleasure. After the chairman's explanation there could be no possibility of any mistake on the part of ' the ratepayers. He thought it was distinctly understood that they, in any sense, endeavoured to claim any special right for the Town Council to have the exclusive control over any electric or other lighting system that might be in- troduced. The opposition was made on thoroughly public grounds, and in addition to that there was a pledge given at the Town Council meeting, which they as ratepayers recognised still, so that no particularly heavy further ex- pense Undersewoul t d be goneege into conditionswithout thheadconaserenattofthe pleasureC o u Din- seconding the chairman's :proposal.—Mr. Bolton said he un- derstood chDaiidnnthane :resiotlduotiensnn ,ct rcrayr ryanayn derstood the expenses of the opposition were not to exceed Town Clerk: £5O was mentioned as the probable expense. yopthaerrticsuumlartlsitiamn .£-50T.—he —Mr. Bolton observed that if the resolution was passed the Council then would be empowered to expend £3,000 or £4,000.—Councillor Monks said half that sum could by no possibility be spent.—The Chairman said £5O would in all probability be all that would be rfluired.—The resolution was then carried, and the meeting concluded with a vote.of I thanks to the chairman.

div.p: ME EGYPTIAN QUESTION.

A. Berlin telegram states that, in compliance with an understanding arrived at by all the European Powers, a representative of each Powtr has been instructed to urge upon the Khedive the necessity of adopting a modification of the constitutional authority now in the hands of the Chanoer of Notables ; And if the Khe&ve or Chamber of Notables object to this demand, the Powers have determinEd: upon joint energetic measures to ensure protection for the interests of Egyptian bondholders.

div.head: LOSS OF THE DOURO STEAMER.
div.p: THE LOSS OF THE DOURO STEAMER.

Further details of the loss of the Douro charge the com- mon seamen on board that vessel with dastardly conduct. It is said that the clew "behaved shamefully. At the critical moment they were amnia into a pitiable state of terror. They rushed frantically to the boats, elbowing aside and trampling down without pity or consideration the women and children. The officers did everything that men could do in such circumstances to protect the passengers and save life, and, when the ship sank-, they went down with her."

AI; ALLEGED MURDERER AT NANTwICR.—On Saturday, a man giving the name of Henry Breeze, and who said he was a book canvasser belonging to Shrewsbury, gave himself into custody at the Nantwich Police Station: He alleged that he had murdered his master and mistress, a Mr. and Mrs. Lewis, of Shrewsbury. He said he was a woollen weaver of Bradford originally, of which piace he was a native. * As it was evilent he was mad from the effects of drink he was handed over to the workhouse authorities.

The fir,t st,twory meeting of the creditors of John Lewis of Altrincharn, baker and cmn dealer, was held on Mcnday The statement of affairs presented showed unsecured liabi- lities £1,G22. and assets an'. Resolutions were passed accepting a composition of 103. in the pound, payable 4s. down, and the remainder guaranteed. Mr. .I),.vitl Morrison, of Altrinchain, was appointed trustee. The principal credi- tors were represented by Mr. Morrison, Mr. F. I. Astbury (Astbury and Eckersley), public accountant, and by the Secretary of the Creditors' Association, Mr. G. H. Russell. Mr. W. E. Cave, Aitrincham, was instructed with the regis- tration of the resolutions.

NORTHWICH GAS BlLL.—This bill came before Dr. Play- fair, chairman of Ways aud Means, on Friday, as an unop posed measure. At the last moment certain amendments were suggested to be made in the clauses, and the bill was, therefore, postponed—the bill came before Dr. Playfair on Tuesday. There was no opposition to its passing. Mr. A. Fletcher, solicitor, Northwich, was present on behalf of the promoters, and proved the preamble of the bill.—Dr. Play- fair asked what was the meaning of their haring such a high maximum as 6s.—Mr. Fletcher said it was due to the sub- sidence of ground in the district, caused by the salt excava- tions. This greatly increased the cost of production, and the percentage of waste on account of leakage was 35 per cent. Hardly a day passed but the company had to take up the streets in order to examine the mains. The present price of gas was ss. per 1,000 feet, but this was owing to the low price of coal —Dr. Playfair said he had intended to dis- allow the 65., but he thought that the promoters had made out their case.—The Parliamentary Agents &Messrs. Taylor, Hoare, and Taylor) explained that the promoters had origin- ally intended to have a sliding scale, but when the bill came before the House of Lords Lord Redesdale struck cut the sliding scale and fixed a maximum at Gs. The preamble Nuts declared to have been proved, and the bill will be re- ported to the House. MORTALITY SW MID-CHESHIRE.—Mr. J. M. Fox, Medical Officer of Health for the Mid-Cheshire Combined Sanitary District, in his summary of the vital statistics of the year 1881, states that the average number of births during 1881 in Altrincham district was 26.5 per 1,000 of the population, and the average in the three previous years was 52 6 ; Con- gleton, 1881, 33 1, average of previous years, 85.6 ; Nant- wich, 1881, 330 against 824; Northwich, last year, 33.1 against 361; Lymm, 31-5 against 31.5 ; Middlewich, 435 against 4U3; Nentwich (urban), 37 5 against 37 7; Sand- Lich, 34 0 against 34 3; Northwich (urban), 400 against 46 4 ; Winsford, 39 3 against 49 3; entire district, 331 against 37.6. 'The annual rate of mortality per 1,000 is as follows for the rural districts of Altrincham, 1881, 151 against 17-1; Congleton, 16 6 against 18 6; Nantwich, 141 against 17.7; Northwich, 130 against 18.4. Urban dis- tricts: Lymm, 11.7 against taB 1; Middlewich, 18.6 against 269; Nautwich, 14.8 against 20 2 ; Sandbach, 129 against • 20.1; Northwich, 18 0 arsainst 257; Winsford, 17 4 against 225; entire district, 15.5 against 205. The rate of more talitv per 1,000 from seven principal zy:notic diseases were in 1881 for the entire district 092, as against an average of 3.12 for the previous three years; and the percentage of deaths under one year to registered births was 105 for the combined sanitary district. CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSION'S. The Cheshire Quarter Sessions were opened on Monday, at the Court-house, Knuts- ford, Mr. Horatio Lloyd (deputy chairman), presiding. Mr. Hilton Greaves, cotton merchant, of Altrincham, was fore- man of the Grand Jury.—Mr. Horatio Lloyd, in delivering his charge to the Grand Jury, congratulated them on the exceptionally small number of cases on the calendar. There were only 17 cases of the most ordinaly character, as against 30 this time last year; while the number for trial at Chester showed no increase.—The Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, M.P., said his father had requested him to sty a few words to the magistrates assembled expressive of his regret that he had been so long a time—the past six months—prevented from attending that court. His own feelings had prompted him last autumn to resign, but, after having consulted a number of Lis brother magistrates in whose judgment he could rely, he had withdrawn his resignation in the hope that when the warmer weather returned be might be able to do some service to the country, and be enabled to move about again. (Applause.)—The Deputy-Chairman moved that Mr. Wilbraham Egerton be requested to convey to the chaii men the hearty congratulations of that meeting on the improved state of his health, andthe expression of an earnest hope for his complete recovery.—Lord de Tabley seconded the motion, which was carried. The chief -constable's return of crime for the quarter showed a total of 1993, apprehended, of whom 68 were committed for trial, 1,617 summarily convicted, and 313 discharged. This was an increase of :174 apprehended, chiefly causal by offences under the Vagrants Act, the Edu- cation Act, and drunkennees. The proceedings for drunken- ness showed an increase of 112 males and nine females. Steps bad been taken to redress vagrancy, with the result that during a single fortnight there had been a decrease of 271 in the number relieved—The Chief Constable reported that on the 21st February last 47 animals remained unaer treatment for foot-and-mouth disease, and, since that "ate, 69 had been attacked in six localities; four had died, GO had recovered, and 52 remained under treatinent.—A motion was on the agenda for a grant of .£9OO for alteration of magistrates' room in the Court-house, but it was reduced to £lOO, en Mr. George Latham's objection, in view of the forthcoming County Government Bill.
