WARRINGTON CHURCHES. Sir,—kfter an absence of nearly three years from War- rington I cannot but feel pleased to find a great change in a few of our churches,—in the accommodation of seating te people, and whatever may be the form of ritual adopted, t! e one great ol4ject ought to be towards freedom,twhic.rt would tend to lesson the interest which may be taken in salvation, blue ribbon armies, or any other nostrum which may be introduced by man. Churchmen, rally round your church.—Ycurs truly, R. S. Warrington, April 4.

div.head: MRS. RIPPON ON DRESS,
div.p: MRS. RIPPON ON DRESS,

Sir,—lt is quite refreshing to read the exhaustive article by Airs. Rippon on the above subject in your last issue. But this is one of those subjects upon -vhich people are not to be taught You may point out absurdities, and you may de- nounce actions, and manners !Ind custOms, which are detri- mental to comfort and health, and the sufferers may acquiesce in your opinion, but there is a demon powerful and uncompro- mising, and that dark angel is fashion! Whether this potentate comes from earth, air, or sea, it would be hazardous to say, but that he is almost omnipotent we cannot deny. Formerly he held sole sway over the fair sex; now he dictates to both sexes, and the gays that some men make themselves is in- sufferable. But, to return to the ladies, poor things, ask them what they can do, and thy will tell you, that however ridiculous the costume may be, you must blame the cos- tumier, whoever he or she wis who invented it. Things have come to such a pretty pass now-a-days, that legislation is almost necessary in a sanitary form to protect the lives of female society, from a horrible self-inflicted penance, or take a leaf from the book of the Dutch Puritans, who enacted in their own free colony in America, how a woman should be dresskd, and the length of the skirt of her gown. Some "woman's rights " legiskttor should certainly bring the sub- ject before the public, .and attempt to nullify this powerful demon of whom we have written. Of course, every allow- ance must be roads for the ladies. If you could instruct how to manage, if you could inculcate moral courage, if you could insure the dear creatures husbands by your teaChings and trainings, then there might be some hope of this bane- ful influence being set at defiance. But, "to be out of the fashion is to be out of the world!" and therefore we come back to the" refrain," viz., that all is conceded that you say, but what you teach must not be learned. Tha tyrant must sway the sceptre, and his votaries are as unflinching as himself; no sensitive girl could stand the jeers and the nods of a fashion-loving world, when she had abjured its trammels, and she swims with the stream. Look to the in- troduction of the fashions ; but then tastes so differ, that we are afraid that we must exist amongst absurdities. Arpley-street. AUNT MARY.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of the Town Council was held on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of the Mayor (Alder- man Pickmere). There were also present Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, Davies, Chandler, Harrison and Kean; and Coun- cillors Broadbent, MilLer, Platt, Taylor, Woolfall, Collin, Ashton, Mackie, Pierpoint, Francomb, Dixon, Wallington, Whittle, Fairclough, Monks, Barker, Brown, Litton, Ridg- way, Jeans, and Burgess; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clet), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), J. H. Gornall (medical officer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), and J. Paterson (gas manager). WATCH COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committee, which were adopted on the proposition of the MAYOR, seconded by Mr. Alderman HARRISON comprised the following: A recommendation that an estimate of the expenditure for the half year ending, . 29th September neat, amounting to £965 lOs. id. in the Watch, and £lO5 17s. in the Fire Engine Department be approved. A letter was read from the Home Secretary, noti- fying that he had the satisfaction of certifying to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, that the Police Force had been maintained in a state .of efficiency during the year ended 28th September last. Richard Spann, of Friars' Green, was appointed the superinteJdent of the Borough Fire Brigade. STREET IMPIZOVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. The nsinutes of this committee comprised the following recommendations: That the following plans be approved. House in Museum-street for Mr. J. Taylor, dentist, Museum- street; house in Lovely-lane for Mr. Wheeldon ; scullery to house in Guardian-street for Mr. John Ellison; office for Monks, Hall and Co. at Atherton's Quay; house in Lilford- street fnr Mr. Wm. Dooley; alterations and additions to house No 24, Arthur-street, for Mr. T. B. Marshall. The estimate of the committee'g department for the half- year amounting to £1,143 14s. was recommended for ap- pi oval. Councillor BROADBENT moved the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor PLArr in seconding the motion, said the num- ber of lamps showed an increase of 50 over the previous half year, but they had been equally distributed over the town.

The motion was carried. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. The following recommendations were made by the Paving and Sewerage Committee:—That the estimate of the expen- diture for the half-year amounting to £2,890 be approved. That the footpath on the east side of Lovely-lane from Sankey Green to Selby-street, and that portion of the foot- path on the south side of Manchester-road from the Ceme- tery gates to the borough boundary be paved with tiles. That the tender of Mr. Samuel Hutton, of Hale Green, Bowdon, for the labour required in completing the forminc, and paving of Catherine and Howard-streets be accepted. That the tender of Mr. John Chorley, of Warrington, for the oupp'y of cast iron pipes for the drainage woilis in Latch- ford be accepted. That the footpath in Bath-street be con• tinned to the entrance of the gardens. Councillor WooLFALL moved, and Councillor WALLING- TON seconded, the adoption of the minutes of this com- mittee. Alderman KEAN (who entered the room at this stage) remarked that the committee intended to deal with Latch- ford, and he hoped it would be to the advantage of all who lived in that locality. The committee bad felt that for along time they had been much kept down by the expenditure of other committees, but no doubt that expenditure was prompted with a view to making the concerns over which they presided into paving concerns. He hoped that would be the end of it, at all events. The minutes were passed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee the Inspector reported that 45 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guar- dians, and school fees allowed in 37 cases for 76 children. Forty-one cases had been taken before the magistrates, and • fines inflicted in 36 cases, two ordered to attend school, two adjourned, and one warrant ordered. It was recommended that the estimate of the expenditure amounting to £149 12s. be approved. Forty-two cases were brought before the com- mittee and dealt with. Alderman WEBs•rEn moved the adoption of the minutes, which was seconded by Councillor Dixon. Alderman CHANDLEY called the attention of those gentle- men who so strenuously contended for the adoption of a School Board to the very Teas mable expense the borough was liable to for the working of the School Attendance Com- mittee. who, he thought, were to be congratulated on their economical management as compared with the amount of good done. The minutes were agreed to. MUSEUM COMMITTEE.

A meeting of this Committee was held on the 10th ult., when the Curator reported as follows for the month of Feb- ruary :—Visitors to the Museum, 2.083, a decrease of 519; volumes issued to subicribers9 2,471, a decrease of 255; volumes issued to readers 1,196, an increase of 161 compared with February. 1881. A circular from the Mayor of Man- chester was read and it was resolved that the Town Council be requested to present a petition to the House of Commons. in favour of the Free Libraries Bill. The minutes also con- tained a resolution that the General Purposes Committee be requested to have the interior of the Art Gallery coloured and painted; and a report of the representatives of this Committee on the recent deputation from Municipal Cor- porations to the Lord President of the Council, which we have already published. Alderman WEnsr:sn, in proposing the confirmation of the minutes, referred to the interview with Mr. Mundella. The result of that interview they anticipated would be very satisfactory, and that the Warrington Museum and those throughout the country would derive advantage from in- creased grants and increased facilities for circulating works of art throughout the provinces. It was thought that the national institutions connected with art should be brought under one management, but it seemed at present the diffi- culties were insurmountable, and there was no hope, at any rate for some time to come, that steps would be taken in that direction. Coancillor BURGESS seconded. Alderman KEAN said all the members of the Council who had carefully read the report of the deputation must be con- vinced that it was an effirt in the right direction, and that good must result. It was pleasing to know that the efforts of the local bodies had been very great in this direction. That spoke wonders for the localities who took an iaterest in the rise and progress of young students of art. Councillor PLATT was glad to see that a more enlightened policy was about to be adopted respecting works of art bought tor the nation,and that the provinces which joined in providing the money for them were to have a share in the benefits. The minutes were then passed. CEMETERY COMMITTEE. On the motion of Councillor BROWN, seconded by Alder- man KEAN, the minutes of the Cemetery Committee were confirmed. They cemprised a report of the registrar that the intermente fr teo past four weeks were, adults 2:5, minors 60, and stillborn 7; and for the corresponding period of last year, adults 27, minors 31, and stillborn 11. Also a recommendation that the estimate of expenditure, amounting to £261 12s, for the ensuing half-year, be approved. The receipts for the past four weel;s were seated to be £76 4s Bd, and the corresponding period last year £62 ss. MARKETS C3MMITTER. • In proposing the confirmation of the minutes of the Markets Committee, Alciernan CHANDLEY said it would be obeerved that the committee had put on one side the sum of £2OO towards the purchase of property hereafter, which they hoped to appropri de to market extension. They thought it wise to make tli;s provision. The MAYOR: Out of revenue? Alderman URANDLEY : Yes. Captain LerroN seconded the motion, which WAS carried. The minutes included a recommendation that the esti-
mated expenditure of £616 13s 6d, for the ensuing half- year, be approved. The receipts from all sources for the past four weeks were stated to be £224 19s 3d.

TOWN HAIL, PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. The MAYOR moved and Councillor RIDGWAY seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Town Hall, Park, and BathrCommittee, which were pissed. The minutes con- tained the estimate of the expenditure for the half-year in the three departments, as follows :—Town Hall, £368 155.; Bank Park, £236 45.; and baths, £164 3s. 10d. This was recommended for approval. The batlikeeper reported that the income from the baths for the fortnight ended 2nd Mar. was ET 6d., and for the fortnight ended 16th March, £6 3s.
THE SANITARY COMMITTEE AND THEIR CHAIRMAN: AN "EXTRAORDINARY PROPOSITION?'

The Sanitary Committee's minutes included the following —Mr. Farmer, of the Adelphi-street Works, Salford, having intimated that the new evaporating machine he had made for the Birmingham Corporation would be together on the following Friday, and that lie should be glad to show it to the members of this committee, it was resolved that a depu- tation of this committee (to con(pt of such members as can find it convenient to go) with the borough surveyor and the medic 11 officer, be authorised to visit the works at Salford to inspect the new machine, and report to this committee. On the 15th March it was recommended that the estimate of expenditure, amounting to £4,611 103., be approved. On the 29th March it was recommended that the following resolution of the Council, passed on the 6th December, 1881, be rescinded, so far as concerns the appointment of Mr. Alderman Burgess as chairman of the Sanitary Com- mittee: Resolved, that Mr. Alderman Burgess be appointed chairman, and Mr. Councillor Monks deputy ohairman for the ensuing year. The offer of Mr. William Sherratt, of Manchester, for the purchase of about 20 tons of lump manure, now in stock, at £4 7s 6d per ton, was accepted. The manure to be delivered on the premises in bags either provided by Mr. Sherratt or supplied by the Corporation and to be returned; terms cash. Inspector Norman was ap- pointed to superintend the working of the Longford Depart- ment in addition to his other duties. _

When in the ordinary course the adopticn of the minutes of the Sanitary Committee should have been mowd, no one appeared to be about to perform that daty. Alderman BURGESS rose to his feet, and said he could hardly be expected to move the confirmation of the minutes of which one of the principal ones was that he should be removed from the chairmanship. So, perhaps, the Mayor would excuse him.

Councillor Moisics said he thought Alderman Burgess was quite right. He (Mr. Monks), therefore, moved the confirma- tion of the minutes. The machine the committee went to see at Salford had, he understood, been removed to Birming- ham, and was in course of erection. When ready the Birmingham Corporation would give them an opportunity of testing the machine to its fullest extent. The estimates were based on what was considered a fair thing. All the manure that was at Longford depot a month or five weeks ago had been sold, ard, be believed, he was quite right when he said there was no stock whatever at Longford. With reference to the resolution passed last Wednesday night rescinding a resolution affecting Alderman Burgess, 'he had nothing to say beyond this: that he had been the colleague of Alderman Burgess on the Sanitary Committee for about I 14 years, and he was very sorry that things should come to a point at which the committee felt it necessary to move such a resolution as this. It was a most unusual one, and he thought such a resolution had never been passed in this Councilo before. He was quite sure that the committee would not have passed any such resolution if they had not I felt themselves practically driven to it. It was no secret that I the committee had not been able to agree upon a certain I policy which it was determined they should adopt, and since the chairman went out of the committee 'room declar- ing he would not come back, the committee had simply had to carry on the work as best they could, and, so fibr as he was able to judge, it had been performed satisfactorily. The I works were now in a much cleaner cendition than they bad been for a very long time. This resolution arose, perhaps, not as much 'from differences in policy as the manner in which the chairman had thought fit to treat the committee, and last Wednesday night, he nas sorry to say, the thing was further complicated by making it practically a personal matter between himself and Alderman Burgess. He had Alder- Burgess's declaration that he would not sit with him (Coun- cillor Monks) for his colleague upon any committee or in connection with anything. Now the thing had come to this, I that he should have to sever his connection with the Sani- tary Committee if Alderman Burgess had to remain. But he had no objaction to do that. He should be quite willing to accept the decision of the Council with perfect good faith and without any bitterness , of feeling. These matters ought not to be made personal and he for one should not make it personal. He wished the Obuncil to deal with the matter for the best interests of the ; town, because they would then serve his interests. He had I no personal interest to serve in promoting the good govern- I ment of the town, which be was anxious to see. It was from a strong conviction ef that sort that he had taken the I course he had done for the last few months in reference to I the policy pursued in connection with the Infectious Diseases I Hospital, and lastly with the machinery at Longford. It I was not a pleasant Oleg, but he thought it was overstepping the province of any chairman to speak to members of his committee in the way in which members of the Sanitary Committee had been spoken to. No apology had yet been made and it came to this—they must either accept such treatment or clear out of it altogether. He had made up his mind as to which course he should take. The committee I would leave this matter entirely in the hands of the Council. He wished to state publicly that no colleague of Alderman Burgess had supported his chairman better than be had when he thought the dhairman was right. He had gone along with him especially in connection with the establish- ment of the Infectious Diseases Hospital in subordinating his own opinions and convictions to the strongly expressed wish of the chairman. Had he to do it again he did not hesitate to say he should oppose the establishment of the Infectious Diseases Hospital to the extent it had been. If the Council confirmed this res)lution, he knew what he had to do, and if the Council would not confirm it then he also knew what he had to do. I Councillor BARKER seconded the resolution.

The DEPUTY MAYOR said he could not support the reso- lution with reference to Alderman Burgess. It was a great pain to him when he first saw that such a resolution had been put upon the books, and he begged to move that the iminutes of the Sanitary Committee be confirmed with the exception of the resolution referring to Alderman Burgess. At the last Council meeting the matter in dispute was thoroughly gone into, and he was in hopes that this matter l would rest quietly until those experiments had been tried. ' He thought if Alderman Burgess was removed from the chairmanship a great many members of that com- mittee wpuld resign, and the committee would be far from ,being settled. He thought it would be much better if tie I , committee would resign, rather than take the step they had. (Hear, hear). Councillor MACKIE, in seconding the amendment, said he was unable to be present at the private and confidential imeeting of the Council, which was held a week or two since, and as reporters were not admitted to the meeting he ' remained in ignorance of what was done there. He rose on the present occasion ignorant of a good deal with which other members were no doubt acquainted. He was simply going to thank Mr Monks for having departed from what seemed to be the usual course there by giving more informa- tion than was customary by the proposer of the resolution for the adoption of the minutes ; at the same time he thought a great many things that were left unsaid—many things at any rate of which those out of doors were entirely ignorant—could be given by some one entering into this , unfortunate disPute more than Councillor Monks had I done. He was speaking correctly when he said it was I decided that this matter would be considered at the private imeeting. At the private meeting the view taken and put I forward was that the matter should be deferred for a month, the time specified to be necessary for the completion of certain experiments; and in connection with that he thought it was understood—certainly he understood it—that Mr. Alderman Burgess was like a good boy to return to his official duties. (Laughter). .In fact he said if a certain I arrangement were made he would go back.. He could not, therefore, help thinking that until those experiments had been made, it was very unwise for any change to take place in such a matter, and it was to be regretted that they should have wrangling and jangling at a period when everything in the shape of peace and order was so abundantly required. They were told by an eminent man of the propriety of keep- ing ail troublesome things out of the sight of the general public ; but he could not help thinking that in the case of such a gentleman as Mr. Alderman Burgess it was by no means satisfactory to find him pitch-forked out of office. Ad rman Burgess, as they all knew, had been something like 30 years a very useful servant of his fellow-townsmen. He had often done things he (Mr. Mackie) had not the sligh- t-at doubt that he would better.not haste done. All of them had done so, but they judged public men by their good in- tentions, and by the fact that they desired to do •good whether they bad succeeded or not. Why, after 30 years service, for the first time according to Mr. Monks, a course of procedure of this kind should be taken to practically turn out and stigmatise Alderman Burgess, was a thing that passed his knowledge, and he trusted would pass the know- ledge of all the other members of the Council. It was no easy in itter to bear such treatment at the hands of one's fellow-townsmen in any position in life, far less in one who had devoted so much time and attention to public work. In fact the time had Comae when, instead of haviag a stigma cast at him of this kind, it would have been more natural to have been crowning Mr. Alderman Burgess with some of those laurels, represented by a public dinner ; or recognising him by some other means as one deserving well of his townsrhen instead of the short curt method of carrying him off from an important office in what was a. certain and intermediate state of that Sanitary Committee's proceedings. If when this new machine waa tried and found to be a SUCCdS4, and Alderman Burgess refused to recognise it, he had no doubt Alderman Burgess would have the good sense to carry out—he (Mr. Mackie) would not say the threat, but the resolution Mr. Alderman Burgess was announced to take at the last Council meeting, of retiring from office. Be had expressed the opinion before, and he strongly expressed it now, that it was a misfortune that by an accident Alderman Burgess should by a cammittee of not more than five or six persons he asked to sacrifice a life long position and retire, certainly not with honour, but. with a certain amount of disgrace, into that quietness of unofficial life which was very ill-fitted to satisfy a gen,lenian of his active habits. They all knew his life and temperament. He had again and again come into conflict with him, and he had always found Alderman I Burgess an able and fair combatant, and one who was always ready to shake hinds after the fight was over. It was for Councillor Monks and the members of the committee to put matter!, in a much plainer light than at present before the eyes of the general public. It was their duty to do that

div.head: Tllt EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 8, 882.
div.p: Tllt EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 8, 882.

first and foremost, and if they failed to substantiate their I position, let them fairly confess that they: had done what they ought not to have done, and ask Alderman Burgess to retain his position, at any rate until the mechanical diffi- culty had been solved. (Hear' hear). He did not, he wished it to be understood, find fault with the the theory at Longford, but he did find fault with the short and sum- mary way in which they had endeavoured to force an old and faithful servant into a course of action which it would have been far better first and foremost to have submitted to the Council as now assembled. (Hear, hear). Alderman SuTTbrr said he would support the resolution because he believed it was perfectly impracticable for the committee, as at present constituted, to perform its work in an amicable or satisfactory manner. He had no desire whatever to say an unjust or disrespectful word concerning Alderman Burgess, and were it not for the reason he had stated, he should be very loth indeed—considering the nature of the resolution appearing on the minutes—to hsve supported it at all. For some time past there had been misunderstandings between the members of the Sanitary Committee, and without desiring to give offence to any one he might almost say that in consequence of what had been considered an arbitrary spirit existing on the part of the chairman upheld by one or two members of the committee, the majority of the committee had not been able to carry on the business with the chairman. The first show of this arbitrary conduct on the part of the members alluded to was a threat to resign unless they got what they asked for. When the Council at the last meeting-r-at the instigation of Alderman Davies, who evidently desired to smooth matters over—tried to bring about a reconcilation, and referred the matter to a committee of the whole Council. Well that committee simply decided to do what tlap Sanitary Commit- tee, ss appeared by the minutes of the last Council, had de- termined to do—and that was to wait—before incurring the. heavy expense in providing additional machine r# at Longford, as recommended by the chairman of the com- mittee, until it was seen what the machinery, which Bir- mingham had offered to supply to them, could do, and which would cost only about a fourth what the other would cost, and be far more effective. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH : Why have you not waited? Councillor SuTTorr, continuing, asked: Was there any- thing in that recommendation for the chairman or anybody else to rebel and to say that unless they got what they wanted they would resign? He maintained, as an individual member of the Council, that the committee was perfectly competent to carry on the work of the committee, and to carry it on satisfactorily to the Corporation and to the public' also, provided that arbitrary spirit was removed and done away with. It was quite evident at the last meeting of the committee that it would be perfectly impossible to go on as at present constituted, and his opinion was the sooner an alteration was made the better. He gave Alderman Burgess every credit for having in times Past rendered valuable service to the town (hear, hear) and he thought the improvements which 1:0 been made in the town in sanitary matters were evidences of what had been ' accomplished by him; but whilst admitting the difficulties of dealing with the refuse of the town—difficulties which almost every large Corporation in the kingdom had had to contend with—they must not at the same time increase the very large expenditure which they had been continually in- curring during the last few years. Under all the circum- stances bethought it would be much better to pass the minutes because he thought that course would bring about alterations which must certainly take place before they could act to- gether. (Hear, hear.) Councillor FRANCOMB also supported the motion, remark- ing that as a member of the committee he did not feel at all ashamed at the course he had taken. When the question of accepting or rejecting Messrs. Manlove's machinery came before the committee, Messrs. Monks, Barker, and himself objected, and asked for time; and they were told that if they did not decide that night Alderman Burgess and two others would resign. As a proof of that, these gentlemen, after they were beaten, stopped away from the meetings something like three or five weeks. Well, in the meantime the members of the committee remaining set to work and disposed of the manure. There were 3,700 tons of it at Longford, but it very soon vanished until there were only 1,100. Since that time at every meeting Alderman Burgess had attended there had been a row or a scene. He (Mr. Franconab) had no feeling in the matter. Alderman Bur- gess was as much respected by him as anybody else, but he could not believe he did right when he charged Mr. Monks, Mr. Barker, and himself with untruthfulness on this question. It was necessary that either Alderman Bur- gess should resign, or that the minority should resign, but he was at the same time perfectly willing to abide the deci- sion of the Council. £B,OOO had, he contended, been spent at Longford on machinery that was only doing a sixth of the work it was expected to do; and he pointed out that while the manure had been sold only recently for £4 7s. 6d. a ton, all that Messrs. Manlove allowed for it was £3 25.6 d. Besides, the manure sold at the latter price contained only 20 per cent. of moisture, while that sold at the former sum contained 35 per cent., an 4 he added that to reduce it to 20 per cent. meant an expenditure of 30s. per ton more, so that they only got £3 2s 6d a ton from Messrs. Manlove fer what they could get £6 per ton at least. Messrs. Monks and Barker had gone thoroughly into this matter, and it would be a great misfortune to the town at large if these gentlemen were removed from the Sanitary Committee.

Councillor MILNER said the conduct of the minority had not been fairly described, and that they had not behaved in an arbitrary and improper manner. [Councillor MONKS: I said the Chairman, not the minority, had behaved arbi- trarily.] Well, Mr. Sutton said the minority. He heat felt all along that sooner or later the question put plainly in the resolution of the committee that night was the question which would have to come before the Council, and on which the Council would have to pronounce a decided opinion. It really WiS whether they would have Alderman Burgess or Couscillor Monks chairman of the committee. There was no doubt whatever that was the difficulty the special meet- ing of the Council held a week or a fortnight ago was caged upon to deal with. He came to that meeting knowing that that was the question to he debated, and he took his seat on the other side of the table because he felt that for the sake of peace and quietness, and in order to re-establish the good feeling hitherto existing on the Sanitary Committee it was worth while to sink all per- sonal matters and to simply place before the Council the question which they had been debating,—as to how and what machinery should be used to deal with the material at ,1 Longford. The result of that meeting was not tlO him alto- gether satisfactory, but still he determined to abide loyally by it, and to leave everything over for a month. Unfortu- nately he was not able to be at the meeting of the Commit- tee when the resolution now on the piper was proposed and adopted by the majority. If he had been he should have known exactly what was the cause of that resolution being there, but he only knew now from hearsay. From what Mr. Francomb said, he gathered the Chairman had stated the report of the Birmingham deputation was not true and that he doubted their word. Well, he thought from what he knew that Mr. Burgess would not put it in that way, but he would doubt the deductions from what they said, and he doubted them himself most decidedly and most strongly. He looked upon the machine very different from what the others did. For the last eight or nine months, as he had said, Councillor Monks had not been in unity with the action of , the Sanitary Committee. Councillor Monks had set himself persistently to obstruct. He had refused to reason and re- fused to argue; he would not listen to the arguments of other people. He said he did not believe this and did not believe that, and argument was Therefore useless. He (Mr. Milner) had given up going to Longford because there seemed to be nothing but objections and trouble; experi- ments satisfactorily going on there were described as so much nonsense, they were told continually that they were getting untruthful reports, and that nothing could be relied on. There were two ways of misleading. One was by stating that which was not correct with the intention to mislead, and the other was by leaving out certain important facts from a statement. The second plan was the course which had been adopted in this case. In the report submitted by the Birmingham deputation facts and com- parisons were stated in regard to the machine, but they heard nothing about the Warrington machine and what was done by it. The money they had spent at Longford I was practically voted as worthless, and it was insinuated I that they had done no good at all. He was quite willing that this matter should be submitted to somebody qualified to hear evidence on both sides, and who would decide between them; but he did not care to say all that he knew, because : he might say more than he ought to do. He was, however, ! impelled to the uncomfortable conclusion that the gentle- ' men who signed the Birmingham report either did not i understand what they were reporting about or they wished to deceive the Council. Now, if there was one thing more striking than another on the Sanitary Committee it was this, that in placing information before the Council everything had been done to give every fact known so that the Coun- cil could form an opinion, but in the supplementary report of those who visited Birmingham that was not the case. The most important facts regareling Warrington were omitted, and statements were made which were physical impossi- bilities. With regard to the Chairman, he (Mr. Milner) could only say that after the persistent opposition of Coon- ' cillor Monks to everything that had been done to carry out the policy approved by the Council, he did not know how Alderman Burgess had been able to conduct himself as he had. Under the provocation he had received, his conduct had been worthy of all praise, arid he was astonished he had not oftener given way to temper than he hart dons. He could not recall any occasion on which Alderman Burgess had given way to his temper in a manner that would offend anyone, unless it was one who was determined before hand to be offended with whatever the chairman did. As to the conduct of the Minority at the meeting with Mr. Fryer, the Council were told that they came to that meeting and said that if their views were not carried out they would resign. He entirely denied that. They argued the question, ant when the vote went against them, they said they would resign. [Several members: Before the vote.] He repeated that it was after the vote, and that ' Mr. Monks looked across the table and said, that it would be mean to leave under such circumstances. Mr. Crosfield said "No, certainly not, we cannot go on with you ; you have ,brought fol ward a fresh policy, and you ifilet he prepared to carry it out." (Herr, hear.) A fresh ministry was brought in, and the majority ought to be pre- pared to carry out their fresh policy. [Several Members again remarked that this took place before the vote] He might, he said, be technically wrong, but he did not believe that he was as to the time of the vote. The vote was, in his opinion, given before anything was said about resignation. He bad no more idea of resigning or making use of such a threat when he entered the committee, than lie had when he attended hundreds of other committees of the Council. The reason for the haste of the minority was simply this : The arrangements with the Nottingham firm had ti he car- ried on through Mr. Fryer, who was going to the Wcst

Indies, and it was necessary that the negotiations should be closed and a decision come to before he sailed. That was the reason why the matter was pressed, and as a proof that there was a determination on the part of Mr. Monks to oppose Alderman Burgess he (Mr. Milner) might mention that when the letter from Messrs. Manlove first came before the committee he entirely declined to allow it to be read. He was supported, and that letter never was read ; and never was entered on the minutes of the committee ; therefore the committee were not fully informed of the Nottingham firm's proposal. Councillor BARKER : That letter was read in this room. Alderman BURGESS: Indeed, Mr. Mayor, it never was read at all.
Councillor MILNER : The majority declined to have it put on the minutes.
Councillor MONKS: But evew member of the committee had a copy of the letter.

Councillor MILNER : Alderman Burgess had a copy and I had a copy, which I lent to you ; I am not aware the other members had. As to the offer Meesrs. Manlove, Elliot and Co. made, it was one which relieved the Corporation from entire respensibility for tile next 3 or 4 years. They agreed to take payment for the machinery they put down in the manure produced, and they guaranteed or were prepared to guarantee that the machinery they put down would do all the work required. They were also prepared to fix a price for the machinery out and out, and if their estimate was wrong to pay the whole extra cost out of their own pockets, and the town would not have been called upon for anything else. There was one fact that he might mention and that was that the great question of dealing with the pail contents of Warrington was solved. (Hear, hear.) A machine could be produced by either Manlove, Forrest, Farmer or some- body else which would relieve them of a tronble and responsibility in this respect, and a manure would be pro- duced as valuable almost as guano for which they would get from £7 to £8 'per ton. Of course the Council could decide to borrow money, put up works themselves, and take the whole responsibility of the success or failure, but in the judgment of the minority in order to get rid of the question and to get rid of the increasing bonded debt of the town it was worth while to accept Messrs.planlove's tender. With respect to the works at Longford being cleaner, he reminded the Council that the majority had come into power atter the wet time had been passed, when the farmers were ar,xious for the manure, and when there was an east wind blowing and everything looked extremely ni6e. (Laughter.) *ln concluding, Mr. Milner said he hoped that the Council would not take the conduct of the affalrs of the Sanitary Committee out of the hands of the gentleman who had de- voted his time to the work for the past 13 years, who had studied this most disagreeable subject deeply; and he added that if they were to go in for ez.peiirnante they must resolve to put money aside for that purpose. He further observed that the machine they were asked to adopt or wait for had never before been used for the purpose to which it was now applied, which was an important matter. Alderman CHANDLEY said the discussion had taken a turn he confessed he was not quite prepared for. It had pained him exceedingly to see on the minutes a resolution by which the committee proposed to do a very undignified, arbitrary, and improper act. The Council had had only one side of the question; and they were asked to judge he thought on an ex pane state- ment as to the conduct of Alderman Burgess. He felt that the committee might.at least have waited until the expira- tion of their term of office in November. (Hear, hear.) They all had peculiarities that might be objectionable of others, and he thought a certain amount of forbearance was required, when they reflected upon the time Alderman Burgess had occupied a seat in that Council. He could, not be one to inflict such pain upon any old member of the Council as the adoption of that resolution would inflict upon Alderman Burgess, who for thirty years had been in the Council.

Councillor JEANS said it appeared to him that this ques- tion, subject to the Town Clerk's ruling, was not one for the consideration of the Council. Each committee bad power to appoint its own chairman, and he thought they were going out of the ordinary course in bringing a matter of this kind before the Council.

Alderman WEBsTEit agreed with the last speaker that it was the duty of a committee to appoint their own chairman and deputy-chairman, and not to come by a side wind to the Council and ask them to rescind the committee's own reso- lution. The chairman was aopointed by the- Banitary Com- mittee, and if they thought proper it was for them to rescind the resolution, and then lay it before the Council for approval or otherwise. [A Voice: That is what they are doing.] What the committee were doing was simply asking the Council to withdraw its approval on their previous re- solution, and they had not rescinded that resolution at all. He admitted that virtually perhaps the result would be the same, but practically it was different. He had listened with great attention to Councillor Monks' statement, and also to that by Councillor Milner. One part of Councillor Monks' address, he thought, urged perhaps the strongest reason that had yet been urged why the matter should not be carried to an extreme at the present time. It was that for 13 or 14 years he himself had worked harmoniously with the chairman, and that on the whole they had acted well, and the results had been satisfactory. Another reason was, that it was a course altogether unusual, and such a course as had never been adopted by that Council, and he thought from his own experience and recollection of the proceedings of other councils it was a course which was rarely adopted. They all knew that in public matters, both imperial and local, concessions had tc be made and compromises effected, and he thought some concession might have been made with a view to working harmoniously on the committee until the time came for the dissolution of the committee. He would be very glad if, without going to the extreme proposed, some course could be adopted by which the matter could be re-considered, 80 that that harmony would again prevail which Councillor Monks hi insel f had candidly and straightforwardly confessed previously existed.

Councillor BROADBENT had observed the difficulty which had arisen on the committee with very great pain indeed, on personal and on public grounds. (Hear, hear.) He was exceedingly sorry that the committee had thought it neces- sary to place the resolution on the minutes, although he could understand when the majority of the committee found themselves opposed by a minority composed of men of very great knowledge and influence, and who had apparently absented themselves to a large extent since the difficulty had arisen, they found themselves in a somewhat awkward position. At the same time he valued, as he had said, both publicly and privately, the services of Alderman Burgess so highly that he could not personally join in the minute relating to him. Whatever was the result of the discussion, and whatever disagreements there might be, th wished the members of the committee to understand that they placed an inesti- mable value on the services which Alderman Burgess had rendered to the town, and which nothing that could happen would ever wipe out. They also, only in a less degree, valued the services of Councillor Monks and others, who ware equally anxious to serve the town. Councillor Wntrun said he was present at the celebrated meeting of the committee when they were told if they did not accept the offer of Messrs. Manlone, All iott, and Co., for the machinery they were a lot of fools and idiots. If that was not enough to make anybody rebellious he did not know what was. _ _

Councillor BURGESS thought that in the present .position of affairs the resolution was uncalled for, and he hoped it would be unhesitatingly rejected by the Council. (Hear, hear.) Councillor DixoN observed that he had been informed the manure made at Longford was the most valuable that had ever come out of any works of the kind. He was very sorry indeed that the resolution had been brought before the Council that night for he had been very anxious that Mr. Crosfield should have been present. If there was in connection with the Conncil any person who more than another had had to do with machinery of that character it was Councillor Crosfield, and he had been very anxious in- deed that they should have had his opinion respecting the process which had brought 'about this state of things. He hoped the amendment would be supported, and that the chairman would be retained in his position until matters got further advanced. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BARKER stated that according to the borough surveyor's report given in November, 1879, it was ex- pected to turn out of the machinery at Longford 3,200 tons of mixed manure, 1,000 tons of sand, 700 tons of charcoal, and 290 tons of concentrated manure. The cost of working the depot under the old system had been £560 a year, but under the new system it would be £46B,—a saving of £92 in wages. This machinery had been adopted, and in the year 1881 the quantity of refuse carted to • the depot was .13,170 tons. '1 he actual results were, instead of 3200, tons of mixed manure there were 3,838, a gain of 638 tons; in- stead of 100 loads of sand there were 50 loads, averaging about 30 cwt. per load; instead of 700 tons of charcoal there were 81 cwts..; instead of 290 tons of concentrated manure there only were 131; and insteadof the wages beingSl6B they reached the sum of £937 Os. 9d., which, with £2OO for the manager's salary made a total of £1,137. When the results were communicated it was natural some of them required an ex- planation. They wrote to the engineers, whose reply was simply this : that when they were induced to purchase the patent right of Firman's Drier they were deceived lsy the patentee as to the quantity it would turn out. There was therefore a failure in this respect which they could\not get over. The engineers proposed additional machinery. He was not present when that proposition was brought forward, but he was at the next meeting, when the amount was put at about £7,000. The proposal was introduced by Alder- man Burgess to the committee in a style which left no doubt that thy could not do better than at once adopt it, and give Mr. Fryer the order before he left England in February. It had been said there was no remark made about retiring. The chairman said—" I know more about this matter than anvoue else does. I have made up my mind that this shall be passed Ly you; otherwise I will resign my position on the Sanitary Committee." This he (Mr. Barker) wrote down at the time, and he stas certain they were the remarks he made. On Wednesday night last the climax came. Alderman Burgess's remarks were then such as no nelson possessed of common sense would put up with. He was surprised himself to see how Councillor Monks kept his temper. The chairman said he would not sit in the same room with him, simply for the reasoi that they would not have this thing thrust upon them—(hear, hear)—because they would not have the proposal of Mr. Fryer which had been proved to be wrong and expensive as well. They simply wanted time, and if after inspecting the machinery at other towns he found they were doing better at Longford, he would cease his opposition at onc. ; but be could not support a proposition emanating from a man whose scheme had already been such a failure in Warrington. Councillor WALLINGTON expressed his surprise on read- ing- the resolution in reference to Alderman Burgess, and said he had come to the conclusion not to vote.

Alderman DAVIES advised Councillor Mackie to avoid the tone of censOrship that seemed to pervade his remarks, and assured him if he did so his remarks would have greater weight with the Council. At the private meeting they resolved that the further consideration of the Abject of the alteration at Longford Depot be postponed until the Sani- tary Committee had seen the result of the working of the machinery then in course of construction at Birmingham, and had laic* further report before the Council. That reso- lution seemed to have the happy result of satisfying both sides. Alderman Burgess was appealed to as to whether he would be prepared to abide the decision of the Council, and he said he would be quite wilang to do so. Nothing more was to be done until they bad had an opportunity of not only seeing the machines, but 'of reporting to the Council; but when he took up the minutes of the committee that evening he read these words :—" Bth March (it appeared that was prier to the meeting of the Council in committee). Resolved that a deputation of this committee (to consist of such members as can find it convenient to go), the borough surveyor and medical officer, be authorised to visit the works at Salford, and inspect the new machinery, and report to this committee." Now they had ,no report from the mem- bers of that committee.

Councillor BARBER said the visit to Salford was made long before the Council meeting. The roport was given to the Sanitary Committee, and if the members had been pre-- sent they would have heard it. Alderman DAVIES remarked that there was noteference to the report in the minkotes and therefore he was right in pre- suming no report had been given. Alderman Webster had said something to the effect that they should put up with each other's temper. As regarded that it was nowhere to be found except in Webster's Dictionary. (Laughter. Alder- man KEAN : "Johnson's, I think?") None of them had as good tempers as they could wish except Alderman Webster, and he had not half so good a temper as Alderman Burgess, Councillors Monks, Sutton, or Barker They were the most amiable men going with the exception of Councillor Wallington. (Laughter.) He pointed out that the gentle- men who said they were not going to vote were not doing their duty, and he therefore appealed to them with such a resolution as would enable them to do so. He propesed "That the minutes of the Sanitary Committee be confirmed with the exception of the minute of the 29th March, 1832, having reference to the rescinding of the resolutions of the Council on the 6th December, 1881; and that the minute be referred back to the Committee for further consideration in the hope that circumstances may arise, and be taken advantage of, to avoid the matter being again brought before the Council."

Alderman HOLMES advised the members of the Sanitary Committee to go to their next meeting determined to let by- gones be bygones. (Hear, hear.) If they would bear and forbear in the future the scenes which had occurred would not occur again. The DEPUTY MAYOR signified his willingness to accept Alderman Davies's addition to his resolution.

Alderman BURGESS, without any attempt on his part to influence the Council in the slightest degree, in one way or another, wished to say that as asked at the last Council meeting—which, as he understood, expressed to him its opinion that he should go back to the the Committee—the very next evening a Committee meeting was held, he went to his place in the Committee room. There had been two meetings held since; the second he did not attend ; the third he did. Now there was no question, and he believed could not be any question, of the relative merits of machinery for some time to come. He accepted with the utmost faithfulness the arrangements come to by the Council; namely, that it should see what the result of the Birmingham machinery was before any further steps were taken. He presumed that this was the feeling which actuated every member of the committee. He knew it actuated Mr. Miler; and he (Alderman Burgess) accepted it, let the result be what it may. And he would go a step further. If evidence could be produced that the Birmingham machine was a more valuable one and did its work better, and was more desirable for the Council to have, he hoped he should not be so silly as to resist for a moment its intro- duction into Warrington. The time for objecting would be when the test had been made. So far as the vote of that night was concerned, he was content to leave his conduct and temper and everything in the hands of the Council. For 13 years he had been chairman of the Sanitary Committee, and it was only very recently, within the last 12 or 18 months—why he did not know—that a word had been said about incompatibility of temper, or anything of that kind. There were plenty of gentleman who were not now members of the committee, who bad yet seats in that room, who could tell whether there was anything arbitrary in the conduct of the chairman of the committee during the time they occu- piel a seat at the table. He did not want to enter into the dispute that took place the other night, nor anything con- nected with it, nor to touch anything that was said that night. If it were true it would bear testing, if it were not true it would crumble away. He was not such a coward as run away. Thirty years' work was too strong, and when he left that place it would be at the bidding of the Council, and not by a resolution of the committee. Councillor JEANS and Councillor WALLINGTON now said they would vote for the amendment.

Councillor PLATT remarked that he should vote for the amendment. He was convinced they had able men on both sides of the committee, and who had the interests of the borough earnestly at heart.—(hear, hear),—and he thought it would be a great pity if 'it should happen that both sec- tions of the committee could not work harmoniously to- gether. If they would only agree there were no men better fitted by training and abilities to carry on the work of the committee than the men who at present composed it. (Hear, hear.) . Alderman KEAN said if the Council was satisfied the amendment would be the means of making friends of the whole committee, he should be most happy to fall in with it. (Hear, hear.) If, however, Councillor Monks still said that if the matter was referred back, Councillors Barker and Francomb would resign —(Cries of "No, no.") Alderman WEBSTER : Such a thing has never been said. Councillor MONKS: I shall be very sorry to hang a threat over the Council. ([Tear, hear.) Alderman HARRISON: I shall be happy to vote for the amendment if it will secure that amicable result which is contemplated. Councillor MONKS observed that he had stated in is opening remarks that it was as painful to the committee as to any member of the Council to recommend such a resolu- tion as was before them and he still said So. The tone of the discussion had not surprised him at all. He knew the difficulty there was before them in this matter, and he had not a word to say beyond this. Not a word had slipped from anybody concerned which gave them any guarantee that they should not be again subjected to the conduct of which they complained. (Hear, hear.) The whole discussion bad turned more upon the qustion of machinery, which had nothing at all to do with the matter. The whole issue hanged upon this fact that the conduct of the Chair- man in the committee's opinion—be wished to say it clearly and definitely—bad been such as to Plead them to lose their confiderce in his judgment and in his impartiality. They also complained:that there was a great want of courtesy in his dealing with the members of the committee. That was the great complaint; that was the principal thing which had caused that resolution.
Alderman HARRISON : Since the last meeting of the Council?
Councillor Moss: Since the last meeting of the Coun- cil.
Alderman HARRISON: Now that is important.

Councillor MONKS continued to state that he should feel free from responsibility after the vote that night. He would sooner leave the Council altogether than consent to attend the committee meeting again without the assurance from Alderman Burgess that the conduct complained of should not be renewed.
Alderman DAVIES. thought there were words which fell from Alderman Burgess that ought to satisfy Councillor Monks.

Councillor MONKS: If Alderman Burgess will stand up in his place and give us the assurance that we shall meet and discuss any question with perfect freedom and cordiality then I have nvt another word to sly. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS observed that there was not much difficulty in this matter. (Laughter.) There never ought to have been any difficulty. He had never done that thing, never meant to do it, and never needed to do it. He should be in his place after the vote was taken. If be received the treatment of a gentleman in the committe-room, the mem- bers would have, through him, no cause for complaint as to the conduct he should exhibit towards them.

div.head: Councillor BARKER : You will have to change then.
div.p: Councillor BARKER : You will have to change then.

Alderman BURGESS: You can understand, Mr. Mayor, what is likely to come. He thought he only needed to siy this that he should do his duty, and he should leave the result. If other gentlemen did not think it right to do theirs, he could not help it, but he shoull not make the work of the committee difficult. (Hear, hear.) The question of machinery was in the long future. It was not likely it •would come up for solution during the present year, and he believed the committee had a clear prospect of disposing in a very satis- factery manner of all that it would produce during that period. Consequently there was no necessity to face, and there was every opportunity for the fullest test to be brought to bear, not only upon the Birmingham, but upon any scheme that might be introduced in the country, It was not to be expected that he should beg of three gentletnen— the committee—to go back. He would not beg. On the former occasion he understood it was the wish of the Council he should, and he went back in perfoct good faith. He should to-morrow night, if all was well, and should do his best to make it a harmonious and satisfactory meeting— (hear, hear)—and he should lee other gentlemen to do their share in promoting that object. Councillor SUTTON said after the explanation which had been giyen. he should support the amendment in ordei to bring about some proper understanding on the committee. ("Quite right.") Alderman WEBSTER remarked that he should like Coun- cillor Monies to bear in mind what he had said before that good government was made up of compromise and conces- sions. He should be sorry if there was any secessions from the committee. Councillor MlLtrEu wished to ash the Town Clerk if it was legal to appoint the nuisance inspector to fulfil any other duties. The TOWN CLERK said he did not know the particular circumstances under which Mr. Norman was appointed. He did not see, however, what there was to prevent the nuisance inspector performing other duties if he had time to do it.
The MAYOR: It would be a very pleasant question to iliseuss at the next meeting of the Sanitary Committee. (Laughter.) Mr. PARKER: It doesn't interfere with his other duties, Mr. Milner.

The MAYOR observed that in concluding the discussion he would remam that he thought Alderman Burgess had spoken very nicely as toEhat he intended to do at the next meeting and other meetings. He did net think be could have said more, and if Mr. Councillor Monks would take them in the spirit which was intended, all things would work harmoniously together.

Alderman- HARRISON: Will you give him another trial, Mr. Monks? (Laughter.) Councillor MONKS : I don't hang any threat over the Council. I take Alderman Burgess's statement, and it will do for me. It is not for me- Alderman HARRISON: I think we ought to present each member of the committee with a little book called the "Amenities of Society." (Laughter.) I think it would go a long way towards promoting this happy result. The amendment was then put to the tneeting, and carried without dissent.
THE RIVERS COMMITTEE. The minutes of the Rivers Committee were passed on the proposition of the DEPUTY MAYOR, seconded by Alderman DATIES.

THE GAS COMMITTEE. The minutes of the Gas Committee, which were passed, included a resolution that the report of the deputation appointed to visit the International Electric Exhibition (which was published last week), be approved and printed. The average illuminating power of the gas for the fortnight ended 3rd March was equal to 18.89 candles, and the fort- night following 18e5.

GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. This committee recommended the approval of its estimated expenditure, amounting to £438, for the half-year ending 29th September, 1882; and also the approval of a resolution that the insertion of legal advertisements in local news- papers be as equally divided as practicable; that a letter, dated 10th March, had been received from the Ratepayers' Association referring to Corpmation contracts being local- ised, and the Town Clerk was instructed to reply that the Corporation would act with reference to the matter in such a manner as would confer the greatest benefit on tne rate- payers generally. The minutes were confirmed. FINANCE.

Orders for the payment of accounts amounting to £4,164 14s. 3d. had been made by the Finance Committee, which recommended that its estimated expenditure of £3,070 12s. 81 for the half-year commencing the 26th ult., be ap- proved. The estimated expenditure of £3,549 Or. 11d. on borough rate account for the next half.year was recom- mended for approval, and a call was made on the over- seers of Warrington, Latchford, and Thelwall for that sum. The estimated expenditure for the half-year on improve- ment rate account was £7,197 ss. 21., and for the sewers rate of £6Ol 2s. 7d., which were submitted for approval. The minutes were passed on the motion of Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Councillor WALLINGTON, the former gentleman remarking that there was a decrease of 3d. in the improvement rate. .

div.head: P.A.TES.
div.p: THE P.A.TES.

Alderman liormEs moved that the following be confirmed :—Borough Rate, amounting to £3,549 Os. I.ld. Itnprovement Rate, as recommended at 13.6 d. in the pound and a Sewers Rate at 2d in the pound. The motions were seconded and carried. PETITIONS.

Petitions were adopted by the Council in support of "A bill to amend the Public Health Acts in relation to private street improvements and expenses," and also in sup- port of "A bill to consolidate and amend the law relating to free libraries." MR. BRAMONT'S PORTRAIT.

Alderman WEBSIER moved, That the portrait of Wm. Beamcnt, Esq., the first Mayor of Warrington, be replaced in the Mayor's parlour." It was one of the best works of art they possessed, and he thought it should be fixed in the place where it could be best seen. On most occasions the light fell upon the picture in such a way that it could not be seen.

The MAYOR, in seconding the resolution, said the picture was put in its present place behind his chair more as an ex- periment than anything else. Alderman DAVIES moved an amendment that the picture remain where it was. (Hear, hear.) He differed very much from Alderman Webster as to the picture being in a bad light. It was admitted by all artists that the light from the south was the worst light to which a picture could be ex- posed, and that the light from the north was the best. In the Mayor's parlour the light from the south fell upon the picture, whilst in that room the light was comparatively from the north—(" It is aarker.")—which was the best. Being "high in heart " of course he was a high authority. (Laughter.) The picture, also, was of too large proportions for the Mayor's parlour. (Hear, hear.) It might be that in some quarrel in the Committee room the picture might come to some danger. (Laughter.) Councillor PIERPOINT seconded the amendment.
Councillor Jeans, Councillor Sutton, Alderman Burgess, Alderman Holmes, and the Deputy Mayor spoke in favour Q f the amendment, which was carried. This concluded the business.

div.head: POISONING CASE AT RUNCORN,
div.p: THE POISONING CASE AT RUNCORN,
THE INQUEST.

On Monday at the Railway Hotel, Runcorn, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, the coroner, held an inquest on the girl Charlotte, who committed suicide on Thursday, the 30th ult. Mr. Francis Fairhurst was the foreman of the jury. The first witness called was

Thomas Parry, who said : I reside at Holloway, Runcorn, and am a dock porter. The body the jury have seen is that of Charlotte Bate, my stepdaughter. She was 16 years of age. Up to a few weeks ago she was a domestic servant, but since that time she had been at home. I last saw her alive at home on Wednesday night about eight or nine o'clock, at which hour she left the house without stating where she was going. At six o'clock on Thursday night, as I was returning from my work, I was met in the street by my wife, who seemed in great distress. She said, "0, Lord, Tom, what shall we do ?" I asked her whatever was the matter, and she replied, "The child's took some of that there stuff." When she told me that I knew in a minute what was the matter. The stuff she had taken was arsenic. I had kept it in a little multard can, suspended from a beam in the ceiling of my bedroom. There was only a small quantity. I had got it about six months ago to poison some rats, with which we were greatly troubled. The de- ceased krKlv what was in the can. She had seen me putting it for the rats, and I told her it was poison, and that she must never interfere with it. After I had killed the rats I was about to throw the arsenic into the fire, lout my wife said, "I would not throw it away ; it might do again.'" The Coroner: When you saw the deceased in the house on this night what did you say to her ?—I never said any- thing at all.—Didn't you say anything at all? Well, I asked her what was up, but she was unable ta tell roe. I said, "Child, whatever made you take that stuff?" and she said, "0, father, I will never do it no more." She gave no reason why she had taken the poison. I sent two or three of the persons who were in /the house to fetch a doc- tor, and I administered to her mustard and water and other things, to make her sick. She did not,vornit, but I believe she had done before I arrived home.
The Coroner: Do you know how the marks on her face were caused ? I cannot tell unless it was the pain. They were not on on the Wednesday.

The Coroner: Did she tell you what quantity she had taken P—No ; but I know what quantity I had. There would be about three-quarters of a teaspoon full. The Coroner: Do you know any reason why she should have taken this arsenic ?—No, I don't. She has had a good rtepfathety I have never given her any cause. She was a girl I was always very fond of, and I could do anything for her. She was a girl that, if anything was said to her, would "run out of herself." I never hit her but once in my life, two or three years since, and she made "fine work," but we were soon friends again. She was bad tempered. Tbe Coroner: Have you seen her mother hit her or do anything to her since then ?—Yes; I have seen her just cuff hnr with her hand.

What effect had that upon her 2—Of course she walked Out of the road of her. Was she keeping company with anybody ?—Yes, with a young man named John Kingsley, with whom she had been a playfellow for a long time. I didn't know she was keeping company until a week or two ago, and I said to her, "Charlotte, you must mind and take c-are of yourself, and don't stop out at nights." She smiled, and I didn't say anything more to her.
Did se seem vexed abut you speaking to her ?-oh, no; not a bit.

By the Foreman: She was away from home all Wednes- day night, and I have since heard she was at Mrs. Bibby's. The'Foreman : Has she ever said in your presence that she was going to take some of this stuff some day ?—No, sir. If she had I should have got'shut of it, and quick. Mr. Croley (a juryman): When she went home on Thursday morning, did her mother thrash her ?--Yes. But I cannot tell anything about that; I was not there. Of course mother did not think she was going to take any- thing like that; and I know mother would not hurt her. _ _

Mary Parry, the mother of the deceased, was then called. The sad end Of her child seemed to affect her greatly, and occasionally whilst being examined by the coroner she broke out into loud lamentations, swaying to anti fro in her chair. She : The deceased was an illegitimate child. I remember her going from the house last Wednesday night. I told her not to be long away. She said she was going to my sister's to fetch a jacket. I waited up for her until 11-15, and next morning I heard she had been at Mrs. Bibby's house, which is across the street. I went for her at 10 o'clock, and found her standing in the house. I said, " Conte, now, why did you stop out so long when I told you not to be long away ?" and she said, " Well, mother, I will tell you." I had a little stick in my hand—a garden peg— and with it I struck her once across the shoulder. I told her to go home, and after hesitating 'a little she went. Ii ten minutes I followed her. When I arrived borne she was combing her hair. I said nothing to her, and she said no- thing to me. She seemed as cheerful as ustid. - Whilst I was away making a little purchase she made her step- father's dinner, which I took to the docks at 12 o'clock. I returned at one o'clock, and she had cooked the dinner for myself and her. She had the baby of on,- of the neighbours in her arms. We had tea at dinner, and I believe she drank a cupful. Immediately after drinking it she became sick, and vomited. I said, " You have been eating something you bad no business." The vomit was so green I thought she bad been eating oranges. I never had the least thought my child would have done this. Shortly after one o'clock a neighbour, named Mrs. Hughes, came in. The deceased kept walking upstairs and down, and vomiting: She wOuld not let Mrs. Hugtes, of whom she was very fond, leave her.

Yes, lam surprised. She had a good father and mother. Do you think she took it herself? Yes. She she did. Mr. Croley : Is it true she was a member of the Sal" 7 Army? Yes. I believe she had been a time or two. Is it that which made her stay out late at night? I ' tell, I am sure. The Coroner: Was the decased a stupid, sulky girl spoken to? She was, sir. Deceased suffered froul head.

Mary Bibby, wife of James Bibby, living at Ii said the deceased went to her house about twelve o'e Wednesday night. She was alone. She stated Der, and mother had gone to bed, and wished to stay au' and as it was a very late hour she permitted her to do.-, has never stopped with me before. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION. ' " The election which has taken place dnring the past week in Widnes has caused no small stir amongst the ratepayers. Indeed, we do not remember such deep interest being mani- fested amongst the Widnesians in any subject for several years past. Whether the fact of the members of the Rate- payers' and Property Owners' Association having some title ago been received at the Local Board meetings in rather a haughty fashion by some of the members has had anything to do with it we know not, but most certainly they have thrown into the contest an amount of energy and determina- tion which hive astonished the ratepayers generally. In former years the members of this society have been treated rather cavalierly by their opponents on the Owners' and Occupiers' Association, who for some period appeared to have but very little difficulty in returning most, if not all, the ' candidates they brought forward. Of late, the rates have been at such a high figure that this, coapled with the fact that trade in the town has been the reverse of good, has created a feeling of irritation on the Dart of many townsmen that, that they have deserted their former favourites, and returned every gentleman whose name was put before the public by the Ratepayers' Association. We need scarcely say that this result has caused the utmost jubilation amongst the members ot that body. ence of Mr. W. H. Kershaw, the returning officer, the faces of the friends of the popular candidates fairly beamed with joy at what mist have been a somewhat unexpected pleasure to them. Hour after hour sped ot and everyone as it passed raised the disheartening figures to a higher total in the case of the Owners' and Occupiers' candidates, whose star appears to have set for the time being. The "old familiar faces," with one or two ex- ceptions, such as that of Dr. O'Keeffe, were absent from the Board room, in which lolled familiarly in the rich chairs, the various friends of the successful men Even Mr. Kershaw appeared to be hobnobbing with the "coming men," and we thought we caught an amused smile on the face of Mr. Thomas Beasley, the late clerk to the Board, as he heard that Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, who had in the past been one of his rather severe critics, was left out in the cold. Mr. Higginson, the surveyor, was present, no doubt thinking to himself that the sewerage scheme which Major Cross had submitted to the Board had, strangely enough, been used by his opponents to damage him with the retepayers, and even put his name below that of our quiet, unpretending friend Mr. Matthews. It will be seen from the return that the rejected candidates include four of the retiring members. Much astonishment and regret are felt in certain quarters that the Major is not upon the Board, as there Is 110 doubt that he has always made a splendid chairman during the twelve or thirteen years dur- ing which he has been associated with it. Many of the enthusiastic friends of the new candidates appear to think that their election necessarily means an immediate reduction in the township rates, but how this is to come about con- sidering the large sum already borrowed, and the engage- ments undertaken by the- Board, is not at all clear. It is also very questionable whether the friends of the Rate- payers' Association upon the Board will have a working majority. We are very much inclined to doubt this fact. The counting of he votes commenced about eight o'clock on Wednesday morning, and amongst those present were I Mr. Allen, clerk to the Board, Messrs. S. Sadler, Webster, I D. Forster, Carlile, T. Sadler, E. Gould, J. Hamblett, J. E. Johnson, Thomas Handley, and Midwood, The Owners' and Occupiers' Association were represented by Messrs. Crabtree, Moss, Hallett, Rogerson, and H. B. Shores, and the Ratepayers' Association by 31essrs. S. Owens; B. Dutton, J. Rimmer, J. Quinn, and It. Farrant. Mr. Thos. Beasley, the late law clerk to the Board, was in attendance as the legal adviser of the ieturning officer in the matter of conducting the election. A large:crowd assembled outside the Board-room during the evehing, who waited patiently until ten o'clock, when the result of the polling was declared as far as the names were concerned. The figures were stated to be as under : Benjamin Brown, Moorside-terrace, ironfounder, 1,027 (9); James Cross, Moss-brook, Farnworth, civil engineer, 1,126 (8) • Holbrook Gaskell, the younger, .Vgburth, Liverpool, alkali manufacturer, 1,259 (6; John Edward Johnson, Widnes-road, and 2, Gladstone-street, Widnes' grocer and provision dealer, 1,370 (5) ; Peter Longton. Derby-road. Farnworth, brewer, 971 (10); Edward Martlev, Victoria-road, Widnes, bookseller and house agent 1,405 (4); John Matthews, Waterloo .road, Widnes, leather merchant 1,233 (7) ; Joshua Midwood, 10, Waterloo-road, Widnes, and Bank Villa, Helsby, Cheshire, gentleman 1,529 (2) ; Richard Webster, Widnes-road, Widnes, grocer and provision dealer 1,454 (3) ; David Wright, 14. Warrington-road, Widnes, baker and grocer 1,680 (1). The first five upon the list are the elected members. Mr. Wright moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Kershaw, the returning officer. Mr. CRABTREE, on behalf of the defeated candidates, seconded the proposition, in cordial and eulogistic terms. He expressed a hope that what had occurred would not prevent the unsuccessful candidates from offering them- selves for election upon some future occasion. Mr. SAMUEL OWENS, who spoke as the secretary to the Ratepapers' and Property Owners' Accociation, said he thought they would all agree that the election had beene one of the best conducted which had ever taken place int Widnes. (Hear, hear.) Their hearty thanks were due to Mr. Kershaw, who bad proved himself a very genial returning officer. He thought they were much indebted to Mr. Allen and the staff of workers by whom he had been sup- ported., The resolution was carried.with acclamation. Mr. KERSHAW, in responding, said his wish throughout the proceedings had been to only do that which was fair to each candidate. He might say it was a grief to him to part with the old mensbrs of the Board—(h ear, bear, and ap- plause)—as he could amine thew it had been a pleasure to I him to work with them. He should now adjourn the poll, as a matter of form, until five o'clock on the following day, ' in order that the figures might, be re-examined. Mr. ALLEN, clerk to the Local Board, also responded, after which the proceedings terminated. On Thursday Mr. Kershaw attended at the Board-room • I and declared the joilowing to be the correct state of the poll: ' —Mr. Wright, 1682; Mr. Midwood, 1533; Mr. Webster, 1459 ; Mr. Martley, 1407; Mr. Johnson, 1370; Mr. Gaskell, 1238; Mr. Matthews, 1233; Major Cross, 1121; Mr. Brown,' 1026; Mr. Longton, 968.
