After some conversation with 'respect to Mr. Linalier's statement, concerning which a general expression of approval was given' the members of the committee passed a resolution that the Commissioaers be asked to allow the committee the use of their board-room for the purposes of the library, from seven to ten in the evening, on two nights in the week; also that the Commissioners place the neces- sary shelves on the walls. The following appointments were unanimously agreed to, namely: Mr. E. A. Chorlton as treasurer, Mr. W. Brooks as secretary, at a salary of £5 per annum, and Mr. J. D. Jones as librarian. at a salary of £l5 per annum. The following resolutions were also passed :—That a cheque for £lB 10s., for the books purchased from the Mechanics, Institute, be drawn. That all cheques be signed by the Chairman and two mem- bers of the committee. That the warmest thanks of the committee be given to Mr. Robert Davies, Warrington, for his donation of Thackeray's works. That the ordinary monthly meeting of the committee be held at 12-15 on the third Wednesday in the month. The Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and Mr. Simpson were appointed a committee to draw up rules and regulations, and Messrs. Handley, Riley, Briscoe. and Frith were elected a committee to prepare the estimates. This concluded the business.
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. ANOTHER STORMY MEETING.

The monthly meeting of the Rural Sanitary Authority was held on Tuesday afternoon, at the Dutton Workhouse. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Charles Rigby, John Mclntyre, Peter Percival, John Ashton, Thomas Andrews, John Challoner, George Whitlow, Joshua Mid- wood, William Jackson, James Darbyshire' William Pickering, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Liraaker (deputy clerk).

div.head: RUNCORN AND ITS PUBLIC LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN AND ITS PUBLIC LIBRARY.

IMPORTANT STATEMENT BY THE LAW CLERK. On Wednesday, at noon, a naeeting of the Runcorn Pub- lic Library Committee was held at the Commissioners' Board-room. The Rev. Canon Barclay occupied the chair, and there were also present:—Messrs. McDougall, Shaw, Briscoe, Riley, Simpson, Handley, Frith, Linaker (law clerk to the Commissioners), and Brookes (secretary).

IMPOUTANT DECISION. It MS decided that the proceedings of tke committee in the past shotild be regarded as yid, in consequence of the legal Statement made by Mr. Linaker at Monday's meeting of the Board of Commissioners, and that other transactions should Commence de note.
APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN. The Rcv. Ct.Nox BARCLAY was elected chairman of the committee.

LECTION OF VICE-CHAIRMAN. It was proposed and seconded that Dr. McDougall should be appointed vice-chairman. Dr. STEELE said he did not see the necessity for appoint- ing a vice-chairman. The CHAIRMAN considered that it would be advisable to have one as there might be occasions when he (the speaker) would not be able to attend the meeting; and, under such circumstances, there would be no difficulty in finding a chairman, if a vice-chairman was elected. Mr. SIMPSON spoke in the same strain; and, after some farther conversation, the proposal that Dr. McDougall be appointed, was agreed to. MR. LINAKER GIVES HIS "OPINION." Mr. LINAKER (law clerk to the Commissioners), having attended for the purpose of explaining the Dowers conferred upon the committee, made the following important state- ment :—" The ratepayers of the district comprised within the limits of the Runcorn Improvement Act, 1852, have under the provisons of the Public Libraries Act, 1855, adopted the latter Act for such district, the Runcorn Im- provement Commissioners have in pursuance of the powers conferred upon them by section 21 of the said Public Libraries Act, vested the general management, regulation and control of the intended public library in a committee consisting of six Commissioners and five gentlemen not being Commissioners- The powers which the Commis- sioners have conferred upon the committee are specified in the 21st section as follbws":—'The committee may from time to time purchase and provide the necessary fuel, light- ing, and other similar mattersoborks, newspapers, maps, and specimens of art and science for the use of the library, and cause the same to be bound anti repaired when necessary, and appoint salaried officers and servants and dismiss the same, and make rules and regulations for the safety and use of the libraries anti for the admission of the public.' The powers of the committee are strictly limited to the portion of the 214 section just quoted. The power to provide the neceAsary room or rooms for the 'library, and of repairing and improving the same, and of fitting up and furnishing

div.head: CLERK'S SALARY.
div.p: THE CLERK'S SALARY.

Mr. JACKSON moved that the salary of the clerk for the year ending Lady Day be VO. The Rev. J. W. N. TANNER seconded the motion. Mr. MiDwoon asked if there were any " bonuses " con- nected with the situation.

The CHAIRMAN replied that there were not. Mr. RIGBY moved, and Mr. MIDWOOD seconded an amend- ment in favour of the salary being fixed at £4O, which they both considered quite sufficient considering the prospects as to payments which were before the ratepayers. Mr. ASHTON remarked that the work which had to be done by the Clerk was heavier, if anything, than it had been in previous years, and he was at a loss to see any reason why the salary should be reduced. Mr. CHALLONER thought the amendment a shameful and ungentlemanly proposal. Nothing could be a greater re- flection upon Mr. H. Linaker's work than the submitting of such a proposition. The CHAIRMAN said the salary had to be fixed by the Authority and approved by the Local Government Board. Mr. Many protested against the insinuation ef Mr. Challoner that he and the seconder of the amendment were ungentlemanly. Were members to attend that Board for the purpose of discharging their duties to the ratepayers, and to be insulted for giving utterance to their opinions? Mr. MIDWOOD think that if anyone is open to the charge of being ungentlemanly, it is Mr. Challoner himself. I protest against his insulting observation, as I maintain that every Guardian ought to be at liberty to express his opinions without being insulted in this manner. Mr. CHALLONBR lam not insulting you. Mr. MIDWOOD (warmly): You never do anything else! Mr. WEIR thought the work of the Clerk had been heavier this year than ever before. The amendment was then put. Only the mover and seconder voted for it; and the original resolution was declared carried.

THE CLAIM By MR. DUTTON'S EXECUTORS. The DEPUTY CLERK read a document, of which the fol- lowing is a copy : "Sewer through land of Mr. Dutton's representatives in Frodsham Lordship. Report of c ,mmittee : The committee have inspected the land, and, after taking into consideratioa the annual amount awarded to Mr. W,ight, and the plsition and surroundings of the two pieces of land (that of Mr Wright and that of Mr. Dutton's representatives) are of opinion that £5O would be a fair and sufficie4 sum to pay to Mr. Dutton's representatives for the wayleava revired. Dated this 4th April, 1882.—John Ashton, Thomas Andrews, Joshua Midwood." Mr. PERCIVAL moved, and 'Mr. WEIR seconded, a resolu- tion in favour of the adoption of the report. The motion was carried unanimously, and on the applica- tion of the clerk, be was instructed to forward the commit- tee'e reportto the executors. Mr. MioWoOD : Mr. Chairman, I understood that Messrs. Henry Linaker and Sons were the claimants in this case. The CHAIRMAN: No, but they were acting for the claimants.
Mr. MIDWOOD: But why do we refer the documents to the executors when the claim came through Messrs. Linaker ? Mr. ASHTON: Out of courtesy to.thon it ought to be sent
through Messrs. Linaker and Son. " Mr. MIDWOOD : Why does Mr. H. Linaker ask for the re- port to be sent to the executors when Messrs. Elenry Linaker and Sons were the claimants? _ _
The CLIME : It must go through somebody. Mr. MIDWOOD: Certainly, but why ask that it should s,:o

to the executors? The CHAIRMAN: Well, the clerk is instructed toseud a copy of it to the executors. That appears to me to be a dis- tinction without a difference. Mr. MIDWOOD : I should also like to enquire whether the counsel's costs have been sent in with respect to the Frod-
sham sewerage scheme. • The DEPUTY CLERK said the costs were, as yet, in the
hands of the taxing-master. The discussion then dropped. MEDICAL OFFICIR'S REPORT.
The annual report of the Medical Officer of Health vrao laid before the Board, and Messrs. Tanner, Challoner and Weir were appointed a committee to consider it.

ME. BANCROFT MAKES HIS DEFENCE. The DEPUTY CLERK read the following communication from Mr. Bancroft Manchester. March 2g, 1882.—Frodsham and Frodsham Lord- ship Sewerage.—Gentlemen,—/n reply to the resolution passed at your last meeting " that Mr. Bancroft gives us the Intorma- tion how It was he did not show the manholes upon the Prod-

.si;;;;:Pfar-i; .a.t-ihefir;C; also how it was he couldf do without them afterwards," I beg to give the following explanations : The manhole and lamphole were shown on the line of sewer through Mr. Weght's land upon the first set of plans submit- ted to you accompanying my report, dated October 18th, 1879. upon the plans of the revised scheme, dated December 27, 1879; upon the plans laid before the Government Inspector at the public enquiries held at Frodsham on Apr/29, 1880, and March 4th, 1881, and upon the duplicate copy of the drawings prepared for and now in possession of the Local Government Board. On Ja,nuary 7th, 1880, I received cne toilowing inAtruettons from Mr. Linaker :—" Kindly furnish me with tracings show- ing quantities of land and wayleaves requi, ed for Frodsham sewerage scheme." In reply I prepared ttre necessary tracings, which included a plan in duplicate giving the length of ease- ment required through Mr. Wright's land. I should state, as I did at the arbitration, that it is not customary in preparing land plans to show details of the propoved works thereon. On July 2nd, 1881, I received written instructions from Mr. Linaker requesting me to furnish him with a section 'of the line of the proposed sewer throuzh Mr. Wright's land, and upon this tracing, which I understand was forwarded to Mr. Wright. was shown the size of the pipe, its inclination, and the , position of the manhole &nil lamphole. On October 17th 1881, I received a farther letter from Mr. Linaker, in which he enquires—" Could it be arranged that the sewer should enter Mr. Wright's field at about 201 t. above the gate, and cross to the north-west corner of Dutton's field ? ' The day following I replied, "I enclose a tracing showing the line 1 think you allude to in your letter. I see no objection to it. It is 13 yards longer than the contract line, but that is o'r: very little moment if terms could be arranged with Mr. Wright." On September 14th Mr. Wright's surveyor called upon me. After explaining the scheme to him I enquired if it would meet Mr. Wright's views if we crossed from Howey-lane in a straight line to the top end of Smithy-lane, as suggested by Mr. Chalioner, but this line, I was informed, could not be enter-

tamed. At the meeting of your Authority on October 13, 1881, which I attended, 1 was asked could not the manhole and laminhole be dispensed with on gr. Wright's land, and I replied that they were shown on the plans for the purposes of ventilating and examining the sewers from time to time, and that they were also shown on the drawings submitted to and approved of by the Local Government hoard, and, after cons,derable dis- cussion, I understood it was decided to leave the question whether they should be dispensed with in the hands of your solicitor aid myself, if during the course of the sabttration we considered by so doing we might probably reduce the amount of the a ward.—l am, gentlemen, your obedient servant, Hr. BANCROFT." The CLERK said he should like the authority of the Board for handing to the press for publication the whole proceedings 'of the Authority from the 18th August, 1879, up to that date with reference to the sewerage of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship. In reference to this matter a great deal of dirt had been thrown up by someone, probably in the hope that some of it would stick. In order to put him- self right with the public and the Authority, he should like the abslract of their minutes to be considered. • No word of his would be found in the minutes, which were simply a -record of the action he had been asked to take as to this matter. After considering these abstracts, he should like the Board to say whether he had done anything which he ought not to have done or anyone, in his office, in the remotest degree. Mr. MIDWOOD said be certainly entirely failed to under- stand the reply which had been sent by Mr. Bancroft. The CHAIRMAN agreed with Mr. Midwood in so far as the fact went that there was some inconsistency between Mr. Bancroft's two statements. Mr. Bancroft appeared to make a distinction between the scheme and the tracing showing the course of the sewer through the land. The DEPUTY CLERK : Certainly. Mr. MIDWOOD : Well, I cannot see into the thing myself. It is all up and down ; in fact, I don't know how it is. The CLERK wished several matters to be very strongly impressed upon the minds of the members of the Authority. In the first place, the notices for the inquiry were not issued by the Authority, but by the ',decal Government Board. They were advertised in certain papers by the last named Board, and the notices were sent down by the Local Govern- ment Board to himself, as clerk of the Authority, with directions to him to have them posted in certain places in Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship, and to have it certified that the notices had been duly posted. That Authority had not anytliing to do with the matter, and he, as clerk, had simply acted under the directions of the Local Government Board in the matter. . A short conversation followed on the interminable man- hole and lamp-hole business. Mr. MID WOOD said he would leave it to the ratepayers of Frodsharn to consider whether it was right they should be put to all this expense, from which they did not derive one .penny benefit, in order that the Marquis of Cholmondeley's purpose might be served in regard to a certain couple of villas, he supposed. Mr. liclyrvnE thought the discussion totally irrelevant There had been an arbitration, and he supposed they would have to abide ty it and pay the bill however long they talked about it. Perhaps they might gather from their ex- perience a little wisdom which might be of use in guiding them in their proceedings in days to come. The CLERK considered it very clear that those gentlemen who had that day moved the amendment in reference to his salary, attributed the blame in the proceedings which had taken place to a certain quarter. If he was correct in this belief, he would ask them to boldly state to whom they personally attributed the blame, but do not let them throw out unfounded insinua- tion which went before the public. This matter had been men- tioned to him several times during the last 'fortnight by gen- tlemen occupying high positions, not only in Cheshlrehut in the adjoining county, who had said, " lain surprised that Mr. Rigby, the secretary to the Manchester and Liverpool Agri- cultural Society, and the Crieshire Chamber of Agriculture, should have made such remarks." He had then Ina', to reply, " But yon are sadly mistaken, for it is not Mr. Thomas Rigby, the secretary to the Manchester and Liverpool Agricultural Society,—a gentleman whose name is well linown, not only in Lancashire and Cheshire, but throughout, the whole country. It is auothcr Mr. Rigby !" (Sensation.) •
- RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMIS-
STONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Monday, at the Board- room, Town Hall. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present n---Messrs. Norman Williams, Fisher, Hazlehurst, J. J. Spea.kman,P. Speakman;Meadowcroft, Lake, Shaw, Briscoe, Taylor, Linaker (law clerk), Barker (surveyor), Mouritz (medical officer), and Brookes (secretary). BREAKING OUT OF SMALLPDX. The CHAIRMAN read the monthly report of the Medical Officer of Health, which showed that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn for the past month was 25. Two deaths had occurred in Halton-in-Runcorn, and one inquest bad been held, making the total deaths 28. The death-rate was 21 wr 1,000. Of the above three were due to zymotic diseases (two scarlatina and one smallpox), one to heart diseap, one to senile decay, nine to abdominal diseases, five to respiratory, and six to cerebral diseases. Three cases of smallpox had occurred during the month. Death had oc- curred in one case; one had recovered, and the other, which was in the Infectious Diseases Hospital, was progressing favourably. No further cases had been brought under the Medical Officer's notice. Dr. Steele proceeded to say that the report was of a tolerably satisfactory nature, with the exception of that part of it which related to the breaking out of smallpox. Dr. Mouritz had suggested that it would be a prudent course to advertise the following notice in the local papers and by placard:—" The Commissioners desire to warn the inhalsitants of Runcorn that a few cases of smallpox have occurred in their district; and they, there- fore, caution all persons having infant children in their charge, to have them vaccinated at the earliest possible moment. They also strongly recommend that young personsl who have attained the age of 12 years ,7hould forthwith be re-vaccinated." In the course of a brief discussion, the MEDICAL OFFICER said he vaccinated his own family every -seven years. There Was no doubt that if the persons who had died (with the exception of the one imported case), had been vaccinated, they would not have succumbed to the disease. Mr. P. SPEAKMAN considered the suggestion of the Medi- cal Officer a very opportune one at the present time, as small- pox was making serious ravages in certain towns. It was resolved that the Medical Officer's proposal be adopted.

Trim LATE MEETING OF RATEPAYERS. A. letter bad been received from Mr. Sutton, assistant overseer, enclosing the resolution passed at the late meeting of ratepayers at Bethesda Congregational schoolroom, in xespect to the Board permitting the present offices to be used for the purpose of the Free Library. The CHAIRMAN began to read the resolution, on which Mr. SHAW suggested that it be taken as read, which was agreed to.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. H. S. Hall (chairman) and W. L. Evans. ALLEGED UNPROVOKED ASSAULT ON A WORKMAN.—Ann Coleburn, a middle-aged woman, was charged with assault- ing Michael Riley, a workman living in Midwood-etreet.— Complainant said he was going home from his work on Sat- urday evening, when the defendant, to whom he had given no provocation, struck hint on the head with a stone.—Mr. W. T. Husband defended, and alleged that the defendant had kept Riley while he had been out of work. He argued that it was most unreasonable to suppose that a woman would set upon such a powerful man, as fear of the consequences would have held her in awe.—John Fitzget;td, a sharp lad, was called for the defence, and said Le saw the quarrel take place. Complaireant was drunk, and on defendant asking him for some money he said he would cut her head open with a Can "if the did not °lose her mouth." Riley after- vo.rds fell, and he supposeLl he received the cut upon his head at this time.—The smartness with which the witness answered all the questions put to him by complainant caused much laughter in court. The magistrates appeared to con- sider the case proved, for they fined defendant ss. and costs 9s. 6d., or in default 14 days' imprisonment.—Complainant asked for his expenses in a very bold style, but he was told he must condnct hi self with a little more deference to the court, and not be so Dertinacious. He would not be allowed any expenses. THE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—Several people were summoned by the Widnes School Board, for whom Mr. G. H. Danby, the clerk, appeared, for not sending their chil- dren to school, and ware each ordered to pay ss. including costs :—William Worthington, John Hill, Patrick Condron, James Stanton, and John Tracey. The cases were proved by attendance officers Woods and Joynson. _

, Before Mr. Brock (chairman) and Mr. Evans. VIOLENT ASSAULT ON TWO POLICE OFFICERS.-1 homaS Quinn was charged with having been drunk and disorderly, and also assaulted P.C.'s Snowdon and Pitt. Snowdon stated that about half-past six on Saturday, the prisoner came to the house where he and Pitt lived, in Moss Bank- road, and caused a great disturbance. Quinn challenged them out to fight, described them by most opprobrious epithets, and threatened what terrible thitzigs he would do if they came out. They walked out to him, and a struggle ensued, in which prisoner gave him three severe blows on the head, and also bit and kicked him. Pitt came to his assistance, on which a crowd of about 300 people assembled, and used both officers very badly. Prisoner was at last secured, and taken into a house in Moss Bank-road. He was afterwards taken in custody upon a warrant. P.C. Pitt gave corroborative evidence, and said the prisoner kicked ' him and struck him several times in the face.—The Chair- man said the coaduct of the prisoner had been of so violent a nature that he would not be offered the option of paying a fine, but would be sent to gaol three months with hard labour.

A HINT TO COAL STEALERS.—A girl named Mary Jane Whalen was convicted, on the evidence of P.C. Barker, of stealing 41tbs. of coal, value 2d., the property of the London and North-Western Railway Co. The father was ordered to pay 215., in default of which the girl was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment. ALLEGED SAVAGE ASSADLT BY A WOMAN, WITH A POKER. I —Catherine Brannon was charged with unlawfully wound- ing an elderly woman named Ann McCormick, the wife of John McCormick.—Complainant, who had to be accommo- dated with a chair whilst giving her evidence, said her husband was a labourer and lived at 93, Penn-street. On the 27th ult., about five o'clock in the afternoon, she was going down Penn-street to the house of a woman named Mrs. Allen. She (witness) had lost the sight of one eye, and she made a mistake and went to the prisoners house in- stead of Alleh's. She did not find out her mistake until she observed the prisoner sitting by the fire. Upon her turning round to leave the house, Brannon took the poker from the fire-place, struck her on the top of the head with it, and knocked her against the door-step. On trying to get up, the prisoner also struck her on the right breast and right shoulder with her fist. She lost a large quantity of blood and became insensible. She was afterwards taken to Dr. O'Keeffe's

surgery by two constables, and her wound was dreSeed. She was and had been unclet the care of the doctor since. She had not had any quarrell with the prisoner during the last two months; and whilst in her house she did not utter a word. She (Witness) was perfectly sober at the time.— Dr. O'Keeffe said that when he examined the woman he found an incised wound, about two inches in length, upon

her head, penetrating to the b.me. She was bleeding pro- fusely.—ln reply to Superintendent Barker, the witness said the wound was of such a character as might have been inflicted with a poker. It was still in a very unhealthy state, and the complainant' would be some time before she recovered. When the woman was brought to his surgery she was not under the influence of liquor.—P.C. Anderson said be apprehended the prisoner, and in reply to the charge, she said that she and the complainant had a row, but there was no instrument used by her (prisoner) though McCormick broke all the windows in her house.—Mr. Hus- band said his defence was contained in the words used by the prisoner when she was apprehended. He thought he should be able to prove that complainant was under the in- fluence of drink, and ran after the prisoner with a knife. Instead of comalainant making the mistake of entering the wrong house through her short sightelness, that accident happened owing to her being no much under the influence of drink that she did not kno* what she was doing. The wound on the head was the result of the woman falling against the fender.—Jimes Levy said he saw the complain- ant seize the prisoner by her shawl on the day in ques- tion, and strike her with a piece of brick.—Wm. O'Brien I also gave evidence, after which the Bench said there was a iprima facie case against the prisoner, and she would be , committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial. Bail would not be allowed.—On hearing thii announcement a number of the fri,T(ls of the prisoncl in court set up a howl of weeping, which resulted in great disorder. STREET DISTURBERS.—RiChard Hunt was charged with having, on the 18th ult., caused a breach of the peace in a public street, by shouting and swearing. This was defen- dant's 19th appearance, and in default of finding sureties himself in £lO and two in £5 to keep the peace six months, he was sentenced to be imprisoned two months.—Ellen Cos- tello was proved to have been guilty of a similar offence, on the 6th ult., upon the evidence of P.C. 1,002. This was her seventh appearance in court, and she was ordered to.fine sureties, herself in £lO and two in £5 each, for two months, or ba sent to gaol seven days. A FORMER SIEIM'S CROSS ACCTIOI,..TEER IN COURT.—Mr. James Irvine,.autioneer, formerly of Simm's Cross, hut now of Manchester, was summoned for obstructing the footpath, lon the 27th ult. Sergeant Strickland said that about one I o'clock in the day, he saw defendant standing on the foot- path in Widnes-rciad, offering goods for sale by auction. Irvine was surrounded by a large crowd, and he called his ' attention to the fact that he was causing an obstructions on which he went inside the shop, but continued to sell. Defendant was upon a table, and on asking for his name he pointed to a board on which was the 'name Hughes. He enquired of defendant if that was his name, and he said it was. Irvine now contended that he was not guilty of the offence charged in the summons, for when he was first seen by the officer, he was standing upon a piece of ground be- longing to the vendor, which did not form part of the foot- path. He argued that he could not wevent the crowd assem- bling, and cnolly asked the Bench if some cause celebre was being tried in that court, and a crowd collected outside, would the magistrates be held responsible for their so doing. 1 He also asked for an adjournment, on the ground that he had only come that morning from Manchester, and had been I unable to get his witnesses together. The magistrates de- ; clined to adjourn the case, and fined defendant 108. and the icosts.

A commun dsbare, and 18th August, 1879.-A letter was this day addressed to received as to the existence of scarlet fever in Fro the Local Government Board by Mr. Henry Beswiek, agent the inspector was ordered to inquire into the matter. to the Marquis of Cholmondeley, complaining of the want This terminated the business. of proper drainage and sewers in Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship. An inspection of the townships complained of price far too . b ad ce. was ordered to be made by Dr. Weaver, the then medical officer of health, who was directed-to furnish the Authority with a report on the existing drainage of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship with his observations thereon, and on the 9th September, 1879, the report of the Medical Officer of Health was submitted to the Authority, in which, after dealing exhaustively with the system of drainage existing in Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship, he gave the follow- ing general aabservations, viz.:-" The preceding sketch shows that the bulk of the sewage from the houses in Fred- sham and Frodsham Lordship is conveyed by drains and ditches, with or without the intervention of cesspools, into watercourses passing through the marsh into the rivers Weaver and Mersey. That various ditches fed by springs and watercourses are polluted and rendered unsuitable for the drinking of cattle kept in the neighbouring fields, and in some cases even becoming nuis- ances injurious to health. That the drains are often road drains improperly used for the purpose of conveying sewage. That the drains are cften shallow,imperfect,and insufficient. That in some cases, notably at Five Crosses, and in Howie- lane, there is no outlet whatever for the sewage. In conclu- sion I may repeat the observations made in my annuals re- port for 1878, viz., In Frodsham the question of drainage is closely connected with that of water supply, the present main sewers are not sufficiently large or deep. New houses are being built, and difficulty arises in disposing of their sewage.' " The above report was submitted to the Local Government Board, andlon the 23rd September, 1879, a let- ter was read from their lordships, in which they stated that "it would appear from their report that a proper system of sewerage is much needed," and recommending the Authority to appoint a competent engineer to advise them as to the steps which should be taken to carry out a suitable scheme; and Mr. Bancroft was accordingly appointed to prepare a drainage scheme for Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship.- 21st October, 1879. Mr. Bancroft's scheme was submitted and referred to the Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship Parochial Committee.-16th December, 1879. The Com- mittee recommended that Mr. Bancroft re-consider his scheme, and provide an outfall at "Sea Flatts," so as. to avoid the necessity of wayleaves and culvert.-30th Decem- ber, 1879. On the recommendation of the Parochial Corn- mittee Mr. Bancroft's revised scheme was adopted.-27th January, 1880. The plans were this day signed and appli- cation was ordered to be made for the sanction of the Local Government Board to borrow £3,880 15s. for carrying out that portion of the scheme considered necessary.-29th April, 1880. A local inquiry was held by S. J. Smith, Esq., when plans of proposed scheme were produced.-lst June, 1880. A letter was read from the Local Government Board concurring in conclusions arrived at by Mr. Smith, as to the desirability of the entire project of sewerage for the township and lordship being carried out at one and the same time.-15th June,lBBo. A deputation from the township of Frodsham Lord- ship attended the meeting of the Authority, and presented a report containing resolutions passed at a town's meeting condemnatory of a sewerage scheme.-27th July, 1880. A resolution was passed-in reply to communication from the Local Government ..Board-that the Authority still consi- dered that a portion only of the sewerage scheme was re- quired at present, and confirming the resolution to apply for the sum of £3,880 155.-16th August, 1880. The Local Government Board intimated that they were advised that it would be preferable Id carry out the scheme in its entirety, but they would net on that ground withhold their sanction to a loan for works proposed to be carried out by the Authority.-4th Mardi, 1881. An inquiry was held by S. J. Smith, Esq., Local Government Inspector, as to appeal by the overseers of Frodsham against the apportionment of cost of searerage works by the Sanitary Authority.-251h May, 1881. The Local Government Board this day forwarded sanction to the following loans for sewerage scheme, viz. : Frodsham £3,118, Frodsham Lordship £762; £3,880.-28th June, 1881. Mr. Dawson's tender accepted, and on the 12th July the contract was sealed by the Authority.-Mr. Wright's way-leave and arbitration: 19th January, 1880. Statutory notice as to way-leave was forwarded to Mr. Wright, accompanied by plan prepared by Mr. Bancroft. tices in similar form to above were also at the same time aemeagded to Mr. Dutton and Mr. Robert Ashton.--21th Janua . 1880. Mr. Robert Ashton's claim for land and r).. way-leave was accepted by the Authority.-29th April, 1880. The first local inquiry was held by S. J. Smith, Esq., Local Ooverntnent Inspector.-4th March, 1881. An inquiry was held by 8. J, 'Smith, Esq., Local Government Inspector, as to apportionment Of expenses.-7th July, 1881. A second notice was forwarded to Mr. Wright, accompanied by plan showing sections, and man-hole and lamp-hole, and asking for particulars of claim for damage or way-leave, a similar notice being forwarded to Mr. Dutton, on thg9th July, 1881. -12th July, 1881. Mr. Dawson's contract sealed by the Authority.-7th October, 1881. Messrs. Wrigley and More- croft wrote admitting receipt by Mr. Wright of notices abcrro referred to. dated 19th January, 1880, and 7th July, 1881, and protesting against the scheme; at the same time submitting an alternative) schetne and offering on behalf of Mr. Wright to contribute £lOO towards the increased cost. -Bth October, 1881. A copy of the foregoing letter was forwarded to Mr. Bancroft asking him for a report, and inquiring if he would advise a special meeting of the Authority. Messrs. Wrigley and Morecroft were informed that their letter had been forwarded to the engineer, for his observations thereon.-13thOctober,1881. An extraordinary meeting of the Authority was held to consider a letter from Messrs. Wrigley and Morecroft, and consult with Mr. Bancroft in the matter. Mr. Bancroft advised that he could not recommend the Authority either of the alternative schemes suggested in Messrs. Wrigley and Morecroft's letter on account of the heavy additional cost which would be en- tailed thereby, and that the scheme as adopted was the most satisfactory for the purpose of carrying off the sewerage from that part of the district. The Authority were unani- mously of opinion that they could not see their way to deviate from the original scheme on account of the serious additional cost to the ratepayers, which would be incurred in adopting either of the suggested alternative schemes, and adducing the following reasons in support of their decision, viz:-1. That ample notice was given to Mr. Wright of the intention of the Authority to carry out the scheme adopted. 2. That Mr. Wright could have attended before the Local Government Board Inspector at the public inquiry and have then raised his objections to the scheme. 3. That the Authority had already entered into a contract for the com- pletion of the whole of the scheme, and that the works un- der the contract are now in an advanced state. 4. That the Authority are advised that the scheme as adopted, is the most satisfactory for the purpose of carrying off the sewer- age from that part ef the district. 13th October, 1881. A letter embodying the foregoing decision of the Authority was forwarded to Messrs. Wrigley and Morecroft.-20th October 1881. Messrs. Wrigley and Morecroft wrote asking for information to enable them to send in claim.-22nd Oct., , 1881. The receipt of above letter was acknowledged and a copy thereof forwarded to Mr. Bancroft for his observations. -29th October, 1881. The requisite information was for- warded to Messrs Wrigley and Morecroft.-24th November. 1881. Mr. Wright's claim for compensation in respect of easement, amounting to £440, was forwarded to the Autho- rity, in which it was stated, that if the Authority were not prepared to pay the above amount, Mr. Wright claimed a reference to arbitration and was ready at once to nominate an arbitrator on his behalf. - 25th November, 1881. The clerk acknowledged receipt of the foregoing claim, and communicated the result to Mr. Bancroft, who replied that he considered the claim very ex- cess've, and in his opinion the Authority would have no alternative but to submit to arbitration.-Nov. 29th 1881. The Authority appointed Mr. Patterson as arbitrator.-10th January, 1832. The solicitor to the Authority reported that he had inquired of Messrs. Wrigley and Morecroft if they would dispense with counsel at the hearing of the arbitra- tion case, and had received a reply as follows, viz. :-" We certainly intend to be represented by counsel on the hearing of this matter. The case is not one in, which it would he satisfactory either to us or to our client to dispense with the services of counsel." It was then decid:d by the Authority that they should also be represented by counsel on the hear- ing of the arbitration case.-71h February, 1882. The soli- citor to the Authority applied for instructions to have an in- terview with Mr. Wright's solicitors, and endeavour to arrange the claim for way-leave in respect of Frodsharn sewerage scheme, in consideration of an undertaking being given not to construct a manhole or lamphole on Mr. Wright's land, and thus avoid the expenses which would be incurred upon the further hearing of the case before the arbitrators and umpire. This course was adopted by the Authority subject to the negotiations being made without prejudice, and the final arrangement to be first submitted to and approved bythe Authority. The following is Messrs. Wrigley and Morecroft's reply to the above suggestion, viz.: [DUPLICATE.] 11, Clegg-street, Oldham, Bth February, 1882.-Wright and Sanitary Authority-Dear Sir,-We have only thts evening been able to see our client about the suggested meeting of whit h you gave us such short notice by telegram. We really do not see ,nuch utility in the proposed meeting if the object be to save expense in connection with the adjourned hearing on the 13th inst., as we imagine that the arbitrators, umpire and counsel having reserved that day will expect their fees whether there, is a sitting or not. Moreover, it is rather unsatisfactory that we should be asked to meet without having any previous knowledge ot the proposition you mean to offer for our con- siderati n. However, it might Terhaps worn rather an un- grae'ons thing to decline a meeting, and we therefore leave it entirely in your hands to say whether we are to meet or not It you desire a meeting, we suggest that you fix it to be held at the Grosvenor Hotel, Manchester, on Friday next, at 1,2 o'clock. In that case we must ask you to wire us by noon to-morrow (Thin sday), so that we may make the needful ar, angernents.- We are, dear sir, yours truly, WRIGLEY and MOP.ECROFT.-W..1 Linaker, Faq. 7th March, 1882. - The ' award was submitted 11 to the A uth ority.-Sol .icitor's remarks. At the ad- journed hearing, before entering upon the sub- ject, a conference took place between the solicitors and counsel for the two parties, and Mr. Wright's conned oared to settle this matter if the Authority would take out the man-hole and lamp-hole and pay Mr. Wright £3OO by way of compensation. CAUTION.—SMALLPDX IN RUNCORN.—VACCI- NATION FOR CHILDREN.—The Runcorn Improve- ment Commissioners desire to WARN the inhabitants of Run- corn that a few cases of SMALLPDX have occurred in their district, and, therefore, caution all persons having infant chll- dren in their charge to have them Vaccinated at the earliest possible moment. They also strongly recommend that young persons who have attained the age of twelve years should forthwith be re-vaccinated—By order of the Commissioners. ROBERT HANHAM MOURITZ, Medical Officer of /I..alth. Runcorn, April 3rd, 1882.

OFEICES at the Works, Eccleston-street, St. Helens. PROSPECTUS. The Company is formed to purchase or otherwise acquire the Foundry known as the Eccleston Foundry, at Eccleston, St. Helens, Lancashire, and the business of an Ironfounder. and the goodwill thereof, lately carried on by the late Mr. Joseph Windus, of St. Helens, Ironfounder, and now carried on by Mrs. Windus, his Widow and Executrix, and the Eltock-iu- Trade. Plant. Machinery, Chattels, and Effects belonging to the said Foundry, and the henefit of all contracts in connection therewith, and also to carry on the said business in all its branches, and also to carry on any of the businesses (connected with the iron trade) mentioned in the Company's Memoran- dum of Association Mr. Windus carried on a successful business up to the time of his death in the year 1880. He had cultivated and estab- lished a large business connection, and the Company is formed to continue, improve, and extend this connection. The Irenfoundry business is considered a profitable one, and with the return of more prosperous times large profits are ex- pected to be realized. Sr. Helens is a large manufacturing town, its Manufactures consisting of Glass, Copper. Chemicals, &c. It is also the centre of an extensive Coal-fie'd. It, therefore, within itself, affords great scope for a business of this character, but in addi- tion to this advantage there are, within a short distance of St. Helens, many manufacturing towns easily accessible by rail, affording a wider scope for the Company's operations, and which the Directors hope to utilize to the Company's benefit. In many of these towns Mr. Windus had established business relations. The Foundry is connected with the London and North- Western Railway by means of a siding into one of that Com- pany's branches. The fact is an advantage in favour of the Company over other Foundries in St. Helens not so connected. No promotion money is being paid to anyone. The only con- tract which has been made is one dated the 3rd day of April, 1882, between Mrs. Jane Windus of the one part, and the Com- pany of the other part, which contract, or a copy thereof, toge- ther with the Memorandum and Articles of Association, may be seen at the office of the Solicitor of the Company. Prospectuses. Forms of Application, &c., may be obtained from the Bankers, Solicitor, or from the Secretary, at the Offices of the Company, Eceleston-s• sect, St. Helens. When no allotment is made, the amount paid on application will be returned in full.
